articles.title: Understanding Stigmatization of Organic and Conventional Farmers: Occupational Taint, Dehumanization, and Perceived Burden
articles.authors: Lucas David; Gaétan Marinho; Michaël Dambrun
articles.abstract: Farmers face substantial physical and mental health risks, yet the role of public stigma toward agricultural groups remains insufficiently understood. This study examined stigmatization of organic and conventional farmers in France, using social distance as the main indicator of social rejection, and investigated whether it was associated with perceived vital forces and burdens, occupational taint, dehumanizing perceptions, and infra-humanization. A sample of 250 French participants completed an online questionnaire assessing perceptions of both organic and conventional farmers. Conventional farmers were evaluated less favourably than organic farmers across all stigma-related dimensions. However, partial correlation analyses showed that the same two dimensions remained robustly associated with social distance toward both groups: perceived burden and biologization. Item-level analyses of the perceived burden dimension further suggested that social distance was especially related to the perception that farmers benefit from collective wealth without sufficient contribution. Overall, the findings suggest mainly quantitative rather than qualitative differences between stigmatization of organic and conventional farmers: conventional farmers appear more strongly stigmatized, but social rejection toward both groups relies on similar social-perceptual pathways.

articles.title: Orthography Shapes L2 Stress PerceptionAcross Development: Evidence from L1 Mandarin Learners of Portuguese
articles.authors: Chao Zhou; Guilherme D. Garcia
articles.abstract: Despite growing evidence that written input shapes second-language speech learning, its role in suprasegmental acquisition remains underexplored. This study examines whether orthography facilitates lexical stress identification through syllable weight. Portuguese is well suited for this question because stress placement is strongly conditioned by syllable weight, which is transparently encoded in the writing system. A total of 186 L1 Mandarin speakers identified stress location in Portuguese pseudowords presented either auditorily or with accompanying written forms. Naïve listeners used syllable weight as a stress cue only when orthographic information was available, whereas experienced learners showed weight sensitivity from auditory input alone. For experienced learners, however, orthography did not further enhance weight sensitivity; instead, it biased responses toward the default penultimate- stress pattern. These findings suggest that orthographic effects change over L2 development, interacting with auditory cue weighting and distributional regularities in L2 stress perception.

articles.title: Selflessness, Self-Centeredness, and Mental Health in Dyads: Indirect Associations Through Affective and Functional Pathways
articles.authors: Lucas David; Michaël Dambrun
articles.abstract: Mental health is embedded in interpersonal contexts, yet little is known about whether psychological modes of functioning can affect the mental health of close others through dyadic processes. Drawing on the Self-centeredness/Selflessness Happiness Model (SSHM), this article examined whether selflessness and self-centeredness were indirectly associated with another person’s mental health through two interpersonal pathways: emotional contagion and functional convergence. Two dyadic studies were conducted among French pairs who knew each other and interacted regularly: a student-close other sample in Study 1 and a general population sample in Study 2. Across both studies, no direct partner effects were found. However, indirect effects emerged via the proposed affective and functional mediators: selflessness was associated with higher partner positive mental health, whereas self-centeredness was associated with lower partner positive mental health and higher partner negative mental health. Additional invariance analyses supported the robustness of these structural paths across samples and relationship types. These findings suggest that selflessness and self-centeredness may have interpersonal implications for mental health through affective and functional mediating pathways.

articles.title: Executive Function and Perceived School Well-Being Across Child- and Adult-Centered Educational Contexts: An Exploratory Study
articles.authors: Laura González; Marina Oliva Lozano; María Jesús Pardo-Guijarro; Silvia Guerrero
articles.abstract: Children’s socioemotional and cognitive development is shaped by the contexts in which they grow, with school playing a key role in well-being and executive function (EF). This study examined whether the association between EF and perceived school well-being differed across school contexts aligned with Child–Environment Interplay (CEI) and Teacher–Text–Centered (TTC) models. 105 preschool and primary school children participated (NCEI = 70; NTTC = 35). EF was assessed through inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility tasks. Perceived school well-being was explored through a structured interview addressing engagement, environment and support, and aggression-related experiences. No overall differences emerged in EF or interview-based well-being. However, higher well-being was associated with lower EF in TTC, but not CEI, schools, while higher perceived aggression was associated with lower EF across both approaches. A qualitative subsample provided insight into how young children interpreted school experiences. These findings suggest that the association between cognitive skills and perceived school well-being may vary across educational contexts and highlight the value of young children’s perspectives into research on school life.

articles.title: The Effects of Group-Based Community Interventions on Social Reintegration of Marginalized Adults with Mental Illness: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Nina Thorup Dalgaard; jakob Kaarup Jensen; Jasmin Sami Adada; Maya Christiane Flensborg Jensen; Elizabeth Bengtsen; Mikkel Helding Vembye; Elizabeth Tipton
articles.abstract:
Background 
Adults with mental illness who also experience social marginalization face interconnected clinical and social challenges, yet scalable interventions addressing both dimensions of recovery remain limited.

Aims 
To evaluate the effects of group-based community interventions on social reintegration and mental health among socially marginalized adults with mental illness.

Methods 
We conducted a preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis of interventions delivered in OECD countries. Searches identified 28,980 records; 62 studies met the inclusion criteria and 49 studies, contributing 349 effect sizes, were included in the meta-analysis. Outcomes were classified as social reintegration or mental health. Meta-analytic models accounted for dependent effect sizes within studies.

Results 
Group-based community interventions improved social reintegration (g = 0.195, 95% CI [0.122, 0.268]) and mental health (g = 0.215, 95% CI [0.090, 0.340]) relative to control conditions, corresponding to effects approximately 2.3 and 1.4 times larger, respectively, than the typical improvements under treatment as usual. Effects varied substantially across studies and outcomes, while measured moderators explained little of this heterogeneity. Effects on social reintegration and mental health were positively associated. Findings were robust across sensitivity analyses and showed little indication of publication bias. Nearly half of studies were preregistered and contributed approximately two-thirds of all effect sizes. Preregistered studies yielded smaller social reintegration effects than non-preregistered studies, although the average effect remained statistically significant and substantively meaningful.

Conclusions 
Group-based community interventions can improve both social reintegration and mental health among marginalized adults with mental illness, suggesting that they may support multidimensional recovery. Their potential value therefore extends beyond scalability and lower delivery costs to substantively meaningful improvements in outcomes. However, substantial unexplained heterogeneity indicates that benefits are unlikely to be uniform across populations, interventions, and settings.

What is already known on this topic
Adults experiencing both mental illness and social marginalization face interconnected clinical and social challenges, while existing systematic reviews on group-based interventions have largely focused on specific diagnoses, intervention types, or psychiatric symptoms.

What this study adds
Across 49 studies contributing 349 effect sizes, group-based community interventions produced positive average effects on both social reintegration and mental health. Effects in the two domains were positively associated, but substantial heterogeneity remained largely unexplained.

articles.title: Affordance-Based Control in Driving Behavior: Integration of Perception and Action by Extending rho Coupling and Satisficing
articles.authors: Takayuki Kondoh; Hiroyuki Mishima; Nobuhiro Furuyama
articles.abstract: Action-control models in ecological psychology have evolved from pursuing a single optimal solution toward affordance-based control within safety regions. However, mathematically integrating these approaches with rho coupling theory remains insufficient. This study theoretically re-examines the "risk feeling formula (RFF)"—a linear sum of two optical variables derived from real-world driving data. Our analysis demonstrates that the RFF is structurally equivalent to rho coupling, yet its "intercept" distinctly functions as a "satisficing" threshold. Rather than representing an internal computational compromise, this threshold signifies direct perceptual attunement for initiating avoidance behavior while maintaining a safety margin. Furthermore, we propose an integrated mathematical representation of affordances as the linear sum of two action-scaled pi values, reflecting the extended body effectivities, corresponding to overt risk (rho_LF) and potential risk (rho_GF). By extending rho coupling to encompass satisficing, this framework elegantly models how actors dynamically balance contextual pressures without error-nulling. This integrated theoretical approach explains diverse human adaptive strategies and provides fundamental insights for future ecological human-centered design, including advanced driver assistance systems.

articles.title: Perceived and evidenced benefits of videogame play amongst neurodivergent populations: A scoping review
articles.authors: Emily J Smith; Jonathan Farnell; Lacey-ann Carter; Roshan Rai; Benjamin Gibson
articles.abstract: There are meaningful concerns that videogame play is harmful for neurodivergent populations, including people with autism spectrum disorders. However, there is a disproportionate focus in the literature on dangers, and there are fewer efforts to consider why such populations may be more likely to play videogames in the first place. In considering benefits to play, this scoping review attempts to map out a more balanced view of videogame engagement amongst a range of neurodivergent populations. A search of academic databases identified 9 articles comprising a mix of qualitative and quantitative studies. Using a narrative synthesis, we found that benefits to play included (1) friendship and belonging, (2) immersion, escapism, and emotional regulation, and (3) development, growth, and autonomy. In the future, we recommend a pivot away from a deficit-focused approach to investigations, and a larger investment in research that considers motivations, attitudes, and consequences of play from a lived-experience perspective.

articles.title: Psychological inoculation against deepfakes
articles.authors: Cambridge Social Decision-Making Lab; Liana Cheetham; Kelly Wong Kar Yee; Sander van der Linden
articles.abstract: Despite growing interest in countering the threat of deepfake misinformation, most interventions aimed at enhancing human detection have thus far proven unsuccessful. In the current study we explore the potential of a popular psychological intervention: cognitive inoculation—which to our knowledge—has not been tested in the context of deepfakes. In a pre-registered between-subjects experiment (N = 297), we evaluate whether an inoculation-based video intervention improves people’s deepfake detection skills compared to a control intervention. The inoculation intervention forewarned participants they may be manipulated by deepfake content and prebunked it by deconstructing deepfake misinformation in weakened form. Following the intervention, participants were asked to classify a series of 10 videos as either real or deepfaked. We find that mean detection accuracy of deepfakes was significantly higher in the inoculation compared to the control group (d = 0.625, 95% CI [0.39, 0.86]) without shifting response bias, indicating that the inoculation intervention substantially improved deepfake discernment. Further investigation of the mechanisms behind the inoculation process finds that both motivation to resist deepfakes and self-reported ability to recognize them increased following the intervention. Overall, our findings highlight the potential of inoculation interventions to build resistance to deepfake misinformation.

articles.title: Examining the Role of Working Memory in Reasoning and Meta-reasoning:  A Fuzzy-trace approach
articles.authors: Leili Rouhi; Zuleykha Gasimova; Valerie A Thompson
articles.abstract: Monitoring processes, such as confidence, are assumed to guide control processes, such as whether to change or persist with a response. Yet whether this monitoring–control link depends on the same working memory (WM) resources implicated in reasoning itself remains unclear. Fuzzy-trace theory (FTT) holds that reasoning relies primarily on low-effort gist representations and that errors arise when a salient but inappropriate gist interferes with the appropriate one. Drawing on FTT and the meta-reasoning framework the role of WM in reasoning, monitoring and control. Participants (N = 998) solved belief-bias syllogisms with and without conflict between validity and believability in a two-response paradigm. They gave an initial answer under a concurrent WM load, a response deadline, or both, followed by a confidence rating and a final answer. Accuracy declined only when load and deadline were combined, and this decline was similar for conflict and non-conflict problems. Confidence was reliably lower on conflict than on non-conflict problems across all conditions, and confidence reliably predicted answer changes and rethinking time regardless of WM constraints. Monitoring resolution, however, was low even without constraints. These results suggest that WM constraints impair reasoning generally but leave conflict detection and control sensitivity largely intact. Reasoners’ limited ability to discriminate their own correct from incorrect responses appears to reflect a more general limitation of monitoring rather than a consequence of constrained resources.

articles.title: From Self to Others? Testing Whether Brief Mindfulness Reduces Intergroup Bias through Decentering or Self-Compassion
articles.authors: Gabriela Gorska; Pawel Holas
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Brief mindfulness reliably changes how individuals relate to their own internal experiences, but whether these intrapersonal changes generalize to intergroup responding remains unclear. This preregistered experiment (N = 91) examined whether mindfulness-related processes—decentering and compassionate self-responding—were associated with socio-affective responses toward in-group and out-group members. Participants completed an adapted Socio-affective Video Task using AI-generated images to assess compassion, personal distress, and prosocial giving. Brief mindfulness was significantly linked to increased decentering and compassionate self-responding. Contrary to preregistered hypotheses, the intervention did not reduce intergroup bias in compassion, personal distress, or the empathic Dictator Game. Findings suggest that brief mindfulness primarily influences proximal intrapersonal processes, whereas changes in intergroup socio-affective responding may be limited.

articles.title: Can Accurate Information Change Identity-Linked Political Beliefs? Evidence From Republicans’ Attitudes Towards Election Integrity
articles.authors: Michael Nicholas Stagnaro; Eran Amsalem; Andrea B Mullin; Hause Lin; Adam J. Berinsky; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: Psychological research suggests that identity shapes beliefs and impedes updating in response to contrary evidence. A prominent example is many Republicans’ persistence in believing that the 2020 election was stolen. We test whether credible factual information can shift Republicans' beliefs about election integrity. Immediately before the 2024 presidential election, we randomly assigned 861 conservative Republicans to an intensive informational intervention or a control matched with civic content. The intervention presented extensive, accurate, politically balanced evidence and encouraged sustained engagement. Treated participants reported stronger beliefs in US election integrity overall, greater confidence in the 2020 election, and more positive expectations for the 2024 election (.5 < ds < .8), including those who started lower in electoral confidence (.5 < ds < .97). Effects were still detectable two weeks later, after Trump’s victory. Though learning was incentivized, belief reporting was not – showing that when attended to, credible balanced evidence can change minds.

articles.title: Displayed judgment certainty reorganizes source selection in self-formed networks
articles.authors: Gaël Carniel; Frédéric Moisan; Alain Barrat; Jean-Claude Dreher
articles.abstract: Collective intelligence in self-formed networks depends on which judgments people choose to observe, as well as on how they integrate those judgments. We tested whether displaying judgment certainty reorganizes source selection and improves subsequent accuracy. Across eight online sessions, 273 participants evaluated 14 true and false news headlines, formed costly directed observation networks, and revised their beliefs over five updates. During network formation, we manipulated the visibility of certainty, defined by the extremity of each source's private probability judgment, while belief direction and source accuracy remained hidden. Displaying certainty produced denser networks and redirected links toward more certain sources; current popularity also predicted selection. Visibility increased exposure to highly certain but incorrect judgments, without a clear improvement in the relative accuracy of selected sources. Accuracy increased across repeated judgments, but certainty visibility did not detectably increase this improvement and reduced reconstructed net scores under the task's payoff structure. Observations with selected sources showed greater improvement than those without, and improvement was associated with selected sources' initial accuracy. Belief revisions moved toward selected sources and decreased with participants' own certainty. Among six compact predictive models, certainty-reinforcing DeGroot provided the best penalized and aggregate held-out prediction, although it did not capture the large first update. These findings distinguish a cue's ability to attract attention from its ability to identify useful information: displayed certainty can reorganize costly information acquisition without a detectable average accuracy benefit.

articles.title: Who can re-enter the loop? A scoping review on cognitive abilities and task re-engagement in human-AI interaction
articles.authors: Han Zhang; Bianca Done; Stefanie Schneider; Nithya Rajan; Manhua Wang
articles.abstract: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) promise a near future in which humans and AI systems work together to solve complex problems. Although offloading tasks to AI reduces immediate cognitive demands, the system may later require human input or decision-making, at which point the human must “re-enter the loop” by redirecting attention, reconstructing the task state, and responding appropriately. Whether individual differences in cognitive ability predict the capacity to re-enter the loop remains unclear. Here, we conducted a scoping review of studies relating cognitive ability to loop re-entry performance. Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Among them, most studies examined conditionally automated driving, and none examined interactions with generative AI systems. Working memory capacity was the most frequently studied ability and was generally associated with better loop re-entry performance, whereas results for attentional control were mixed. The evidence was further limited by small samples, single-task measures of cognitive abilities, and inconsistent outcome measures. As human oversight becomes increasingly central to AI safety, understanding who can re-enter the loop effectively remains an important open question. We offer concrete recommendations to guide future research.

articles.title: From Psychological States to Self-Reports: A New Perspective on Response Bias
articles.authors: Jess Grimmond; Scott Brown; Quentin Frederik Gronau; Guy Hawkins
articles.abstract:
Self-report measures are a cornerstone of psychological science, yet little attention has been
devoted to the processes through which internal experiences become observable responses. We
propose a theoretical account of self-report in which responses reflect two concurrent sources of
information: the latent states individuals seek to communicate and the response processes
governing how those states are expressed. We formalise this framework for Likert-type data using
the Latent State and Response Style (LASARS) model, an ordinal-threshold approach that
separates latent state expression from response style processes. Across applications to novel and
previously published data, we show that response styles are stable across time and survey
instruments, while individuals retain the capacity to modify their response style without changing
the latent states they wish to express. We further demonstrate a novel prediction of the
framework: that response style information obtained in one context can be used to reduce
response style confounding in another. Together, these findings support a view of self-report as a
communicative decision process rather than a direct reflection of latent states. More broadly, they
suggest that understanding psychological measurement requires explaining not only what people
experience, but also how they choose to express those experiences

articles.title: A Megastudy of Behavioral Interventions to Increase Voter Registration Ahead of the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
articles.authors: Katherine Anne Mason; Kayley Okst; Don Green; Robb Willer; James Druckman; Jan G. Voelkel; Yash Patel; Claire Robertson; Wooyoung Choi; Jasmine Sanchez
articles.abstract: In the United States, in nearly all cases, one must register in order to vote—yet, a substantial portion of the eligible electorate remains unregistered. Despite this, relatively little is known about how to increase the likelihood that a voter registers. Here, we tested the impact of 10 expert-crowdsourced, theoretically-based psychological interventions on a sample of eligible, yet unregistered, U.S. voters ahead of the 2024 presidential election (N = 12,896). Eight of the interventions increased intentions to vote, and five led individuals to click on the voter registration website. Escalating Commitment, which sequentially employed several social pressure strategies, was the strongest intervention across these outcomes. However, none of the interventions had a significant effect on actual voter registration or voter turnout. The results highlight a substantial disconnect between voters’ intentions and their ultimate behaviors. We discuss potential structural and psychological barriers that undermine the translation of intent into action.

articles.title: Beyond Lineups: An ROC-Expected Utility Framework for Eyewitness Identification
articles.authors: Yueran Yang; Justice Healy; Janice Burke; Max Guyll
articles.abstract: How should the legal system and scholars evaluate lineup performance? To answer this important question, this paper introduces a receiver operating characteristic-expected utility (ROC-EU) framework, which bridges two prominent evaluation methods in eyewitness research. The framework emphasizes investigators as the primary decision-makers who use eyewitness evidence for classifying suspects’ guilt. This perspective shift not only helps clarify confusions in interpreting lineup ROC analysis but also expands the scope of lineup evaluation. Specifically,  the expected utility component of the framework enables a holistic assessment across distinct investigative stages: the prior probability of guilt captures independent incriminating evidence collected before a lineup; likelihoods of investigator classification outcomes capture factors that shape witness responses during a lineup; and utilities of investigator classification outcomes capture the real-world legal and societal consequences that follow investigator classification decisions after a lineup. articles.title: Weak Links between Speech Perception and Speech Production at the Subphonemic Level
articles.authors: Brian W. L. Wong; Arthur G. Samuel; Efthymia C Kapnoula
articles.abstract: Recent research has shown individual differences in gradiency, defined as sensitivity to fine-grained acoustic differences at the subphonemic level. Consistency also varies, with some listeners providing more stable responses than others to repeated presentations of the same stimuli. However, it remains unclear whether gradiency and consistency are linked between perception and production. Across two experiments, 160 Spanish speakers completed a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) task measuring perceptual gradiency and consistency along a Spanish /ba/–/pa/ continuum manipulated in 7–8 ms steps of voice onset time (VOT). The same participants also performed an explicit imitation task using the same stimuli. Results revealed only weak relationships between perceptual gradiency and imitation accuracy, as well as between perceptual consistency and imitation consistency, even after accounting for other factors related to speech perception and imitation. These findings suggest that models proposing strong perception–production coupling may not extend to the subphonemic level.

articles.title: Self-Referential Social Processing in Schizophrenia and Bipolar Disorder: Advancing Theoretical Precision and Clinical Insights with Model-Based Neuroscience
articles.authors: Carly A Lasagna; Jacob Kraft; Michael D. Nunez; Takakuni Suzuki; Tyler Grove; Stephan F Taylor; Ivy Fei Tso; Timothy Joseph Pleskac
articles.abstract:
Background. Individuals with schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BD) often misjudge whether social cues, like eye contact, are meant for them, which can fuel symptoms and functional impairment. These difficulties appear to stem from disruptions in how social information is dynamically processed (“evidence accumulation”). We used neurocognitive joint modeling to investigate which neural signals shape evidence accumulation during gaze perception and whether these brain-behavior links help explain disrupted self-referential social processing.

Methods. Leveraging EEG data from N=99 SZ, BD, and healthy controls (HC) during a self-referential gaze perception task, we built joint drift-diffusion models characterizing how different trial-level EEG features translated to evidence accumulation and behavior. Joint models were compared against each other (and models using task-averaged EEG or behavior only) for their ability to predict task behavior and relevant clinical dimensions, including paranoia, functioning, and cognition. We examined whether the best-performing model differentiated patients and HC.

Results. The best-performing joint model explained evidence accumulation through trial-level fluctuations—not task averages—in two neural signals: CPP and frontal midline theta, implicated in subjective deliberation/certainty and top-down modulation, respectively. Less reliable translation of trial-level CPP signals to evidence accumulation impaired gaze perception in SZ and BD. Mapping how trial-level theta dynamics translated to evidence accumulation captured paranoia and functioning better than behavior or task-averaged neural metrics alone.

Conclusions. Model-based approaches that embrace the within-person variability of neural signals may reveal more nuanced, clinically relevant perspectives on the pathophysiology of SZ and BD than those using task-averaged brain activity or behavior alone.

articles.title: Mapping Behavioural and Psychological Factors Associated with Engagement in Online Activism: A Critical Scoping Review
articles.authors: Benjamin Gibson; Jekaterina Schneider; Mark J. Forshaw
articles.abstract: Online activism can be a powerful means of supporting social and political engagement. However, there are genuine concerns that online behaviours do not translate into social and political action, while nascent research suggests that online activism may affect well-being and feelings of identity more negatively compared to traditional (i.e., in-person) forms of activism. This scoping review attempted to map out the evidence so that the reader may better understand the psychological and behavioural factors associated with engagement in online activism. A search of academic databases and registers identified 24 articles comprising 28 studies and examined various forms of online activism including hashtag campaigns, online petitions, and social media engagement. Online engagement was shown to support a range of (further) online and offline activist behaviours, to foster collective identities, and to provide psychological benefits such as increased self-efficacy and feelings of empowerment (which in turn encouraged further political action). However, contextual and individual factors likely influence both behaviours and opportunities for psychological benefits. This review highlights the blurred boundaries between online and offline activism, while evidencing that even “passive” digital engagement may serve as a gateway to broader civic participation.

articles.title: Low family income and behavior problems in early childhood: Is family stress the causal mechanism?
articles.authors: Gülbin Şengül-İnal; Nicolai T. Borgen; Eric Dearing; Henrik Daae Zachrisson
articles.abstract: The Family Stress Model (FSM) provides a causal theory for how a family’s economic situation influences children’s behavioral outcomes through increasing income-related stress on parents, existing research on FSM is overwhelmingly correlational. We compared between-family FSM associations—the analytical approach typically used in cross-sectional and longitudinal FSM studies—with within-family FSM associations. The latter provides a more stringent causal test by eliminating bias from time-invariant confounders and unobserved between-person heterogeneity. We used longitudinal data (N=80,349) on maternal distress, relationship satisfaction, and child externalizing and internalizing behavior problems, assessed when the children were 18, 36, and 54 months from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study (MoBa). For household income, we used registry data. In both between- and within-family models, lower income was associated with more behavior problems, with total effect sizes being approximately two to three times larger in the former models. The proportion of indirect effect explained by family stress mediators was sizable in the between-effects model. In contrast, the within-effect model showed no indirect effect of family stress mediators. These results are consistent with the concern that between-family estimates of the FSM are confounded by unobserved factors that vary across families.

articles.title: When the Same Leader Helps and Harms: Inconsistent Leadership Behavior in Team Meetings
articles.authors: Amelie Verena Güntner; Kai N. Klasmeier; Catrin Millhoff; Nora Gosch; Simone Kauffeld
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The same leader often displays constructive and destructive behaviors at once, a
phenomenon known as inconsistent leadership. Inconsistency has been linked to negative
follower outcomes, yet it has almost exclusively been studied as a follower perception. This
study examines inconsistent leadership as enacted behavior, asking how and under what
conditions the co-occurrence of instrumental and destructive leadership shapes team behavior in
meetings.
Design/methodology/approach: Using a multilevel moderated mediation model, we tested our
model on 30 videotaped team meetings (5,430 coded behaviors), rating leaders' instrumental and
destructive behavior and coding leaders' action planning and team members' conflict-related
communication.
Findings: Instrumental leadership was associated with more action planning, which in turn
reduced conflict-related communication, but only when destructive leadership was low. When
leaders behaved destructively alongside instrumental leadership, this indirect effect disappeared.
Practical implications: Occasional destructive behavior can undo the benefits of otherwise
constructive leadership, so what matters for teams is not only what leaders do well but whether
they do it consistently. Organizations can address this through leadership development that helps
leaders recognize and reduce inconsistent behavior in meetings.
Originality/value: Inconsistency has almost always been studied as a follower perception. This
study extends its consequences beyond follower attitudes to observable team communication and
to the leader's own planning, showing that inconsistency also shapes the enacting leader. It offers
a behavioral, micro-level operationalization that complements existing perception-based
measures.

articles.title: Perceptions of Profit Motive: For-Profit Companies are Judged Less Favourably Than Non-Profits Even When the Societal Benefits of Profit-Seeking are Made Salient
articles.authors: Zuleykha Gasimova; Martin Harry Turpin; Alexander C. Walker; Jonathan Albert Fugelsang; Derek J. Koehler
articles.abstract: People tend to view profit-seeking businesses more negatively than otherwise equivalent non-profit businesses or organizations. This tendency puts people at risk of missing out on the potential societal benefit that can emerge when profit-seeking motivations are aligned with prosocial goals. When making judgments about firms and businesses, people may simply neglect the possibility that profit-seeking could result in gains for society. The current research finds that people’s attitudes are more ambivalent (as opposed to strictly negative) when they consider, in a broader sense, examples of how profit-seeking companies could positively or negatively affect society (e.g., consumer and employee welfare, technological advances, etc.). Study 1 (N = 101) showed that people are open to endorsing both general (pro-profit) statements about how profit-seeking businesses may produce socially beneficial outcomes and general (anti-profit) statements about how profit-seeking businesses may produce socially harmful outcomes. In Study 2 (N = 301), we examined whether exposure to such statements highlighting the potential positive (or negative) societal impacts of profit-seeking affected participant’s judgements of for- and non-profit firms. Exposure to pro-profit and anti-profit statements did not impact people’s judgments of profit-seeking businesses. Instead, people consistently exhibited a tendency to judge for-profit companies as having a less positive societal impact in comparison with their non-profit counterparts. This anti-profit bias persisted even among participants who had expressed agreement with general statements about the ways in which profit-seeking companies can deliver societal benefits.

articles.title: Relationships Between Auditory Statistical Learning and Reading Skills in Children with Reading Difficulties
articles.authors: Anqi Hu; Brynn Siles; Monique Montoute; Kelly Hay Yee Chan; Sarah Young-Hong; Amanda Van Horne; Morten H. Christiansen; Zhenghan Qi
articles.abstract:
Purpose. This study evaluated the psychometric implications of a novel gamified SL task for school-aged children with reading difficulties and examined the relationships between auditory syllable-based statistical learning (SL) and literacy skills.

Methods. Two groups of children aged 7–11 with reading difficulty were recruited. In Experiment 1, 13 children piloted a child-friendly, non-gamified auditory SL task at two timepoints, with learning assessed via a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) test at both timepoints and a statistically induced chunking recall (SICR) test at Timepoint 2. In Experiment 2, 22 children completed a gamified version of the SL task, with learning assessed via 2AFC and SICR at both timepoints and reading skills (nonword and sight-word fluency) assessed at Timepoint 1.

Results. Children showed learning at the group level across timepoints, as measured by SICR in both gamified and non-gamified tasks, and as measured by 2AFC in the gamified task only. SICR showed higher internal consistency than 2AFC across tasks. Test-retest reliability for 2AFC was higher for the gamified (r = .64) than non-gamified (r = .14) task.  Children’s performance on 2AFC and SICR in the gamified task were significantly associated with their nonword and sight-word reading fluency.

Conclusions. Gamification and the use of a statistically induced chunking recall task in an auditory SL task improved the task’s psychometric properties in school-aged children with reading difficulties. Auditory SL was also associated with concurrent reading skills in these children, suggesting that the implicit learning of regularities in spoken language input may additionally support reading development.

articles.title: Facilitation and Attenuation of Learning to Novel and Familiar Stimuli Through Contextual  Mismatch: Experimental Evidence and a Computational Model
articles.authors: Jialin Shi; Mark Haselgrove
articles.abstract: Learning about the relationship between a stimulus and an outcome typically progresses more successfully when the stimulus is novel, compared to when it is familiar. This phenomenon, referred to as latent inhibition, is widespread across the animal kingdom and continues to motivate the development of theories of learning. Recently, Haselgrove et al. (2025) reported a series of experiments that revealed conditions under which this influential phenomenon could be reversed. They demonstrated, using pseudoword stimuli, that successful associative learning about a novel or a familiar stimulus was a function of the mismatch between the novelty of the stimulus and the context in which is trained. Thus, in a context that sustains novelty, learning about a stimulus-outcome relation progressed more successfully to a familiar stimulus than a novel stimulus (reversed latent inhibition). Here we report three experiments that reproduce and extend the generality of these findings. We show that the effect can be obtained with images as stimuli, and when participants are equated for the effects of cognitive load during familiarization. To explain these results, we propose that novelty and familiarity are stimulus elements that can compete for associative strength alongside the elements of a stimulus that are activated by its physical characteristics (e.g. its colour, saturation, etc.). We then describe a simple computational model that serves as proof of this concept, and which reveals that latent inhibition, and its reversal, can be simulated without appeals being made to learned variations in attention or memory/response interference.

articles.title: Varying Dimensions of Language Input Predict Language and Executive Function Development Across Socioeconomically Diverse Families
articles.authors: Rachel R Romeo; Alexus Guadalupe Ramirez; Klaudia I. Kulawska; Amy E. Carolus; Katie A McLaughlin; Meredith Rowe; Liliana Lengua
articles.abstract: Children’s early language experiences are linked to their language and executive functioning (EF) development, and vary by socioeconomic status (SES). However, unique features may support different cognitive domains because input is multifaceted. The present study characterizes the dimensional structure of maternal language input and examines how these dimensions vary by SES and predict language and EF development across the preschool years. Thirteen metrics of maternal speech were extracted and/or manually coded from semi-structured play with 275 mother-child dyads when children were 3 years (137 male, 138 female; 65% White, 4% Black, 2% Latino, 2% Asian, 28% multiracial). Children’s language and EF were assessed four times between ages 3 and 5 years (data collected 2008–2012). Exploratory factor analysis revealed four input dimensions: linguistic quantity, linguistic complexity, interactiveness, and conceptual input. These differentially predicted children’s baseline language and EF performance, but not growth. Specifically, interactive and conceptual input predicted language skills, while complexity predicted EF skills. The four dimensions jointly mediated the relationship between SES and baseline language (β=0.053), and a serial pathway linked SES through input and language to EF (β=0.052). These findings reveal distinct pathways through which specific features of early input support children’s language and EF.

articles.title: The precision hierarchy hypothesis: A unifying framework to explain opposing serial effects
articles.authors: Carina Ufer; Helen Blank
articles.abstract: Serial dependence, the phenomenon where current perception is biased toward the previous stimulus, has been interpreted as a mechanism for perceptual stability, smoothing variability in sensory input. However, analyses that include both the previous stimulus and previous response unmasked repulsive effects at the sensory level that were otherwise concealed. Moreover, attractive serial biases fail to scale with environmental correlations, challenging their primary role in maintaining stability. We propose the Precision hierarchy hypothesis, grounded in predictive processing, as a unifying framework for these seemingly contradictory findings. Repulsive effects naturally emerge when priors - shaped by recent trials - are highly precise, making small deviations in incoming input more probable under alternative priors. We further propose that prior precision decreases across hierarchical levels. A higher precision at lower sensory levels leads to repulsive effects, as even small deviations in incoming signal are in conflict with the prior. In contrast, attractive biases emerge at higher, more abstract levels, where deviations are integrated with broader conceptual priors. By dynamically shaping prior precision according to environmental correlations, perception remains adaptive, balancing the need for stability with the sensitivity to detect meaningful changes in the environment. This framework reconciles diverse findings on serial effects and provides testable predictions for future research.

articles.title: A Browser-Based Remote Photoplethysmography Method for Live Heart Rate Estimation
articles.authors: Mariana Von Mohr; Manos Tsakiris; Gianluca Finotti
articles.abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) enables contact-free heart-rate estimation from facial video, but most web-based implementations process recordings offline, limiting their use in real-time experimental applications. We developed and, to our knowledge, provide the first ECG validation of a live rPPG implementation embedded directly within Gorilla Experiment Builder, a widely used platform for online behavioural research. We validated the method in 27 participants against simultaneously recorded electrocardiography (ECG) across nine trial durations ranging from 10 to 50 s. rPPG-derived heart rate showed excellent agreement with ECG-derived heart rate, with a mean absolute error of 1.48 bpm, a root mean square error of 2.19 bpm, and an ICC(A,1) of .960. Mean bias was small (0.40 bpm), with repeated-measures 95% limits of agreement from -3.85 to 4.66 bpm, and heart-rate error did not differ significantly by trial durations. These findings support the feasibility of live rPPG within a browser-based experimental platform for physiological feedback and adaptive online experiments without requiring webcam videos to be stored or processed offline.

articles.title: From Prediction Accuracy to Prediction Use: A Monitoring-Centered Framework for Interactive Sport Expertise
articles.authors: Yingzhi Lu; Mengkai Luan; Xiaoran Gao; Wenzi Wang; Chen Yiheng; Chenglin Zhou
articles.abstract: Action anticipation is widely recognized as a cornerstone of expert performance in interactive sport. Decades of research have shown that skilled performers predict upcoming actions more accurately than less-skilled performers by extracting kinematic cues and integrating them with contextual information. This literature has provided a powerful account of how anticipatory predictions are formed. Yet, interactive sport rarely ends when a prediction is generated, because opponents continue to move, sensory evidence changes, contextual priors may mislead, and performers must determine whether an initial prediction remains useful for action. In this narrative review, we argue that the field should move beyond anticipation accuracy toward the adaptive use of anticipation during unfolding interaction. Drawing on sport expertise research, predictive-processing accounts, performance-monitoring theory, observed-action error studies, and sport-specific neurophysiological evidence, we propose a monitoring-centered framework for interactive sport expertise. In this framework, anticipation generates probabilistic reference states, monitoring evaluates whether these states remain aligned with unfolding input, and functional discrepancy processing determines whether mismatch matters for action goals, affordances, and motor plans. We further argue that discrepancy processing is graded and functionally meaningful rather than binary. From this perspective, expert performers may not only predict better; they may also detect diagnostic mismatch more selectively, tolerate irrelevant variability, and couple action-relevant discrepancy information with sport-specific motor preparation and adjustment. The framework yields testable predictions for assessment, training, and future research on expert performance in sport.

articles.title: The broken brain? Prevalence and consequences of brain framing of mental disorders
articles.authors: Olha Guley; Sanil Shashank Pandhare; Elena Pasquinelli; Daniel Nettle
articles.abstract: Public discourse often frames mental disorders as brain disorders, yet little is known about how this framing shapes lay beliefs. We combined large-scale text analysis of 55,068 New York Times articles with one correlational study (N = 204) and four preregistered vignette experiments (total N = 2,445) to examine both the prevalence and consequences of “brain talk” about mental disorders. We find that brain framing has become much more prevalent since 1980, and especially since 2004. We find evidence that brain framing increases belief in other biological and genetic causes; reduces belief in psychological and environmental causes, and strengthens beliefs in the efficacy of medication as a treatment. Effects on pessimism about recovery varied across studies and disorders. Brain framing had no robust effects on perceived age of onset, duration, severity, or beliefs about efficacy of psychotherapy treatment. Public beliefs about mental disorders are malleable and can be shaped by framing, highlighting the cognitive and societal consequences of brain framing in communication about mental health.

articles.title: Longitudinal and Latent-variable Extensions of the Triadic Actor-Partner Interdependence
articles.authors: Shiyao Wang; Jennifer Dang Guay; Karla Van Leeuwen; Evelien Schat; Eva Ceulemans
articles.abstract: When modeling interpersonal processes within triadic systems, researchers commonly encounter two types of analytical complexity: observations collected repeatedly over time, and constructs measured via multiple items. The current study introduces longitudinal and latent-variable extensions of the standard triadic Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (tAPIM) to accommodate these data structures. The longitudinal extensions, the concurrent tAPIM and the temporal tAPIM, account for temporal dependence and temporal precedence in repeated observations, while the latent-variable extension models each member’s construct as a latent variable measured from multiple observed items. In addition, we identify measurement invariance across triad members as a challenge specific to triadic data analysis and conduct a simulation study to investigate the consequences of its violation for the estimation of actor and partner effects. The results indicate that: 1) imposing invariance constraints that are not empirically supported may bias the estimation of nonzero actor and partner effects associated with the noninvariant member, while effects of invariant members and zero effects are accurately recovered; 2) relaxing invariance constraints avoids bias in point estimates, but standard errors of effects associated with the noninvariant member were still inflated, reducing power to detect true effects. The current paper offers practical guidance for researchers modeling interdependence in triadic systems using multi-item or longitudinal data.

articles.title: It's a small world of signs: Semantic network structure in American Sign Language based on free associations
articles.authors: Zed Sehyr; Karen Emmorey; Elana Pontecorvo; Naomi Kenney Caselli; Erin Michelle Buchanan
articles.abstract: Semantic network analyses have shown that words in spoken languages are organized into efficient "small-world" structures that support rapid lexical access and retrieval. However, little is known about whether similar organizational principles generalize to sign languages. We present the first large-scale analysis of semantic network structure in American Sign Language (ASL) using a free semantic association task. Deaf ASL signers (N = 45) produced three associations to 2,714 cue signs drawn from ASL-LEX, resulting in almost 100,000 cue–response pairs. We constructed (a) directed associative networks based on cue-response relationships and (b) undirected conceptual similarity networks based on cue–to-cue cosine similarity and compared ASL with English using matched subsets of the Small World of Words norms. We estimated network statistics and evaluated network topology using bootstrapping and degree-preserving random graphs. Both languages exhibited small-world organization indicating similar pressures on efficient semantic organization across language modalities. However, the languages differed in topology. Across network types, ASL exhibited longer average path lengths, and in conceptual similarity networks, lower clustering, suggesting reduced integration. In associative networks, ASL showed lower modularity, while in the conceptual similarity networks, ASL showed higher modularity than English, indicating a more compartmentalized semantic space. Further, more frequent signs occupied denser and more diverse semantic neighborhoods, whereas iconic signs exhibited fewer semantic connections and lower response diversity. These findings suggest that semantic memory is shaped by modality-independent organizational principles while also reflecting language-specific network topologies and structural pressures. The dataset and tools provide a basis for future cross-linguistic investigations.

articles.title: Partisans are more likely to entrench their beliefs in misinformation when political outgroup members correct claims
articles.authors: Diego A. Reinero; Elizabeth Ann Harris; Steve Rathje; Annie Duke; Jay Joseph Van Bavel
articles.abstract:
Misinformation has become a global issue with potentially dire consequences (e.g., election
results, COVID-19 vaccines, international conflicts). The most common strategy to reduce
beliefs in misinformation is to issue corrections or fact-checks. However, fact-checks are often
ineffective for polarized issues and there has been debate over whether misinformation
corrections sometimes "backfire," causing people to become more entrenched in misinformation.
Across three experiments (N = 1,217) we identify a key feature – the partisan identity of the
source – that explains when corrections will be effective and when they will be most likely to
backfire. We found that while corrections work on average, backfires still occurred 23% of the
time and were 52% more likely to occur when the correction came from a political outgroup vs.
ingroup member – leaving people with more entrenched beliefs in misinformation. Indeed, the
effect of partisan bias on initial belief in misinformation was 5x larger than the effect of
corrections. Partisan bias was most prominent and corrections were least effective when famous
politicians were involved. In sum, corrections have small effects compared to partisan identity
congruence, and sometimes backfire–especially if they come from a political outgroup member.

articles.title: Gender Differences in Self-reported Emotional Sharing in Social Interaction: A Meta Analysis
articles.authors: X. Jia; Karen Holtmaat; Y. Mo; ZIHAO Zeng; M. Kaneva; Annet Kleiboer; Sander L. Koole
articles.abstract: Through emotional sharing, individuals can make their emotional experiences available to others, creating opportunities for interpersonal emotion regulation. Although gender differences in these behaviours have been documented across various domains, findings regarding their magnitude and consistency remain inconclusive. This meta-analysis examined gender differences in emotional sharing among adults. A systematic search identified 32 articles comprising 37 independent samples, 155 effect sizes, and 13,147 participants, including 8,504 women and 4,643 men. Overall, women reported higher levels of emotional sharing than men, g = 0.31, 95% CI [0.18, 0.44]. This effect was not significantly moderated by (1) functions (emotional expression, emotional disclosure, emotional expression as coping), (2) temporal level (dispositional, situational), (3) emotional valence (negative, positive or unspecified), (4) specific negative emotion (anger, sadness, fear/anxiety, shame/guilt, and unspecified negative emotions), and (5) the interpersonal target (romantic partner, friend, other, or no partner specified). Despite the absence of significant moderation effects, pooled estimates within most subgroups remained significantly positive, indicating higher levels of expression and disclosure among women than men across a wide range of emotional contexts and interpersonal relations.

articles.title: Political Emotions Shape Preferences for Leaders’ Facial Traits: Anger Favors Dominance, Fear Favors Trustworthiness
articles.authors: Mariana Von Mohr; Manos Tsakiris
articles.abstract: Past work shows that conservatives prefer more dominant-looking political leaders, whereas liberals prefer more trustworthy-looking ones. We extend this by showing that, beyond partisanship, discrete political emotions independently shape preferences for leaders’ facial traits. A balanced sample of U.S. Republicans and Democrats identified the political issue that made them most angry or most afraid and then chose which leader would best address that issue using computer-generated faces varying in dominance and trustworthiness. Participants chose a more dominant and less trustworthy-looking leader more often when angry (49.5 percent) than when fearful (46.5 percent). Mechanistically, anger shifted choices toward more dominant-looking leaders by increasing reliance on dominance cues and reducing reliance on trustworthiness cues, whereas fear selectively increased reliance on trustworthiness cues. These findings show that political emotions exert distinct influences on leader evaluation with implications for democratic decision-making and electoral choices.

articles.title: Infants’ learning of tones and VOT contrasts in the lab
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract: Infants likely home in on the speech categories in the ambient language(s) by attending to the acoustic cue distributions present in the input, but direct experimental evidence for this remains scarce. Young infants’ discrimination of /d-t/ and Mandarin Chinese tones T2-T4 was assessed over the course of a repeated exposure-test pro- cedure. In addition to being the first to document the emergence of perceptual categories through repeated testing of the same infants, this study suggests that perceptual learning through acoustic cue distributions could also account for the development of lexical tone perception.

articles.title: Rescripting suicidal mental imagery in young people: A pilot study of feasibility, acceptability and safety
articles.authors: Lianne Schmaal; Georgie Paulik; Zamantha Munoz; Laura van Velzen; Pemma Davies; Martin Mitrevski; Eleanor Bailey; Phoebe Gleeson; Lisa Incerti; Samantha Galea
articles.abstract: Suicidal mental imagery – vivid, intrusive mental images of suicide or death - is common among young people experiencing suicidal ideation and may increase risk of suicidal behaviour, yet interventions directly targeting these images are lacking. We conducted a single-arm pilot study evaluating the feasibility, acceptability and safety of a brief, therapist delivered imagery rescripting intervention targeting action-facilitating suicidal mental imagery in help-seeking young people aged 16–25 years with mood disorders and current or recent suicidal ideation. Fourteen participants were recruited; 12 were eligible for the intervention and 11 (92%) completed treatment and follow-up. The recruitment target (N=25) was not met, largely due to service disruptions and clinician capacity constraints. Acceptability and safety criteria were met: 73% reported that sessions were not distressing, none felt less safe following treatment, and no participant showed increased suicidal ideation from baseline to follow-up. Two serious adverse events occurred but were judged unrelated to the intervention. Exploratory analyses showed reductions in suicidal-image frequency, realness, compellingness, intrusiveness and distress, alongside a 52% reduction in suicidal ideation severity. Our pilot study indicates that directly rescripting action-facilitating suicidal mental imagery showed encouraging short-term safety and acceptability signals in young people, supporting evaluation in a larger randomised controlled trial.

articles.title: Towards an Integrative, Interdisciplinary, and Multidimensional Approach to Curbing Epistemically Suspect Beliefs: A Commentary on Bronstein et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Magdalena Adamus; Jais Adam-Troian; Maria Chayinska
articles.abstract: In this commentary, we endorse the recent call by Bronstein et al. (2026) to open a polyphonic debate and bring clinical psychology into the dialogue on the nature, causes, and consequences of epistemically suspect beliefs. We concur with the authors’ call for creating an integrative approach that would triangulate findings across different disciplines in a much-needed attempt to harmonise knowledge about individual, situational, and structural factors that contribute to the endorsement of epistemically suspect beliefs. Using economic anxiety as a model case, we then show how the integration of clinical insights could inform innovative, cost-effective, and scalable intervention programmes. Finally, we call for careful consideration of the risks associated with incorporating the clinical perspective, particularly the potential pathologisation of epistemically suspect beliefs and stigmatisation of those who endorse them, as well as the need to carefully distinguish delusions from ill-informed beliefs and rational suspicions.

articles.title: Assessing Person-Specific Symptom Networks From Brief Narratives: Development and Initial Evaluation of the Narrative-to-Network (N2N) Approach
articles.authors: Felix Vogel; Carla Paulus; Julian Reichert; Jonas Tesarz; Stefanie Jungmann
articles.abstract: Person-specific symptom networks formalize which problems characterize an individual and how those problems are perceived to influence one another, making them increasingly relevant for individualized case conceptualization, treatment planning, and personalized psychotherapy. However, existing approaches typically rely on structured causal assessment or intensive longitudinal data, both of which can increase assessment burden. We developed and initially evaluated the Narrative-to-Network (N2N) framework for deriving directed person-specific networks from brief spoken narratives in which individuals describe their psychological difficulties and perceived relations among them in their own words. Following a development phase (N = 22), an independent evaluation sample (N = 50) completed a narrative assessment and a Perceived Causal Networks (PECAN) assessment. Narratives lasted approximately three minutes. Manual coding showed relatively high agreement for node identification (Dice = .76) and edge direction conditional on a shared relation (agreement = .81), with lower agreement for edge presence (Dice = .62). Narrative-derived and PECAN networks showed partial but incomplete convergence (mean Jaccard = .29). Most problems identified in narratives were also identified through PECAN (62.6%), whereas only 36.7% of PECAN problems appeared in the corresponding narratives. Despite containing substantially fewer problems and relations, narrative-derived networks were perceived as highly representative; among participants with complete ratings (n = 39), mean representativeness scores were 33.26 for narrative-derived networks and 34.10 for regulated PECAN networks, with no statistically significant difference (p = .527). Narrative node count was positively associated with psychological distress both concurrently (ρ = .34) and at follow-up (ρ = .40). These findings provide initial evidence that structured person-specific symptom networks can be reproducibly derived from brief prompted spoken narratives and may offer an economical, complementary representation of individuals’ difficulties.

articles.title: The Development of Compositionality in Language and Thought
articles.authors: Eulalie Péquay; Isabelle Dautriche
articles.abstract:
Compositionality is the property of a representational system whereby com-plex meanings
arise from the combination of simpler meaningful elements. Here we take a developmental
perspective to understand the origins of compositional representational systems and their
relation to language—an issue that bears on longstanding debates in cognitive science about
the structure of the human mind. Based on our review, we conclude that (a) well-controlled
evidence for compositional abilities during language acquisition remains scarce, although
some studies suggest infants begin to understand specific multiword combinations during the
second year of life, and (b) the key computation underlying compositionality—function
application—can be observed in infancy during the first year of life, well before, and even out-
side, compositional language. These findings suggest the mind may support compositional
operations prior to the emergence of compositional language, while leaving open questions
about how the development of compositional thought and compositional language interact.

articles.title: Moral Concern for AI in an Economic Game
articles.authors: Carter Allen; Joshua Lewis; Lucius Caviola
articles.abstract: How will people morally regard increasingly human-like artificial intelligence systems? We introduce the AI Harm Game, a novel paradigm examining whether people will harm AI for personal gain. In our study, 498 U.S. participants interacted with GPT-4o in a three-round economic game. In each round, participants chose whether to harm the AI for a small monetary bonus (causing it to vividly simulate suffering) or refrain from harming it (eliciting gratitude). Although participants were overwhelmingly skeptical that current AIs can suffer, their decisions and reasoning about whether to harm the AI varied considerably. Participants harmed the AI in 1.4 out of 3 rounds on average. Women and older participants were more reluctant to harm the AI, while participants higher on measures of selfishness and psychopathy were more willing. These findings reveal that even without attributing consciousness to them, many people hesitate to harm responsive AIs, suggesting people’s moral impulses may generalize to future human–AI relationships.

articles.title: Evaluating dyadic interdependence between cannabis attitudes and parental monitoring processes among parents and adolescents
articles.authors: Tram Doran; Emily Olenik; Sarah Ryan; Alexandria LeVert; Jane Metrik; Pearl Ayiku; Samuel Meisel; Jack Rusley; Anthony Spirito; Sarah Ann Thomas
articles.abstract: Cannabis is a commonly used substance during adolescence. As US legalization expands, public perception of cannabis increasingly reflects the view that it is less harmful than other substances. The extent to which parents monitor and know about their adolescent’s activities and whereabouts is an important tool to manage risk behaviors like substance use. However, it is unclear how parental monitoring may vary based on cannabis attitudes. The current study investigated how parents' and adolescents’ attitudes toward cannabis (risk of harm to teens, disapproval, and ease of availability) are associated with parental knowledge about adolescents’ whereabouts/activities and its sources (adolescent disclosure, parental solicitation). We hypothesized that lower perceived risk of harm and less disapproval of cannabis use would be associated with lower levels of parental monitoring among both parents and adolescents. Our sample was N = 73 adolescents ages 14–17 (59% female) and their caregivers. Lower parental perceived risk of harm to teens from cannabis use was associated with less adolescent-reported parental solicitation. Lower adolescent perceived risk of harm to teens from cannabis use was linked to less adolescent disclosure to parents. Greater adolescent-perceived cannabis availability was associated with (a) both adolescent- and parent-report that parents knew less about adolescents’ whereabouts and activities, and (b) lower adolescent-report of less disclosure to parents. Results highlight the interdependent nature of parent and adolescent cannabis perceptions in relation to monitoring processes. Parents may benefit from public health initiatives that provide them with information on the potential negative health and emotional consequences of cannabis use in adolescence.

articles.title: “A Freeing of My Mind”: Narrative Accounts of Perinatal Mental Health in the Context of   Rx Kids, a Prenatal and Infant Unconditional Cash Transfer Program
articles.authors: Caroline Doenmez; Crystal L. Cederna; Mona Hanna
articles.abstract:
Background: In 2024, a new program called Rx Kids began providing unconditional cash transfers to all expectant mothers and infants in Flint, Michigan. Through a lump sum payment provided mid-pregnancy and monthly payments for up to a year after birth, the place-based maternal and infant health program is aimed at providing economic stability to improve the health, hope, and happiness of mothers and newborns.  

Objective: This study examined how mothers who had received Rx Kids cash transfers discussed perceived impacts on their perinatal mental health while participating in the program.  

Design: Qualitative.  

Methods: Thematic analysis was used to analyze interviews conducted between July and October 2025 with 46 mothers from Flint, Michigan, who participated in the Rx Kids program. Conceptual frameworks from medical anthropology and psychology were utilized to interpret their narratives.  

Results: Three dominant themes emerged pertaining to mothers’ experiences of perinatal mental health in the context of receiving Rx Kids cash transfers: 1) financial relief and perinatal well-being; 2) postpartum time affluence; and 3) program communication as a form of care.  

Conclusion: For mothers in Flint, Michigan, financial concerns play a central role in their narratives of their perinatal mental health struggles with stress and postpartum depression. Analyzing their descriptions of perceived shifts, adaptions and relief associated with their participation in Rx Kids, we find that the program was often depicted as equally impactful in terms of improving mothers’ mental health as it was in easing financial pressures.

articles.title: The beliefs at the heart of multilingual family language policies: A corpus-assisted discourse study of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism
articles.authors: Ruth Kircher; Melanie Brouillard; Alexa Ahooja; Erin Quirk; Susan Ballinger; Linda Polka; Krista Byers-Heinlein
articles.abstract: This study focuses on parental language beliefs, which we approach from an attitudes perspective. Language attitudes are at the heart of multilingual family language policies because they shape parents’ language practices and language management – and thereby, ultimately, children’s multilingual development. Based on French and English corpora (over 30,000 words in total) comprising 742 Quebec-based parents’ responses to an open-ended survey question, we present a corpus-assisted discourse study of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism. We analyse frequencies and collocations to attest statistically significant patterns, and we examine concordance lines and longer text segments to establish meaning in context. Our findings confirm the multidimensionality of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism, providing new insights into the nature of the three previously-established dimensions – status, solidarity, and cognitive development – as well as revealing a potential fourth dimension: personality development. The study thus makes a contribution to the family language policy framework and to language attitude theory more generally. Moreover, the findings show systematic differences between parents transmitting multiple societal languages versus parents transmitting heritage languages alongside one/more societal languages. The study thus also makes a practical contribution by facilitating the development of tailored support measures for different types of multilingual families.

articles.title: Playing for fun, playing to escape: Gaming motives and problematic video game use in a French sample aged 6 to 45 years
articles.authors: Chloe Nguyen; Quentin Hallez
articles.abstract: Data on the prevalence of problematic gaming in France are scarce, and few studies have compared gaming behavior, gaming motives, and their correlates across developmental periods with identical instruments. We surveyed 676 French participants aged 6 to 45 years (52.4% male), spanning childhood (6–14 years; parent-reported), adolescence (15–17), young adulthood (18–25), and adulthood (26–45), using the Game Addiction Scale (GAS-7), the Motives for Online Gaming Questionnaire (MOGQ), the WHO-5 Well-Being Index, and the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-15). Overall, 79.6% of participants played video games. Problematic gaming (monothetic GAS criterion) characterized 4.8% of gamers, with no significant differences across age groups and rates three times higher in males than in females. Although symptom levels were similar across age groups, motive profiles were not: recreation dominated at every age, whereas coping and escape motives were rare in childhood and markedly higher from adolescence onward. In hierarchical regressions, escape and competition motives and gaming frequency were the strongest unique correlates of problematic use, statistically attenuating the bivariate contributions of gender, impulsivity, well-being, and gaming time. Motive–symptom associations were invariant across age groups, whereas the association between gaming time and symptoms was stronger in older age groups. These cross-sectional findings suggest that motivational assessment may be more informative than screen-time metrics for the prevention and screening of problematic gaming.

articles.title: Getting Closer or Stepping Back? Personal Space Adjustments Following Facial Emotion Imitation and Observation
articles.authors: Ivan Patané; Clément Desoche; ALESSANDRO FARNE; Fadila Hadj-Bouziane
articles.abstract: Regulating personal space (PS) is essential for navigating social interactions. Although emotional cues are known to influence PS, the mechanisms underlying this modulation remain poorly understood. The present study investigated whether active facial emotion imitation is followed by changes in PS regulation and whether these changes differ from those observed following passive emotion observation. Participants completed a Virtual Reality Stop-Distance task to assess their preferred interpersonal distances from angry, happy, and neutral virtual agents, before and after an imitation session, during which they actively imitated angry or happy facial expressions. Following emotion imitation, participants exhibited a bidirectional modulation of PS: they increased their distance from angry virtual agents and decreased it from happy virtual agents, while no changes were observed for neutral agents. These findings suggest that active facial imitation enhances sensitivity to emotional signals and adaptively modulates interpersonal distance. Eye-tracking analyses revealed no significant changes in gaze behavior between pre- and post-imitation sessions, indicating that the reported effects were not driven by differences in overt visual attention. In a second experiment using a similar pre-post design, a new group of participants passively observed the same emotional expressions without imitating them. Results showed that, after emotion observation, angry virtual agents elicited an increased interpersonal distance, whereas no changes in distance from either the happy or neutral virtual agents were observed. Together, these results indicate that defensive distancing from others’ angry expressions followed both active imitation and passive observation, whereas the approach-related reduction in distance in response to happy expressions was evident after active imitation only. These findings highlight the contribution of emotional-cue exposure to personal space regulation in social contexts and provide further evidence that emotional experience can dynamically shape interpersonal behavior.

articles.title: Linking Traits and Behavior Through Computational Modeling of Neuroethical Decisions
articles.authors: Brian Kim; Kianté Fernandez; John Medaglia
articles.abstract: Individual differences in psychology are often measured through self-report questionnaires or behavioral performance, yet these approaches capture different constructs and rarely align. Computational modeling provides a framework for connecting both measures, as it extracts a process-level description of cognition from observable behavior in the form of latent variables. These latent variables represent repeated patterns of decision-making that should relate to psychological traits. We applied this approach to neuroethical decision-making, where evidence shows that both behavioral performance and self-reported psychological traits are related to how individuals weigh uncertain risks against potential benefits of emerging brain technologies. Participants completed a neuromodulation task in which risk and benefit probabilities were systematically varied. To capture how decisions unfolded, we used a temporally sensitive diffusion decision model that estimates when and how risks and benefits are evaluated. These model parameters described general trends in task behavior: individuals considered risks earlier and weighed risks more highly than benefits. Additionally, model parameters described how individuals modified their behavior: individuals who considered benefits first according to the model tended to endorse neuromodulation, but shifted towards rejection when risks were evaluated earlier. Importantly, self-reported psychological traits related to these computational parameters. Cognitive factors such as risk propensity and numeracy related to risk sensitivity and evaluation timing, while prosocial traits were also related to evaluation timing and benefit sensitivity. By contrast, Religion & Spirituality and Moral Commitment measures showed lower than expected associations across parameters. By capturing process-level mechanisms, computational modeling served as a bridge between self-reported traits and observed behavior, showing how stable individual differences shape the dynamics of decision-making in neuroethical contexts.

articles.title: When Effort Stops Meaning Something: A Cognitive Systems Model of Persistence, Disuse, and Re-entry
articles.authors: Arya Jadhav; Lawrence R. Burns
articles.abstract: Learning depends not only on task performance, but on whether effort remains coupled to interpretable signals of progress, competence, and continued agency. External cognitive systems can disrupt this coupling when they absorb cognitive work that would otherwise sustain internal learning dynamics. We introduce the Cognitive Cost Comparator (CCC), a mechanistic agent-based model of engagement-gated learning under external offloading. In the model, heterogeneous agents allocate effort between internal cognition and an external aid across 300 discrete time steps. Although the present simulations instantiate the external system as AI assistance, the architecture is intended to generalize to cognitive tools that alter the perceived cost of task completion. The model couples three feedback processes: a confidence-engagement loop that gates learning opportunity, an offloading-disuse loop that erodes internal confidence and raises engagement thresholds, and a scaffolding-interpretability mechanism that determines whether effort produces meaningful progress signals. Learning states are modeled as dynamic attractors rather than fixed outcomes. Across simulations with 4,500 agents, engagement reliability was the strongest predictor of terminal confidence (Spearman r = 0.72). Scaffolding primarily prevented entry into disengaged failure states, but did not reliably restore agents once disengagement had stabilized; recovery increased meaningfully only when scaffolding was paired with explicit re-entry mechanisms. These findings suggest that cognitive systems involving human learners and external aids must be evaluated not only by performance support, but by whether they preserve the conditions for effortful re-engagement after failure.

articles.title: Lines We Cross: Identity Complexity at the Boundary Between Activism and Radicalism
