articles.authors: Michelle Blaya-Burgo
articles.abstract: Violent radicalization and politically motivated violence pose significant threats to global peace, security, and social cohesion. These problems are costly, and reactive approaches have not effectively reduced their incidence. Because conflict is inevitable, prevention efforts should take precedence. This paper examines social identity complexity as a potential buffer against violent radicalization, proposing that complex identity structures – perceptions of having multiple, distinct ingroup memberships – may reduce susceptibility by preventing individuals from fixating on a single identity and pushing it to extremes. Two studies tested this idea. Study 1 (N = 226) used a 2×2 design manipulating identity complexity (simple vs. complex) and self-uncertainty (low vs. high). Results showed that simple identity structures increased radicalism intentions, resulting in a greater relative preference for activism among those with complex identities. Study 2 (N = 240) examined political identity and natural levels of identity-uncertainty. Results showed that higher uncertainty predicted more radicalism. Further, when political identity was highly salient, uncertainty increased intentions to engage in radicalism. Across studies, most participants favored activism over radicalism; however, the findings suggest that uncertainty can push intentions toward more extreme forms of action, while access to multiple identities may help protect against fixation on a single identity.

articles.title: Remote Digital Cognitive Assessment in a Trial-Ready Alzheimer’s Cohort: A Scalable Approach for Early Intervention Studies
articles.authors: Andrew J. Aschenbrenner; Hannah Wilks; Matthew Welhaf; Samhita Govindan Katteri; Sarah H. Stout; Martin Sliwinski; Tammie Benzinger; Brian A Gordon; Yan Li; Richard J. Perrin
articles.abstract:
Background: Early detection of cognitive decline in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), particularly in preclinical stages, is critical for evaluating therapeutic interventions. Traditional cognitive assessments often lack reliability and require lengthy in-person visits, limiting scalability for younger, trial-ready populations.
Objectives: To evaluate the feasibility, reliability, and validity of high-frequency remote digital cognitive assessments in individuals with autosomal dominant Alzheimer’s disease (ADAD).
Participants: 162 mutation carriers and non-carriers from DIAN-TU from 20 international sites (Ages 19-69 years).
Measurements: Participants completed remote assessments via personal smartphones, prompted four times daily for seven days (approximately 3 minutes per session), and conventional in-clinic cognitive testing at baseline. Adherence, test–retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficients [ICCs]), construct validity (confirmatory factor analysis), and sensitivity to clinical impairment were evaluated.
Results: Average adherence was 41%. Despite this, remote measures demonstrated excellent reliability (ICCs > 0.90 after 10 sessions) and strong construct validity, with tasks loading onto memory, attention, and executive function domains. Model fit was poorer in symptomatic individuals (CDR > 0), consistent with cognitive dedifferentiation during disease progression. Both remote and traditional composites were sensitive to clinical impairment, with similar effect sizes and increasing group differences near expected symptom onset.
Conclusions: High-frequency remote cognitive assessment is feasible, reliable, and valid in a relatively young international ADAD cohort. This approach offers substantial advantages for clinical trials, including reduced participant burden, improved accessibility, and enhanced reliability, supporting its integration into early-intervention studies.

articles.title: A questionnaire survey on context-dependent requirements for the trustworthiness of artificial intelligence and humans
articles.authors: Satoshi Nishida
articles.abstract: Trustworthiness has become an important focus of artificial intelligence (AI) research. Although trustworthiness is a multifaceted concept and its requirements may depend on the context in which AI is used, little is known about how the public perceives these requirements. To address this issue, we conducted a questionnaire survey with nonexpert participants to examine the requirements that the public considers important for trustworthy AI and how their perceived value differs between social and nonsocial contexts. We further compared these context-dependent patterns with those observed for human trustworthiness. Our findings showed that, across social and nonsocial contexts, confidentiality and privacy protection were among the most important requirements for AI trustworthiness whereas the relative importance of other requirements depended on the context. In nonsocial contexts, transparency and interpretability of decision-making were particularly important whereas in social contexts, the ability to collaborate and communicate and a positive public image and attractive appearance were predominantly significant. Although similar context-dependent patterns were observed for human trustworthiness, findings consistently highlighted the ability to collaborate and communicate as a requirement for trusting humans, regardless of context, in contrast to AI trustworthiness. These findings provide insights into the public’s perception of trustworthy AI and highlight the importance of considering the context in which AI is used when examining AI trustworthiness requirements.

articles.title: New Ecological Paradigm Scale Revised (NEPS- R): Evidence for a Two-Factor Structure and Measurement Invariance
articles.authors: Marília Montenegro; Filipa Nunes; Ana Rodrigues de Lemos; Joana Cadima; Paula Mena Matos; Tiago Ferreira
articles.abstract: The New Ecological Paradigm Scale-Revised (NEPS-R) is among the most widely used measures of ecological worldview, yet there’s a lack of consensus on its factorial structure, and evidence on its measurement invariance across gender, particularly within parental dyads, is scarce. This study examined the psychometric properties of the NEPS-R in a sample of 255 mothers and 219 fathers of preschool-aged children in Portugal. Confirmatory factor analysis compared the original unidimensional structure, the theoretical five-factor model, and a two-factor Ecocentrism-Anthropocentrism structure. A refined 10-item two-factor solution provided the best fit for both mothers and fathers, outperforming the unidimensional and five-factor alternatives. This model demonstrated full configural, metric, scalar, and strict invariance across parental gender, indicating that mothers and fathers interpret and respond to the NEPS-R items equivalently. These findings support a bidimensional conceptualization of ecological worldviews and provide novel evidence of measurement invariance for the NEPS-R using dyadic parental data. This study provides a psychometrically robust and gender-invariant instrument capable of comparing mothers' and fathers' ecological worldviews within the same family, with implications for research on intergenerational transmission of pro-environmental values and for family-based environmental interventions.

articles.title: Grounding meaning in social and emotional experience: Challenges and opportunities
articles.authors: Pablo Solana
articles.abstract: Within the broader debate on how the mind and brain represent meaning, multiple representation theories have positioned social and emotional experience, along with their underlying neural systems, as key sources for concept grounding. In this article, I review the current evidence for this proposal and discuss several conceptual and methodological challenges, including the limited capacity of behavioral evidence to support this view, the difficulties associated with interpreting neuroimaging findings, the need for stronger causal evidence, and the importance of adopting open science practices. I argue that these limitations converge on a common concern: in their current form, many findings taken to support multiple representation theories of socio-affective grounding do not provide sufficiently diagnostic evidence to empirically adjudicate between them and competing accounts of semantic representation. In response, I outline a set of methodological recommendations and underexplored ideas that may help refine the theoretical framework, generate more decisive tests, and guide future research.

articles.title: Investigating which type of maltreatment has the largest impact on health:  The challenge of measurement error
articles.authors: Milan Zarchev; Henning Tiemeier
articles.abstract: To answer the question of which type of maltreatment has the largest impact on health outcomes, researchers often simultaneously enter multiple maltreatment predictors in a single regression model. However, this approach of mutual adjustment is problematic, as some maltreatment types (e.g. physical neglect) are often measured with more error than others (e.g. physical abuse). Greater measurement error attenuates effect sizes and reduces statistical power to detect associations, implicitly creating the appearance that better measured maltreatment types are more impactful. The attenuation is particularly severe in mutually adjusted models, as maltreatment types tend to correlate with each other. Researchers comparing maltreatment types should routinely report on reliability estimates such as McDonald’s omega and present separately-estimated associations next to the mutually adjusted model.

articles.title: Relationship Microcultures Theory
articles.authors: Maya Rossignac-Milon; Emma S Miller; Lydia Emery; Joshua Conrad Jackson; Eli Finkel
articles.abstract: Just as groups of people form large-scale macro-cultures, close relationship partners construct their own microculture. Dyads invent their own language (the word “muddles” for homemade ceramics), stories (rescuing their cat), rituals (weekly backgammon), morality (conflicts require mutual apologies), identity (activists), and sense of reality (belief in UFOs). We contend that the emergence, development, and maintenance of this co-created microculture predicts key relational and personal outcomes. We introduce Relationship Microcultures Theory (RMT), which complements prevailing relationship theories by examining how particular words and behaviors are interpreted within the history of the specific relationship in which they acquired idiosyncratic meaning, shaping in turn the well-being of the relationship and the individuals involved. In our Microcultural Unit Model, we describe a meta-theory for understanding how particular dyadic interactions become microcultural units (e.g., inside jokes) by acquiring mutual, idiosyncratic, and referential meaning. In our Aggregate Microculture Model, we advance a theory of how more extensive microcultures—those comprising more units, used more frequently, and spanning more life domains—contribute to relational outcomes (e.g., relationship satisfaction and longevity) and personal outcomes (e.g., meaning in life and self-regulatory success). We also theorize that microcultural extensiveness can undermine relational and personal outcomes when mutuality, idiosyncrasy, and referentiality are low. By examining the dyad as a culture in miniature, RMT opens novel research directions for relationship science.

articles.title: Quantifying the relative associations of time of social media use and addictive social media use with emotional distress among U.S. adults
articles.authors: Hyosin Kim; Jakub Helvich; Giselle Lee; Brian Primack
articles.abstract: Both time of social media use (TSMU) and addictive social media use (ASMU) have been associated with depression and anxiety. However, their relative associations with emotional distress remain unclear, and research involving middle-aged and older adults has been limited. We examined associations of TSMU and ASMU with depression and anxiety in a probability-based nationally-representative sample of 1512 U.S. adults aged 30–70 years. Depression and anxiety were measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7, respectively. TSMU and ASMU, assessed using the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale, were both operationalized in quartiles to facilitate direct comparison. In separate weighted logistic regression models, both TSMU and ASMU were associated with depression and anxiety. However, when TSMU and ASMU were included in the same models, associations between TSMU and both depression and anxiety became non-significant, whereas associations between ASMU and both outcomes remained strong (p<0.001 for both). Compared with participants in the lowest quartile of ASMU, those in the highest quartile had between 4 and 5 times the odds for depression (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 4.94; 95% confidence interval [CI], 3.20–7.62), and anxiety (AOR, 4.59; 95% CI, 2.76–7.63), even after adjusting for TSMU. These findings suggest that ASMU may be more strongly associated with depression and anxiety than overall amount of social media use among U.S. adults.

articles.title: Daring to leave the laboratory: Why operational neuroscience requires a different research strategy
articles.authors: Jerome I. Rotgans
articles.abstract: In this opinion paper, we highlight why taking neuroscience into complex operational environments requires a different analytical logic from that used in controlled experiments. Laboratory paradigms are powerful because they isolate cognitive processes, repeat conditions and compare averaged responses. Operational work removes much of that control. A critical event may occur only once, several cognitive processes may unfold together, and the meaning of a neural response depends on what the individual or team was doing at that moment. We describe a pragmatic approach developed through our neuroergonomics work. We transform continuous haemodynamic signals into discrete ROI-specific activation events, producing an event-by-ROI activation matrix (Spearfish code). These events are then linked to synchronized video and operational data and compared with expert or desired-performance benchmarks. This approach does not recreate laboratory causality in the field. It provides a structured way to identify when and where potentially meaningful activation occurs and to interpret it against performance and context. We discuss its use for training, cognitive-load mapping, human-centred automation and team workload allocation, while making explicit the limits of the resulting inference.

articles.title: Accounts Balanced: The Contingent Role of Rhetoric in Who Survives Political Scandal
articles.authors: Pierce D. Ekstrom; Marti Hope Gonzales; Allison Williams; Elliot Weiner; Rafael Aguilera
articles.abstract: When accused of misconduct in their private or public lives, people choose whether to apologize or to defend their character or reputation. Previous experiments have found that when misconduct is severe or offends outgroup members, transgressors may benefit by defending themselves and denying culpability for wrongdoing. In this study, we explore whether these tendencies can successfully reduce politicians’ accountability for wrongdoing in the context of a U.S. congressional election. We constructed a novel dataset documenting Representatives’ public remarks in response the 1992 House Bank Scandal, during which Representatives from both major parties were accused of misusing funds. Contrary to predictions, conciliatory remarks were not associated with electoral failure among more severe House Bank “offenders.” Consistent with predictions, defensive remarks (refusals) lost their typical association with electoral failure when the incumbent’s party controlled the district. Results suggest that groups may allow their leaders to escape blame for wrongdoing and retain power.

articles.title: Trial After Trial: Temporal Dynamics Reveal a Distinct Computational Phenotype of Chronic Cannabis Use
articles.authors: Samuel Poelker-Wells; Kendra Leigh Seaman; Galston Kok Yi Wong; Francesca Filbey
articles.abstract:
Background: Studies of effort-based decision-making (EBDM) related to chronic cannabis use have yielded inconsistent findings. This variability may reflect the limited ability of behavioral measures alone to distinguish the mechanisms driving observed choices. Computational modeling can help these discrepancies by isolating alterations in valuation, evidence-accumulation, and temporal processes.
Methods: Forty-one individuals who chronically use cannabis (CU) and 45 individuals who do not (NU) completed the Effort Expenditure for Rewards Task (EEfRT).  Drift diffusion, subjective value, and temporal dynamics models were used to characterize latent decision processes of effortful choice. Model-derived parameters were compared between groups and examined in relation to cannabis-use characteristics.
Results: Greater effort allocation via hard-option choice in CU was characterized by less baseline effort avoidance during evidence accumulation and a weaker starting bias toward the easy option, implicating multiple decisional processes. They also showed lower between-participant variability in starting bias and, less definitively, decision caution. Subjective value modeling showed that both groups used similar decision strategies. Incorporating trial progression improved modeling and indicated that greater sustained hard-option choice in CU was related to weaker temporal decline in evidence accumulation and subjective value. Cannabis use characteristics showed no significant associations with latent parameters.
Conclusions:  Adults who use cannabis showed lower effort avoidance both at baseline and during evidence accumulation, greater homogeneity in selected decision processes, and attenuated decline in hard-option valuation. These findings suggest that cannabis-related differences in physical EBDM reflect altered evidence accumulation and temporal stability rather than broad differences in integration of reward, probability, and effort.

articles.title: A Brief Need-Supportive Manipulation and Subsequent Task Performance: A Randomized Experiment
articles.authors: Chen Erez; Leo Wolmer
articles.abstract: Within self-determination theory, basic psychological need theory proposes that social environments supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness foster autonomous motivation, engagement, well-being, and effective functioning. Yet experimental evidence that a brief need-supportive context affects subsequent behavioral performance remains limited. In a randomized experiment, psychology undergraduates (N = 121) completed two trials of a timed word-generation task used as a behavioral performance proxy. Between trials, they received an experimenter-delivered multicomponent scripted manipulation intended to support or thwart these needs or a neutral interaction, followed by a stress induction manipulation. In an analysis of covariance with HC3 standard errors, condition predicted Trial 2 performance after adjustment for Trial 1. Participants assigned to the need-supportive condition scored higher than those in the neutral control. The thwarting-control estimate was small and imprecise. A brief need-supportive context may therefore carry over to performance on a subsequent task, conditional on initial performance. Because the manipulation also varied feedback, expectancy, warmth, and contact, the finding is preliminary and does not isolate need support as the operative mechanism.

articles.title: Young Children Engage in Choice-Relative Moral Reasoning
articles.authors: Talia Waltzer; Gail D. Heyman; Alan Leslie; Sydney Levine
articles.abstract: A central challenge in moral reasoning is evaluating actions not only by their outcomes, but also by the alternatives that were available at the time of choice. The present study examined whether preschool-age children engage in this form of choice-relative moral reasoning. Using a child-friendly version of the trolley problem, 3- to 5-year-old children (N = 124, 51% girls) judged a protagonist who moved a barrier to protect three children’s cookies from being eaten by a mean squirrel. Children typically judged this action as morally good when no better alternative was available, even when it caused harm to another child. However, they judged the same action as morally bad when a non-harmful alternative was available but not chosen. These findings suggest that preschool-age children evaluate actions in light of available alternatives rather than solely on the basis of outcomes. Thus, even young children appear to consider what else could have been done when making moral judgments.

articles.title: Learning Whether Work Can Still Move: Repairability Cues, Hope, and Organizational  Demoralization
articles.authors: Robin Umbra
articles.abstract:
Employees often remain in work states that are blocked, harmful, stagnant, damaged, or 
otherwise unwanted: chronic workload strain, stalled career progression, ignored voice, 
unresolved conflict, failed change initiatives, or damaged relationships. In these situations, 
employees are not only appraising whether work is unpleasant, stressful, or controllable; they are 
also learning whether the state can still move. Building on cue–appraisal learning, this article 
develops repairability cue meaning as a movement-specific form of conditioned appraisal 
meaning that explains how recurring organizational cues come to signal whether unwanted work 
states remain meaningfully movable. Repairability cue meaning captures whether a recurring 
organizational cue has come to signal movement, stagnation, increasing changeability, or closure 
in relation to a particular unwanted work state. The theory’s central contribution is to show that 
employees do not need full repair to regain hope; they need credible evidence that a blocked state 
is becoming more movable. When recurring cues instead teach that movement has disappeared, 
workplace sadness and organizational demoralization become more likely. Organizational 
demoralization is defined as a learned affective-motivational occupational state centered on 
perceived lost movement. The theory explains why renewed engagement can remain viable 
before full repair, and why withdrawal, silence, redirection, or exit may become understandable 
when movement disappears.

articles.title: The Youth-GEMs project: genetic and environmental interactions underlying trajectories of youth mental health
articles.authors: Bart P. F. Rutten; Sinan Guloksuz; Bochao Lin; Covadonga M. Díaz-Caneja; Ian Kelleher; Elisabeth Binder; Jonathan Mill; ESMERALDA RUIZ; Karim Lekadir; Maria Bulgheroni
articles.abstract: Most mental disorders emerge before age 24, yet the mechanisms shaping youth mental health trajectories remain poorly understood. Here, we present the Youth-GEMs consortium performing a multidisciplinary, multisite research project funded by a European Union Horizon-Staying-Healthy-2021 grant. The Youth-GEMs project (Gene Environment interactions in Mental health trajectorieS of Youth) has an integrated, developmental framework that examines how genetic, epigenetic, and environmental factors dynamically interact to influence risk and resilience across adolescence and young adulthood. The project combines developmental (epi)genomic mapping of the human brain, genomic analyses of trans-syndromal phenotypes, exposome-wide environmental assessment, and Artificial Intelligence-based modelling to identify predictive and actionable markers of mental health trajectories of young people. By harmonizing multimodal data from existing population-based cohorts and by establishing the first international, trans-syndromal clinical cohort of help-seeking young people, Youth-GEMs is generating biologically informed polygenic and exposomic scores, cell-type-specific regulatory annotations, and interpretable machine-learning models. Continuous engagement with young people, clinicians, and stakeholders ensures that findings translate into tools for early detection, monitoring, and personalized intervention. Together, these efforts aim to advance mechanistic understandings of youth mental health, improve prediction of emerging illness, and support the development of evidence-based, developmentally sensitive approaches to prevention and care.

articles.title: The Architecture of Academic Safety: Supervisory Communication, the Impostor Phenomenon, and Doctoral Psychological Well-Being—A Mixed-Methods Study"
articles.authors: Varsha singh; Rajnesh meena; Saloni vishwakarma
articles.abstract:
NOTICE: This manuscript is currently under peer review at a journal. This version is the Author's Original Manuscript (AOM) and has not yet undergone formal peer review.

The doctoral journey increases risks for poor psychological well-being and the impostor phenomenon. This mixed-methods study examined how supervisor communication style influences these experiences among PhD scholars. Quantitative data were gathered via an online survey from 90 scholars, alongside qualitative interview data from 20 participants. Quantitative results indicated that scholars generally perceived their supervisors’ communication positively (M = 3.78, SD = 0.42), reported moderate levels of the impostor phenomenon (M = 2.42, SD = 0.99), and demonstrated relatively high psychological well-being (M = 4.26, SD = 0.70). Supervisor communication style was not significantly related to the impostor phenomenon (r = .074, p = .484) but showed a significant positive relationship with psychological well-being (r = .206, p = .049; R² = .043). The impostor phenomenon was negatively, but not significantly, related to well-being (r = -.196, p = .061). Crucially, however, qualitative findings explained this disconnect by revealing that specific, nuanced communication types heavily dictate these experiences. Qualitative findings revealed that instructive clarity, affective support, autonomy, scholarly inclusion, academic recognition, and constructive feedback characterized positive communication, whereas structural ambiguity, inconsistent feedback, intellectual exclusion, systematic invalidation and controlling behaviours induced stress and experienced high imposter phenomenon

articles.title: Navigating consumer uncertainty: Curiosity and individual differences in exploratory consumer behavior
articles.authors: Collin Kather; David M. Lydon-Staley
articles.abstract: Consumers differ not only in whether they explore marketplaces, but also in how they explore them. We examined whether multidimensional curiosity helps explain two forms of exploratory consumer behavior: exploratory acquisition of products and exploratory information seeking. Across two independent samples of adults (Study 1, N=461; Study 2, N=337), participants completed measures of six curiosity dimensions and exploratory consumer behavior. Stress tolerance was uniquely associated with greater exploratory acquisition in both studies after accounting for the other curiosity dimensions. Covert social curiosity was uniquely associated with greater exploratory information seeking in both studies. Associations between thrill seeking and acquisition and between overt social curiosity and information seeking emerged in Study 1 but did not replicate in Study 2. Joyous exploration and deprivation sensitivity showed bivariate associations with exploratory behavior but did not explain unique variance consistently. These findings indicate that a multidimensional curiosity framework provides a more differentiated account of the psychological heterogeneity underlying how consumers navigate uncertain marketplaces.

articles.title: Context-specific adaptation of cognitive processing in changing virtual environments
articles.authors: Ulrike Senftleben; Daniel Zeidler; Stefan Scherbaum; Matthew McGinity; Caroline Surrey
articles.abstract: Human cognition is sensitive to context cues, as indicated by the context-specific proportion congruency (CSPC) effect. This effect demonstrates that individuals implicitly adapt their cognitive processing to contextual cues that predict the likelihood of conflict. However, CSPC paradigms typically rely on simple, two-dimensional context cues, raising questions about their validity for complex, real-life environments. In this preregistered study, we examined whether CSPC effects emerge in three-dimensional, naturalistic contexts delivered via virtual reality (VR). We presented a numerical Stroop task in two virtual environments—a forest and an office—alternating on a trial-by-trial basis. Unbeknownst to participants, each environment was paired with either a high (80%; mostly congruent/MC context) or low (20%; mostly incongruent/MI context) proportion of incongruent trials (counter-balanced). Our results show the typical CSPC effect: reduced response time differences between incongruent and congruent trials in the MI environment relative to the MC environment. This finding indicates that context-dependent adjustments of cognitive processing extend to complex, semantically meaningful virtual environments. This supports the ecological validity of CSPC learning and highlights the importance of context cues in real-life cognitive processing. Further, our study highlights how VR opens up new avenues for studying context-dependent cognition beyond conventional laboratory stimuli.

articles.title: Robust Measurement of Habits with the Forced-Response Task A Multiverse Analysis
articles.authors: José Juan León; Pablo Martínez-López; Francisco Garre-Frutos; David Luque
articles.abstract: Instrumental behavior reflects a balance between two systems: an outcome-oriented, goal-directed system and a cognitively efficient habit system that gradually gains control with repeated instrumental responding in stable contexts. While overtraining reliably induces habits in animal models, human participants often retain goal-directed control when their performance is assessed using devaluation paradigms. To address this translational gap, the forced-response method has emerged as a promising approach for studying goal-directed and habitual behavior by constraining the time available to respond. This method imposes a dual task in which participants must respond accurately to an instrumental discriminative stimulus at a specific time signaled by a sound. Because the onset of the discriminative stimulus varies across trials, the time available for response preparation is systematically manipulated. Restricting this time can unmask stimulus-driven responses when the goal-directed system has insufficient time to override them. Although the forced-response method has become increasingly popular, its use has also been accompanied by growing flexibility in data analysis, creating a potential “garden of forking paths.” Using four independent datasets, we generated 48 a priori valid preprocessing pipelines to assess variability in two discrete measures of habitual behavior—the proportion of habits and the habit index—as well as their split-half reliability and the proportion of habits as a continuous function of the available response time, modeled using generalized additive models. Results indicated that both habit measures were generally robust across preprocessing pipelines. The proportion of habits was more sensitive to specific preprocessing choices, particularly accuracy and timing-synchrony exclusion criteria, but also showed greater reliability. In all cases, however, the resulting variability was small. Reliability analyses yielded acceptable estimates in most analytic universes. Overall, these findings support the forced-response method as a robust paradigm for studying habit formation and expression in humans.

articles.title: Personality Differences among Men and Women of Various Sexual Orientations, Including Asexual and Pansexual Individuals
articles.authors: Jakub Fořt; Dominika Benešová; Petr Freudenfeld; Jaroslava Varella Valentova; Jan Havlicek
articles.abstract: Several theoretical approaches explain variance in personality related to sexual orientation. Drawing on the minority stress theory and the gender shift hypothesis, this study explores personality differences across people of various sexual orientations, including underrepresented groups, such as asexual and pansexual individuals. The minority stress theory posits that non-heterosexual individuals experience heightened social stressors, contributing to higher neuroticism. The gender shift hypothesis further suggests that prenatal hormonal influences may lead to sex-atypical development, explaining some personality variation in sexual minorities. Using a large Czech and Slovak sample (N = 6,476), we administered the Big Five Inventory (BFI-10) to heterosexual (N = 2,598), gay/lesbian (N = 1,943), bisexual (N = 1,412), pansexual (N = 389), and asexual (N = 165) cisgender individuals. We found that non-heterosexual men scored higher in neuroticism than heterosexual men, consistent with both the minority stress and gender shift hypotheses. Pansexual and bisexual individuals of either sex were higher in openness to experience than heterosexual individuals, and asexual individuals scored lower in extraversion than same-sex individuals of any other sexual orientation. We recorded mixed results for conscientiousness. No differences were found in levels of agreeableness. Effect sizes of the recorded differences are, except for few, generally small.

articles.title: Made in the Image of the Creator? AI Use in Creative Work Reduces Authenticity, Love and Other Psychological Benefits
articles.authors: Jessica Carson; Paul H.P. Hanel; Wijnand A. P. van Tilburg
articles.abstract: Across psychological, philosophical, and theological traditions, creations have been understood as being “made in the image of their creator”—they reflect the person who made them. The rise of generative artificial intelligence, however, has blurred the throughline between creator and creation. Across three experiments (one pre-registered, U.S. and U.K. samples; N = 651), we examined differences in creator outcomes associated with AI-assisted versus human-only creative work. Compared with human-only work, AI-assisted work was associated with significantly lower self- and identity-relevant indicators, including authenticity, self-creation connection, positive affect, and intrinsic motivation, and with higher levels of the “existential ick” emotions of disgust, guilt, and shame. Additionally, we found that the authenticity gap was statistically mediated by the creators’ perception that their AI-assisted work contains less of their love, above and beyond differences in perceived effort, uniqueness, quality, and expensiveness. We also ruled out effort justification as an alternative explanation. Together, these findings suggest that AI reshapes not only how creative work is produced, but also the extent to which creators experience their work as an authentic expression and extension of themselves.

articles.title: Selflessness, Self-Centeredness, and Mental Health Dynamics in Daily Life
articles.authors: Lucas David; Michaël Dambrun
articles.abstract: Experiences of selflessness and happiness are interconnected in everyday life. Both between-person and within-person variations in selflessness are associated with higher and more stable happiness. However, little is known about the role of selflessness in shaping negative mental health at the experiential level. Moreover, self-centeredness, the second regulatory process proposed by the Self-centeredness/Selflessness Happiness Model (SSHM), has received little empirical attention. This experience sampling study addresses these gaps by examining the dynamic effects of selflessness and self-centeredness, between and within individuals. These effects were assessed on positive and negative mental health, as well as on relationship quality with others and nature. Results reveal distinct yet complementary roles for selflessness and self-centeredness: selflessness fosters and stabilizes mental health, self-centeredness undermines it and introduces greater variability. These findings offer insights into the psychological mechanisms underlying complete mental health and illuminate how these processes shape our connection with the social and natural environment.

articles.title: Differential Effects of Self-centeredness and Selflessness: A Six-Month Longitudinal Study Across Mental, Relational, and Ecological Domains
articles.authors: Lucas David; Michaël Dambrun
articles.abstract: The Self-centeredness/Selflessness Happiness Model (SSHM) posits two complementary modes of self-based psychological functioning, selflessness and self-centeredness, relevant across multiple subfields of psychology. Shaped by developmental, social and cultural influences, selflessness and self-centeredness differentially forecast multiple variables from individual mental health to ecological concerns and behaviors. Addressing the largely correlational nature of prior evidence on the model, we conducted a two-wave longitudinal study over six months (N = 316) to test the middle-term prospective effects of selflessness and self-centeredness on mental health, relationship quality, and ecological orientation. Controlling for autoregressive stability and within-wave covariation, cross-lagged panel models indicated that selflessness prospectively predicted higher positive mental health and lower negative mental health and ecoanxiety. By contrast, self-centeredness predicted lower positive mental health, relationship quality and relationship with nature, and higher negative mental health. Additional findings revealed the mutual inhibition between the two dispositions. These findings extend cross-sectional research on the SSHM by demonstrating medium-term prospective associations and by positioning selflessness and self-centeredness as transdisciplinary predictors of holistic forms of health spanning intrapersonal, interpersonal, and ecological domains.

articles.title: Semantic Interference in Blocked-Cyclic Word Production with Different Stimulus Types, Tasks, and Response Modalities
articles.authors: Stefan Wöhner; Andreas Widmann; Sophia Forchner; Erich Schröger; Jörg D. Jescheniak
articles.abstract: Theories of word production rely heavily on semantic context effects. For example, when pictures are named repeatedly and sorted by semantic category, it takes longer to name them than when they are named in an intermixed manner. Wöhner et al. (2021) found that semantic interference in blocked-cyclic naming was approximately three times greater for sounds (e.g., barking) than for pictures (e.g., a dog). This study explored possible reasons for this differential interference pattern. When the stimuli were presented briefly, the differential interference was replicated, ruling out the possibility that it results from a large overlap between stimulus processing and phonological response preparation. When the sounds and pictures were replaced with spoken and written words that the participants translated into their second language, the size of the interference was similar, showing that the differential pattern does not result from different stimulus modalities (auditory vs. visual). When participants typed their responses, the differential interference was replicated again, showing that it does not depend on a certain response modality (spoken vs. written). Additionally, pupil dilation data suggest that sounds, compared with pictures, may activate additional representations that contribute to the interference. Overall, the data imply that semantic interference in word production is shaped by early, stimulus-specific, perceptual and semantic “lead-in” processes that precede lexical selection. More attention should be given to these early processes in word production research.

articles.title: Evaluating biomarkers and prediction models: predictive utility analysis with E2P Simulator
articles.authors: Povilas Karvelis; Daniel Felsky; Anissa Abi-Dargham; Guillermo Horga; Andreea Andreea
articles.abstract: Precision psychiatry aims to identify biomarkers and develop prediction models to improve diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment selection. Despite extensive research, translating findings into clinically useful tools remains challenging. Here we argue that one important contributor to this translational gap is a pervasive misalignment between routine statistical analytic practices and the requirements for real-world decision making. To help address this, we introduce predictive utility analysis: a statistical workflow for estimating the practical significance of biomarkers and prediction models by accounting for outcome base rates and measurement reliability. Starting from effect size or model performance estimates, the workflow simulates expected real-world performance in a target population and summarizes it across complementary metrics including positive and negative predictive value, Precision-Recall AUC, and Net Benefit. Analogous to how power analysis is used for determining the conditions needed to achieve statistical significance, predictive utility analysis can help determine the conditions needed to achieve practical significance. We implement and illustrate this workflow using E2P Simulator, a recently developed open-source web tool that makes predictive utility analysis accessible through interactive simulations and publication-ready visualizations. We demonstrate its application using specific examples in three key areas: diagnostic (depression, Alzheimer’s disease), treatment response (antidepressants), and risk (suicide attempts and psychosis onset) prediction, highlighting conditions under which we may expect clinically meaningful advances. While we focus on translational challenges in psychiatry, the workflow and tools presented here address general statistical challenges and are broadly applicable across biomedical and behavioral sciences.

articles.title: Artificial Neutrality: Bias and Omission in Large Language Models’ Descriptions of Urban Wildlife
articles.authors: Sam Gowland; Lauren Scott; djt.vanderlinden@gmail.com; Shaun Lawson
articles.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly prominent AI applications, but they remain vulnerable to bias rooted in their training data. Such bias matters in the context of animals, since LLM outputs can influence human attitudes and behaviours toward wildlife. To explore this, we conducted a word association experiment with human participants (N = 300) and with three LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini). Each was asked to provide five keywords for species commonly viewed positively (hedgehogs), negatively (rats), and with mixed attitudes (foxes). Sentiment analysis showed that humans exhibited greater variability, generally reflecting expected
attitudes toward each species. LLMs, by contrast, did not reproduce these distributions. Their responses leaned toward neutral or ecological terms rather than emotive words, diverging from typical human conceptualisations.
Our findings suggest that while LLMs may reduce bias through neutralisation, they risk introducing new distortions, underscoring the need for careful, balanced application in wildlife-related contexts.

articles.title: Heritability is not destiny
articles.authors: Emma Meaburn; Mahitab Elgamal; Qidong Song; Michael Thomas
articles.abstract:
High heritability estimates for behavioural traits such as cognitive ability and educational attainment are often misinterpreted as showing these traits are resistant to environmental intervention. However, heritability describes sources of variation within a population, not how outcomes would change under alternative environments - the counterfactual relevant to education policy.

We illustrate this using a computational model of English past-tense acquisition, an established model of experience-dependent cognitive development. In an artificial neural network, simulated genetic influences were implemented through a polygenic architecture affecting neurocomputational parameters, while environmental variation reflected differences in the richness of linguistic input. By varying these influences, we generated populations with low or high trait heritability and compared their responses to (a) behavioural interventions and (b) improvements in environmental quality.

Population intervention effects depended on how strongly adverse environments had constrained prior development, rather than heritability. Gene x environment interactions were small and only appeared in high heritability populations – environments worked similarly for all genotypes. Improving environmental quality across cohorts benefited populations similarly regardless of trait heritability. To test an exemplar policy counterfactual, interventions were targeted to reduce achievement gaps: prior performance was more effective for targeting intervention than environmental disadvantage or polygenic scores.

These findings support the view that heritability is not destiny. Because cognitive development is plastic and experience-dependent, environmental change can improve outcomes across genotypes. The policy relevance of genetics lies not in predicting immutable outcomes, but in identifying where intervention can be most effective. Genetics is not about destiny, it is about opportunity.

articles.title: Uptake, Barriers, and Facilitators of Open Science in Clinical Psychology: Findings from an Exploratory Survey in German-speaking Countries
articles.authors: Anja Christine Feneberg; Jakob Fink-Lamotte; Helen Niemeyer
articles.abstract: Open Science practices (OSP) aim to enhance transparency, reproducibility, and research quality, yet empirical research regarding their uptake in clinical psychology remains scarce. The present survey examined OSP across clinical psychological research, teaching, and psychotherapeutic practice at universities and university clinics in German-speaking countries. Based on responses from 130 participants (M=37.13 ± 9.75 years of age, 61.54% female) preregistration, a-priori sample size planning, and open access publishing were the most commonly reported OSP. Concerns regarding data protection and ethics, time constraints, and fear of mistakes were the most prominent barriers, while access to infrastructure and incentives were the most needed types of support. Teaching activities addressed Open Science topics, whereas implementation in clinical practice remained limited. Overall, the findings highlight the need for field-specific guidelines, institutional support, and aligned incentive structures to foster sustainable adoption of OSP across career-stages and contexts.

articles.title: Introspection and Difficulties in Documenting Subjective Experiences of Meditation
articles.authors: Ndabenhle Siphesihle Mthembu
articles.abstract: Introspective research into subjective experiences of meditation is constrained by an inability to document meditative experiences in a manner that addresses their irreducible qualities. Meditators' integration attempts are negatively affected due to this methodological gap. Thus, more responsive documentation methods need to be developed within introspective research. This paper theorizes that documentation failure in introspective research stems from a fundamental linguistic flaw embedded in how pre-linguistic felt-significance relates to downstream documentation methods. During a subjective meditative event, an experience possesses felt-meaning, defined as the direct perception of a quantity of meaning within the event itself. This felt-meaning is pre-linguistic and serves as the raw material out of which expressed meaning—the formal linguistic description—is constructed. The primary cause of documentation difficulty arises when pre-linguistic events are perceived to be devoid of felt-significance. When an experience presents no identifiable pattern from which to construct a linguistic description, generating expressed meaning becomes increasingly difficult, exposing a hard limit of language itself.

articles.title: To whom should punishment communicate? Children's and adults' perceptions of punishment's message
articles.authors: Young-eun Lee; Sophie Noëlle Charles; Larisa Heiphetz
articles.abstract: Why do people punish? Legal and political theories describing punishment as expressive argue that one of punishment's functions is to communicate information (e.g., which behaviors are unacceptable). While this work emphasizes communicating to transgressors, punishment may also show victims that others take their pain seriously. In two studies, we asked how laypeople perceive the communicative nature of punishment. Study 1 found that adults (n=156), but not 4- to 7-year-old children (n=84), evaluated communicating punishment to transgressors more positively than communicating it to victims. Study 2 (n=188 adults and n=87 children) revealed that adults also evaluated communicating the reason underlying punishment to transgressors more positively than communicating it to victims, whereas 5- to 7-year-old children showed a more balanced evaluation of the two targets. Indeed, children provided more favorable evaluations than did adults of scenarios that did not include transgressors as targets of punishment's message. Together, these findings suggest that adults, but not children, consistently prioritize informing transgressors over informing victims, potentially contributing to social responses to wrongdoing that place insufficient emphasis on victims’ informational and emotional needs.

articles.title: Formal Properties of Spontaneous Figure Drawings are Associated with Contemporaneous Affective State
articles.authors: Jake Hooper; Jennifer Mitlehner; Margaret E. Sereno
articles.abstract: Does the way a person draws reveal how they feel? Expressionist theory proposes that affect leaves traces in the formal properties of art, yet existing evidence relies largely on exceptional artists or on drawings created to depict a specified emotion. Adult participants completed a spontaneous figure drawing and reported their current affective state. Each drawing was quantified using two complementary approaches: (1) rater-coded formal elements and (2) computational image statistics. The resulting set of 40 drawing features was reduced to 9 interpretable components. Controlling for drawing time and artistic skill, these drawing components explained meaningful variance in affect, with the strongest and most robust associations emerging for negative affect. Critically, human ratings and computational image features each captured unique information not accounted for by the other, and these effects were observed in ordinary, untrained participants who were never instructed to communicate emotion. Spontaneous figure drawings thus appear to contain recoverable signatures of contemporaneous affective state embedded in their formal structure, independent of artistic skill. These findings position everyday drawing as an accessible, information-rich, and compact behavioral window into affect and provide a reproducible framework for quantifying how emotion is externalized in visual form.

articles.title: Usage of Digital Technology and Its linkage with the Development of Life Skills, Mental Health, and Psychological Hardiness among university students
articles.authors: Kadim Lovakumari; Tosendra Dwivedi
articles.abstract:
Background: The pervasive use of digital technology among Indian university students has raised concerns about its implications for life skills, mental health, and psychological hardiness. While moderate use may enhance learning, excessive use is associated with adverse psychological outcomes.
Objective: This study examines (a) prevalence of digital technology usage, (b) differences in life skills, mental health, and psychological hardiness across levels of digital technology usage, and (c) interlinkages among these variables.
Methods: The study adopted a two-phase design. In Phase-1, a Self-constructed Digital Technology Usage Scale was developed and standardized on 1,000 university students from Delhi-NCR. In Phase-2, data were collected from an independent sample of 600 postgraduate university students (300 professional, 300 non-professional) from government and private universities in Delhi, using stratified random sampling (Gender x Stream x University Type). Tools used: (1) Life Skills Assessment Scale (Nair et al., 2010), (2) Mental Health Inventory (Jagdish & Srivastava, 1983), and (3) Psychological Hardiness Scale (Singh, 2008).Analysis: Descriptive statistics, independent-samples t-tests, Pearson correlation, One-way ANOVA, and Multiple Regression were performed using SPSS v26.
Results: Moderate users (2-5 hrs/day) showed significantly higher life skills (M=198.60), mental health (M=158.2) and psychological hardiness (M=105.80) compared to low (<2 hrs) and high (>5 hrs) users (F=8.73 to 10.21, p<.01). Mental health (β=.38) and hardiness (β=.32) significantly predicted life skills.
Keywords: Digital Technology Usage, Life Skills, Mental Health, Psychological Hardiness, University Students

articles_hidden.title: Assessing Parent and Youth Perceptions of Attachment:  Validation of the Adolescent Attachment Anxiety and Avoidance Inventory (AAAAI)
articles_hidden.authors: Jason W. Payne; Sebastian Dys; Sherene Balanji; Marlene Moretti
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Attachment is a robust protective factor for youth mental health. This study examined the factor structure and validity of the Adolescent Attachment Anxiety and Avoidance Inventory (AAAAI), a 16-item measure of youth (8–18 years) attachment in parent and other caregiving relationships. Structural validity was assessed using parallel youth and parent report formats among over 2,000 respondents from both clinical and community samples.
Method: Participants were caregivers in three independent clinical samples and one community sample (N = 571, 407, 220, and 551) and youth self-reporting in the first clinical sample (N = 571). Youth were 7.5 to 18 years old (sample means 13.4 to 14.6), 51% to 61% female, and 61% to 78% White. Caregivers were predominantly mothers (80% to 96%). Confirmatory factor analyses were followed by multi- informant models and tests of associations with caregiver-reported internalizing and externalizing problems.
Results: A two-factor structure replicated across all samples under a single specification, whereas a one- factor model fit poorly. Differential associations with youth internalizing and externalizing problems supported the discriminant validity of each subscale. Multi-method analyses confirmed that anxiety and avoidance were distinguishable across informants, while moderate parent-youth convergence suggested complementary rather than interchangeable perspectives.
Conclusions: The findings support the AAAAI as a measure of attachment anxiety and avoidance in both parent and youth report. For research and clinical practice, the two subscales capture distinct attachment patterns, and parent and youth forms together show where caregivers and youth see the relationship similarly and where they differ.

articles_hidden.title: Individual differences in eye movements dynamics of free viewing conscious and unconscious naturalistic scenes
articles_hidden.authors: Shaked Lublinsky; Yoni Pertzov lab; Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg; Liad Mudrik
articles_hidden.abstract: Different individuals produce different gaze patterns while exploring the world. Here we examined whether these differences occur also when viewing a scene unconsciously. We reanalyzed the data collected in Lublinsky et al., 2025, looking for two types of individual differences; content-based individual differences, which depend on the visual stimulus presented, and content-free individual differences, which do not relate to the observed stimuli. In two experiments, 52 participants viewed scenes consciously and unconsciously, rendered invisible via Continuous Flash Suppression (CFS). We found reliable content-based individual differences in the conscious condition only, suggesting that unconscious processing of scenes does not evoke consistent patterns within individuals. On the other hand, we found consistent content-free individual differences in both visibility conditions. In the unconscious condition, these most likely reflect consistent gazing patterns on the CFS stimulation (i.e., the changing color patches). Yet these content-free measures showed differential strength for seen vs. unseen trials, thereby validating participants' subjective reports. These findings provides novel means to support a dissociation between conscious and unconscious processing under CFS, which is notoriously difficult due to methodological challenges.

articles_hidden.title: Baselines Matter: Cardiovascular Baseline Procedures in Affective Psychophysiology
articles_hidden.authors: Maciej Behnke; Wadim Leszek Krzyżaniak; Szymon Jęśko-Białek; Patryk Andrzej Maciejewski; Audrey-Ann Journault; Sylvia D Kreibig; Jeremy Jamieson; James Gross
articles_hidden.abstract: A baseline is necessary to define biological reactivity in psychophysiological research. However, the conceptualization and implementation of baseline measurements are often underdescribed and weakly justified. This poses a problem because poor baseline decisions have the potential to introduce noise, reduce comparability across studies, and bias interpretations of data. In this article, we focus on laboratory studies using cardiovascular measures to examine how baselines are described and used in affective psychophysiology. To describe heterogeneity in baseline procedures, Study 1 reviewed 310 psychophysiological studies and coded baseline activities, durations, analyzed intervals, and theoretical justifications. To examine within-baseline stabilization, Study 2 analyzed the POPANE dataset to assess minute-by-minute changes in cardiovascular activity in 1,010 participants during a standard 5-minute baseline. To test whether these patterns replicated and whether baseline estimates differed across sessions, Study 3 analyzed the CEPAV dataset in 300 participants across two separate laboratory visits. Finally, to assess generalizability across a larger and more heterogeneous sample, Study 4 replicated these analyses using compiled laboratory data from 2,395 participants. Across studies, results indicate that baseline procedures vary considerably, are often insufficiently reported, and may meaningfully impact the interpretation of cardiovascular data. Although different cardiovascular indices may stabilize differently during a 5-minute baseline, findings suggest that this procedure is a reasonable, pragmatic choice and that separate-session baselines should not be assumed to be superior. More broadly, findings highlight the need for stronger justification, standardization, and reporting of baseline procedures in psychophysiological research.

articles_hidden.title: Near-random behavior in strategic games
articles_hidden.authors: Tal Boger; Dorsa Amir; Sami Ryan Yousif
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans struggle to produce random behavior when asked to do so, leading some to suggest that our ability to randomize is attenuated (or even absent). Here, we demonstrate that the capacity for random behavior is much greater than previously acknowledged: Humans can behave in (near) optimally random ways when the context demands it. We created a custom, online version of the game Battleship in which participants competed against one another. On each turn, one player chose a tile on a 3x3 grid to place a ship, while the other player tried to guess the ship’s location. Across six preregistered studies, this strategic context led to dramatic increases in random behavior relative to closely matched non-strategic tasks. Such random behavior was also remarkably flexible and optimal depending on context; both players readily incorporated varying information about the game (e.g., that tiles can differ in value) while simultaneously accounting for their opponents’ knowledge of that information. A computational model validated these findings and revealed nuanced differences across contexts. Contrary to decades of work finding that humans fail to randomize, we find that strategic games promote highly flexible, near-random behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Is it Difficult to be a People Pleaser? An Item Response-Theoretical Examination of the People Pleasing Scale
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Blötner; Johanna Werner
articles_hidden.abstract: The phenomenon of people-pleasing—meaning the tendency to sacrifice one’s own needs and obligations to help others—has gained a lot of interest in lay psychology. Only recently have scientific endeavors been devoted to the development and validation of suitable measurement tools such as the People Pleasing Scale (Blötner, 2026; https://doi.org/10.1007/s12144-026-09519-2). The measure provides desirable psychometric properties from the perspective of Classical Test Theory, but in this framework, several statistical assumptions about item and scale characteristics remain untested. To address this gap, we subjected the People Pleasing Scale to item response-theoretical examinations as per the polytomous graded response model (N = 2,538). Its three subscales (Responsibility, Neglect of Own Needs, and Others’ Expectations) provided favorable item discrimination, widely dispersed item thresholds (even though the thresholds to obtain high scores were located at best at moderate levels), and ample levels of item information and reliability across the three latent trait spectra. These findings underscore that people-pleasing, as measured with the People Pleasing Scale, refers to an everyday rather than a clinical construct. As such, it is apt to be used to assess people-pleasing in studies across diverse areas of academic psychology and for applied contexts alike.

articles_hidden.title: Development and characterization of a standardized stimuli set of 240 famous faces in Quebec
articles_hidden.authors: Nastasia Maria Mitrikeski; Mélodie Leclerc; Zihao Geng; Maxime Montembeault
articles_hidden.abstract:
Famous faces are especially well suited to studying the semantic component of face processing because they carry a sense of familiarity shared across individuals. Recognizing famous faces is not only relevant to research, but it is also clinically informative. Famous-face recognition deficits are observed in prosopagnosia and neurodegenerative disease. They are differentially affected across dementia syndromes, making their assessment useful for differential diagnosis. Testing familiar face processing requires stimuli suited to a specific geographic and sociocultural context, which has led to the development of standardized famous-face databases in France, Great Britain, Spain, and Portugal. However, no such standardized set currently exists for the Quebec population. We therefore created a stimuli set of 240 locally and internationally known famous
people across four categories (politicians, singers, actors, and athletes), spanning different time periods and including famous people of different races, ethnicities, ages, and genders. Through an online survey on Qualtrics, adults aged 40 to 79 from Quebec are rating the famous faces on distinctiveness, familiarity, valence, and name frequency, alongside measures of famous face recognition, naming, knowledge, and agreement. Descriptive statistics were obtained for each famous face, and the standardized stimuli set will be available in open access once data collection is complete. Future directions include the development of new cognitive tests for face processing impairments, notably in neurodegenerative disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Meta-Analytic Evidence for an Ecological Account of the Relationship between Acculturative Stressors and Adaptation
articles_hidden.authors: Dinh-Hung Vu; Kinga Bierwiaczonek; Mike W.-L. Cheung; Rongtian Tong; Jonas R. Kunst; Nora C. G. Benningstad; Evita Willemiek van Duin; Karine Lindholm; Colleen Ward
articles_hidden.abstract: Acculturative stressors, reliably associated with poor migrant adaptation to receiving societies, are highly context-dependent. Yet, how context shapes the stressor-adaptation relationship remains poorly understood. In two pre-registered meta-analyses, we tested the moderating role of structural, cultural, and temporal factors in cross-sectional data (Study 1) and examined the temporal dynamics in longitudinal data (Study 2). Study 1 (k = 229, N = 66,409) modelled origin and receiving country contexts simultaneously to test specific migration routes. Structural factors, such as the receiving country’s poverty, inequality, and unemployment, intensified stressor-adaptation associations. Effects of cultural factors mostly concerned socio-cultural adaptation, most notably stronger stressor-adaptation associations when migrants moved from collectivistic to individualistic societies. For temporal context, longer residence in the receiving country was linked to weaker stressor-adaptation associations. Study 2 (k = 22, N = 8,555) validated the cross-sectional finding that stressor-adaptation associations attenuate over time: effects were stronger and reciprocal at earlier timepoints.

articles_hidden.title: The Modulation of Mood Through Absorption in Music Listening
articles_hidden.authors: Bradley Austin-Keiller; Frank Russo; Karina J Linnell
articles_hidden.abstract: Music listening is widely used to regulate emotion, yet the listener-level processes underlying affective change remain under-specified. This longitudinal study examined musical absorption as one such process, testing a novel Musical Absorption Training (MAT) protocol designed to scaffold absorptive engagement. Adults aged 55 and older (analytic N = 49) completed 16 listening sessions over four weeks. Participants were randomly assigned either to eight sessions of guided MAT followed by eight unguided sessions, or to unguided listening throughout. Valence and arousal were rated before and after each session, state absorption after each session, and trait absorption (AIMS) at baseline, Session 8, and Session 16. Mixed-effects models showed that greater state absorption predicted larger within-session increases in valence and arousal, driven mainly by within-person fluctuations. MAT did not raise state absorption during the guided phase, but after guidance ended, absorption was preserved in the MAT group. Trait absorption increased over time without a significant Group × Time interaction; however, higher state absorption during the maintenance phase predicted higher trait absorption at study end. These findings identify absorption as a promising listener-level correlate of music-related mood change and offer preliminary evidence that structured attentional guidance may help sustain absorptive engagement across repeated listening.

articles_hidden.title: Low-certainty modals not future tenses cause increased psychological discounting
articles_hidden.authors: Cole Robertson; Sean Roberts; Asifa Majid; Tammy Lu; Phillip Wolff; R. I. M. Dunbar
articles_hidden.abstract: Speaking a language that obliges the future tense for linguistic Future Time Reference (FTR) has been hypothesised to cause speakers to perceive delayed outcomes as temporally distal and therefore less valuable (“temporal discounting”). Conversely, we hypothesise that the obligation to use low-certainty modal verbs, e.g. may, causes speakers to construe risky and delayed outcomes as riskier and therefore less valuable (“combined discounting”). We experimentally elicited free-text FTR responses and measured construals of future temporal distance and discounting of (risky) delayed rewards in speakers of Dutch (which does not oblige FTR marking) and English (which does). We used statistical mediation models, which parse out an indirect effect of a predictor on an outcome via a mediating variable, a direct effect of a predictor on an outcome, and a total effect—the other two combined. English speakers construed future events as temporally proximal, which in turn caused less (rather than more) temporal discounting (indirect effect). The direct effect went in the opposite direction, meaning there was no population-level difference in temporal discounting (no total effect, Study 1). When we measured combined discounting, English speakers discounted more (a total effect, Study 2). Further, English speakers used more low-certainty language and this caused increased combined discounting (an indirect effect). Future tense use did not impact construals of temporal distance, meaning future tense use did not mediate an effect on combined discounting (Study 2). We addressed possible cultural confounds by testing Dutch-English bilinguals (Study 3). When bilinguals were tested in English, they used more low-certainty modal verbs, which in turn caused increased combined discounting (an indirect effect). This was moderated by self-reported English proficiency, indicating language, not culture, is responsible for effects. Results suggest effects of FTR grammar are not driven by obligatory future tenses affecting temporal discounting, but by obligatory low-certainty modals affecting combined discounting.

articles_hidden.title: A Revolution in Search of an Estimand: On the Idionomic Proposal of Hayes et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Magnus Johansson; Matti Vuorre; Nils Olof Wilhelm Hentati Isacsson; Kristoffer Magnusson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Hayes et al. (2026) argue that clinical psychology is stalled by an “ergodic error”, the application
of group-level statistics to individuals, and propose idionomic analysis as the remedy. We agree
that pooled associations do not need to describe individuals and that treatment effects vary
between people, but the proposed remedy does not answer the clinical question. Personalizing
treatment is a causal problem, yet Hayes et al. never state which causal quantity, or estimand,
they target. Their evidence consists of observational within-person associations, which cannot
separate effects from confounding that varies over time. Applied to observational data, none of
the recommended methods can identify a causal effect. Non-ergodicity shows only that pooled
and individual associations may differ, not that causal effects do. The reported heterogeneity is
also questionable, in part because person-level estimates from short series are imprecise. The
reliability Hayes et al. cite against this concern describes person means rather than within-
person variation, and the statistics summarizing heterogeneity have not been adequately
checked against simulated data in which there is no heterogeneity. Designs that randomize
treatment within or between persons can target person-level and conditional effects, within
limits set by carryover and irreversible change. Rather than the proposed idionomic revolution,
clinical psychology needs to join the causal revolution, in which the estimand is stated before
the data are analyzed.

articles_hidden.title: Five More Items Matter: Comparing Structural Validity, Response Bias, and Nomological Networks in 10- and 15-Item Big Five Measures Across Nations
articles_hidden.authors: Zhangchu Xu; Yuke Yang; Zhihao Ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Ultra-short Big Five measures are widely used to reduce respondent burden while retaining acceptable measurement quality. Yet when personality domains are represented by only two or three items, it remains unclear whether modestly greater item coverage translates into better measurement performance across cultural contexts. The present study compared the Ten-Item Personality Inventory (TIPI), the 10-item Big Five Inventory (BFI-10), and the 15-item Big Five Inventory-SOEP (BFI-S) across four sources of validity evidence: factor structure, measurement invariance, response bias, and nomological networks, using three large-scale cross-national datasets. Conventional confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) models showed inadequate fit across all three measures and were frequently affected by Heywood cases. Exploratory structural equation modeling (ESEM) analyses indicated that BFI-S showed better recovery of the expected five-factor structure than TIPI and BFI-10, although cross-cultural variability remained. TIPI and BFI-10 were not subjected to measurement invariance testing because their baseline structures did not support meaningful comparisons, while BFI-S demonstrated relatively robust demographic invariance but weaker cross-national invariance. All measures showed directional response bias, with the largest contribution observed in BFI-10 and the smallest in BFI-S. Moreover, greater response bias was associated with larger deviations in personality–criterion associations across countries. Despite limited item coverage, all three measures reproduced theoretically expected nomological associations, with BFI-S showing greater cross-national consistency. Overall, expanding from two to three indicators per Big Five domain was associated with improved structural recovery, reduced response bias, and more consistent external associations. However, this modest increase in item coverage did not eliminate the inherent limitations of ultra-short personality assessment, highlighting the continued importance of considering measurement purpose, context, and cultural applicability.

articles_hidden.title: Do God Primes Prime God? Converging Evidence Against the Efficacy of Experimental Religious Priming
articles_hidden.authors: Will M Gervais; Meara Geraty; Aiyana Koka Willard
articles_hidden.abstract:
How does religion change people? Religious priming has been used to scientifically ask this question for nearly two
decades, linking religious cognition to varied outcomes – especially prosociality. Priming research has proliferated
in the absence of direct evidence that religious priming tools work as implicitly assumed: by activating religious
cognition. Here, we evaluate this assumption. Across a bias-adjusted meta-analysis (k = 66) and two experiments
(total N = 2960), we report strong and converging evidence: 1) against the validity of the most commonly used priming
methodology, 2) against even overt primes’ abilities to robustly affect prosocial cognition or behavior, 3) against a
meaningful relationship between cognitive activation of religion and prosocial behavior; further, evidence was 4) in
favor of even ineffective primes nonetheless inviting participant suspicion. Combined, this suggests that the evidential
strength of existing priming research is likely overstated, with critical assumptions now contradicted by evidence.

articles_hidden.title: Is it Difficult to be a People Pleaser? An Item Response-Theoretical Examination of the People Pleasing Scale
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Blötner; Johanna Werner
articles_hidden.abstract: The phenomenon of people-pleasing—meaning the tendency to sacrifice one’s own needs and obligations to help others—has gained a lot of interest in lay psychology. Only recently have scientific endeavors been devoted to the development and validation of suitable measurement tools such as the People Pleasing Scale (Blötner, 2026; https://doi.org/10.1007/s12144-026-09519-2). The measure provides desirable psychometric properties from the perspective of Classical Test Theory, but in this framework, several statistical assumptions about item and scale characteristics remain untested. To address this gap, we subjected the People Pleasing Scale to item response-theoretical examinations as per the polytomous graded response model (N = 2,538). Its three subscales (Responsibility, Neglect of Own Needs, and Others’ Expectations) provided favorable item discrimination, widely dispersed item thresholds (even though the thresholds to obtain high scores were located at best at moderate levels), and ample levels of item information and reliability across the three latent trait spectra. articles_hidden.title: A puzzling situation: How cooperation and social observation influence visuospatial problem-solving
articles_hidden.authors: Federico Cassioli; Nellia Bellaert; Mandy Rossignol; Clay B. Holroyd; Rudi De Raedt
articles_hidden.abstract: Human problem-solving rarely occurs in social isolation. Yet how cognitive performance and subjective experiences vary across social situations, and whether these effects depend on individual differences in social anxiety (SA), remains underexplored. In this preregistered, within-subject experiment, 101 healthy young adults completed a visuospatial problem-solving task, involving tangram puzzles of different difficulty levels (1,818 trials total) across three social conditions: alone or joined by an experimental confederate acting as either a scrutinizing observer or an active cooperator. Using hierarchical Bayesian modeling, we modeled task performance and post-trial self-reported experiences, and tested whether SA, measured with the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale, moderated the effects of social condition. Both performance and self-report ratings were modulated by task difficulty and social condition. Relative to performing alone, being observed was associated with a decrease in the probability of success and higher post-trial anxiety. Cooperation facilitated performance and reduced perceived difficulty. Crucially, SA moderated the effect of cooperation on post-trial anxiety: cooperation produced the largest reduction in post-trial anxiety among participants with greater fear of being observed. This buffering effect was specific to social-evaluative fear rather than general trait anxiety or task performance. Our findings reinforce the view that cognitive performance and participants’ experiences are jointly shaped by the social context in which they occur.

articles_hidden.title: On the importance of effort perception in stroke care: From evidence to an ideal care pathway – An opinion paper
articles_hidden.authors: Maëlle Charonitis; Fabienne Collette; Benjamin Pageaux
articles_hidden.abstract:
Post-stroke rehabilitation has traditionally relied on objective assessments of motor and cognitive abilities. However, one crucial factor remains underestimated in current practice: the perception of effort, that is, the conscious experience of task intensity and difficulty. Effort perception is strongly influenced by internal states such as fatigue and pain, two symptoms frequently reported after stroke, even without major neurological deficits. While these symptoms are often treated separately, they converge into a shared experience: heightened perceived effort.
Recent literature suggests that both physical and mental fatigue, along with pain, increase perceived effort by impacting available resources and motivation to engage and persist in cognitive and physical tasks. This modulation can directly affect patient engagement and adherence to rehabilitation. When effort is perceived as disproportionate—even for a simple task—it may lead to reduced participation or withdrawal from the care plan. Conversely, a better understanding of effort perception could pave the way for personalized interventions that consider not only patients’ actual capacities but also their subjective experiences.
It is therefore urgent to consider the perception of effort as a clinical indicator in its own right—one that sits at the intersection of body, brain and lived experience.
