By integrating this dimension, research could better explain why some patients disengage from post-stroke care, despite good recovery potential and clinical practice could refine motivational strategies and therapeutic adherence models. The stakes are twofold: improving the understanding of the mechanisms underlying effort perception and harnessing it as a lever for optimizing post-stroke care trajectories.

articles_hidden.title: Bounded rational world modelling
articles_hidden.authors: Samuel David Jones; Antonia Reul; Paul Rauwolf
articles_hidden.abstract: The effective navigation of complex environments requires forming and acting on memories of actions, states, and values; features collectively referred to as a 'mental model'. But what are the decision rules that shape world model acquisition? Dominant normative responses to this question characterise the decision about what information to engage with, and the fidelity in which to encode that information, in terms of cost-value optimisation. However, this is untenable in natural environments of any complexity. The current report presents new empirical support for a complementary characterisation of world model acquisition based on realistic assumptions about human decision-making. Across two pre-registered experiments, N=108 people explored a virtual machine in which combinations of action switches map to symbolic information with associated values. In experiment one, participants were incentivised to maximise value acquisition under costs, while in experiment two participants were incentivised to explore the machine without costs. Each experiment involved a test battery assessing participants' understanding of the machine. We show that varying value structure dramatically shapes world model acquisition - in particular, knowledge of low-value options is sparse under search costs. Search is affected by lapses in memory, and metacognitive awareness of learning progress is poorly calibrated with accuracy. Most importantly, comparison to optimal benchmarks suggests that shortfalls in human performance are attributable to satisficing against a subjective aspiration threshold and updating world models locally in light of the feedback elicited. These results demonstrate that noisy myopic satisficing is a core decision rule shaping world model acquisition.

articles_hidden.title: An Integrative Theory of the Noradrenaline System: Meta-Control through Expected Information Gain
articles_hidden.authors: Riccardo; Giovanni Pezzulo
articles_hidden.abstract:
Living organisms constantly balance exploration and exploitation to adapt to changing environments.
While the neuromodulator noradrenaline (NA) is known to regulate arousal, attention, and information
seeking, its precise computational function remains elusive. Here, we propose an integrative theory of
the noradrenergic system, suggesting that it encodes expected information gain (EIG), a measure of how
informative the environment is over time, and that it uses this quantity for the meta-control of adaptive
behavior. We illustrate this theory using a hierarchical active inference model in which the NA system
acts as a higher-level meta-controller that dynamically adjusts a set of parameters (η) of a lower-level
behavioral controller, modulating exploration rate, the balance between deliberative and habitual control,
perceptual precision, learning rate, and cognitive flexibility. Simulations demonstrate that NA-based
EIG estimation and meta-control enhance performance in volatile environments by promoting directed
exploration, facilitating rapid shifts away from maladaptive habits, sharpening sensory evidence, and
accelerating learning following context changes. These results unify multiple facets of noradrenergic
function under a single computational objective, providing a novel perspective to explain tonic and
phasic NA activity in estimating EIG and meta-controlling behavior. Summing up, this framework
provides a principled link between neuromodulation, exploration, and adaptive behavior, suggesting
that the noradrenergic system implements a fundamental mechanism for inferring and exploiting the
informational richness of the environment.

articles_hidden.title: Nausea and disgust as aversive interoceptive signals in psychopathology.
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Bagley; Camilla Nord
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Disruptions in reinforcement learning are reliably seen across
psychiatric disorders. Yet the origins of reinforcement learning are in interoceptive
signals: we learn to pursue primary interoceptive rewards, such as calories, or avoid
primary interoceptive punishments, such as nausea. Interoceptive punishments may
drive diverse aspects of psychopathology, from enhanced disgust processing in
obsessive compulsive disorder to restricted eating behaviour in anorexia nervosa.

Aims: To determine the role of interoceptive punishments in psychopathology, we
tested a) whether the experience of the interoceptive punishment of nausea covaried
with psychiatric symptoms and b) whether learning about a close proxy of
interoceptive punishment—disgust—predicted psychopathology.

Method: In a large representative sample (n=308), recruited online, participants
completed a battery of questionnaires, on which we conducted a factor analysis, and
a learning task, to which we fit computational reinforcement learning models. This
enabled us to quantify both disgust-related and unrelated psychopathology as well
as reinforcement learning measures from disgust-based, fear-based and points-
based outcomes.

Results: Self-report measures of nausea were strongly and generally predictive of
psychopathology, unexpectedly spanning nearly all symptoms and syndromes. A
similar pattern emerged for self-reported disgust. This suggests that enhanced
experience of interoceptive punishment is a general feature of psychiatric
symptomatology. Additionally, a subset of questionnaires (contamination OCD,
blood-injury phobia and spider phobia) related to computationally-derived measures
of behaviour on a disgust-learning task, indicating a potential mechanism of
interoceptive punishment learning.

Conclusions: These findings provide insight into a previously-unexplored symptom
of mental health problems, nausea, and demonstrate a potential mechanism by
which aversive interoceptive learning may contribute to psychopathology, revealing a
new potential interoceptive treatment target.

articles_hidden.title: Sex and gender differences in functional and participation experiences of students with developmental coordination disorder in higher education
articles_hidden.authors: Clare Copley; Kim Petersen; Madeleine Pownall; Lucy H Eddy
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) is a common neurodevelopmental condition characterised by persistent motor coordination difficulties that negatively impacts daily functioning and participation across the lifespan. Despite a high prevalence (5-6%), DCD remains under recognised in adulthood, creating particular challenges in contexts requiring high levels of independent participation, such as higher education. Sex and gender are also important to examine, given their potential to influence the recognition, presentation and lived experience of DCD. However, there is a notable lack of research exploring how sex and gender identity may impact these experiences. 
Aims: This exploratory study aimed to investigate whether functional challenges and participation experiences differed according to sex and gender identity among higher education students with DCD.
Methods: Data were collected via an online self-report questionnaire completed by 77 higher education students with DCD/dyspraxia across the UK and Ireland.
Results: Findings indicate high levels of functional difficulty and participation restriction across the sample, with fatigue often reported as a consequence. Females with DCD were significantly more likely than males to report challenges related to gross motor skills (p<.05, d=.60) and executive function skills (p<.05, d =.60). Participants who identified as a gender minority reported a higher incidence of difficulty with fine motor skills (p<.05, d=–.63) and executive function (p<.05, d =–.60) compared to cisgender participants. 
Conclusions: Findings indicate that students with DCD experience persistent functional challenges that restrict participation in higher education.  Experiences and support needs may also differ based on sex and gender identity.

articles_hidden.title: Detecting Response Styles in Visual Analogue Scales
articles_hidden.authors: Dominik Vollbracht; Tanja Lischetzke; Mirka Henninger
articles_hidden.abstract: Response styles are prevalent in self-report data and may bias parameter estimates. While there are various approaches for detecting response styles in Likert-type data, models for visual analogue scales remain scarce. We propose a novel modeling framework that extends the beta item response model by Noel and Dauvier (2007) to jointly detect extreme response style, midpoint response style, and acquiescent response style. Estimated in a Bayesian framework using Stan, the model performed well in a comprehensive simulation study. Parameter recovery was primarily influenced by the number of (reverse-scored) items and the variance of response styles, whereas sample size had a negligible effect. The model’s practical utility is illustrated using empirical data (Kuhlmann et al., 2017), for which it demonstrated superior model fit compared to the original beta item response model. Overall, the proposed framework provides researchers with a principled approach to account for response styles in visual analogue scale data.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-cultural and Indigenous perspectives on music and social bonding
articles_hidden.authors: Danya Vivianne Pavlovich; Patricia Opondo; Juan David Leongómez; Yuto Ozaki; Zixuan Jia; Suzanne Purdy; Patrick E. Savage
articles_hidden.abstract: Experimental studies of primarily Western participants have suggested that musical synchrony facilitates social bonding. Critics question the validity and cross-cultural generality of synchrony-bonding relationships, as well as the causal role of music. Drawing on new data from large-scale Registered Reports co-designed and implemented with over 100 collaborators (“Many Voices”), we show that group singing enhances social bonding significantly more than speaking, across 901 participants speaking 30 languages. We share lessons from this collaboration regarding evolutionary hypotheses about the origins of music and language, as well as the importance of collaborating with Indigenous and non-Western researchers. By making the psychology of music research more inclusive, we may broaden our understanding of music and social bonding in humans and beyond. Indigenous knowledge does not oppose science: it improves science.

articles_hidden.title: Assistive AI in Counseling Psychology for Dyslexia (AAIC-D): A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing the Therapeutic Alliance
articles_hidden.authors: KHAIRUL KORAI
articles_hidden.abstract:
Individual with dyslexia frequently experience persistent reading difficulties that extend far beyond academic environments, contributing to heightened anxiety, low self-esteem, and chronic psychological distress. In traditional mental health counseling, literacy-heavy tools such as written intake questionnaires, thought journals, and dense psychoeducational handouts impose a heavy extraneous cognitive load. This load exhausts working memory and triggers reading anxiety, effectively diverting mental bandwidth away from core therapeutic processing. To address this barrier, this paper introduces a conceptual framework: Assistive AI in Counseling Psychology for Dyslexia (AAIC-D). Grounded in a narrative synthesis of existing literature, this model positions artificial intelligence not as a replacement for human clinicians, but as an accessible cognitive scaffold managed under ethical oversight. The framework synthesizes Cognitive Load Theory, the Triadic Therapeutic Alliance model (Client, Therapist, and AI), and Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles. By leveraging Generative AI summaries, speech-to-text journaling, and multimodal text-to-speech presentation, AAIC-D offloads reading and writing effort, restoring the client's emotional capacity for therapeutic engagement. Finally, we address critical counseling practice governance concerns including algorithmic bias, data privacy under HIPAA/GDPR, and client over-reliance offering actionable guidelines to humanize and democratize psychological care. 

Keywords: Dyslexia, Assistive AI, Therapeutic Alliance, Cognitive Load Theory, Universal Design for Learning, Counseling Psychology, Cyberpsychology

articles_hidden.title: The Hidden Friction of Action: A Framework for Autistic Inertia
articles_hidden.authors: Hari Srinivasan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Autistic inertia describes difficulty initiating, sustaining, stopping, or shifting action and cognitive state despite conscious intention. Existing accounts, including executive dysfunction, monotropism, predictive processing, autistic burnout, and disability-oriented perspectives, capture important aspects of the phenomenon but remain fragmented. We propose the Hidden Friction Framework (HFF), which addresses how intention can remain intact while its translation into flexible action becomes disrupted. The HFF proposes that autistic inertia may emerge from interacting predictive, transition, sensory–motor, executive–cognitive, emotional, and environmental forms of friction. Rather than treating inertia solely as a problem of action initiation, the framework considers difficulty flexibly entering, sustaining, exiting, or shifting cognitive, sensory, emotional, and behavioral states. It also helps explain why inertia may vary across contexts and why similar behavioral outcomes may arise from different configurations of friction. The HFF integrates cognitive, embodied, environmental, and lived-experience perspectives and generates testable predictions about how different sources of friction may independently and cumulatively shape action and state transition in autism.

Keywords: autistic inertia, autism, embodiment, epistemic injustice, neurodiversity, disability theory.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of Stoic Training on Fear of Negative Evaluation and Responses to Social-Evaluative Stress: A Randomized Controlled Trial
articles_hidden.authors: Michael William Lewis; Charles Kalarchian; Alexander MacLellan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: Stoic philosophy has influenced cognitive and behavioral therapies, but Stoic training has received limited empirical evaluation. This preregistered randomized controlled trial examined whether Stoic training reduced fear of negative evaluation (FNE), improved broader psychological outcomes, increased Stoic attitudes and behaviors, and altered subjective and cardiac responses to acute social-evaluative stress.

Methods: Undergraduate students (M age = 19.16 years, SD = 1.05; 81% women) were randomized to eight days of online Stoic training or an active control involving literary-fiction readings. Ninety-eight participants completed pretraining and posttraining self-report assessments (Stoic training, n = 46; control, n = 52). Seventy-eight subsequently completed a modified Trier Social Stress Test (TSST), of whom 66 provided usable electrocardiography data for the preregistered cardiac analyses. Before speech preparation, participants in the Stoic condition completed a five-minute Negative Visualization exercise, whereas control participants waited quietly.

Results: Relative to the active control, Stoic training was associated with lower posttraining FNE when controlling for pretraining scores, b = −2.77, p = .016, adjusted d = −0.50, and higher posttraining Stoic Attitudes and Behaviours Scale scores, b = 6.06, p = .038, adjusted d = 0.43. Exploratory subscale analyses suggested possible effects on Beliefs About Control and Beliefs About Happiness, although neither remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Between-condition effects on resilience, self-efficacy, and rumination were not significant. During the TSST, cardiac effects were contrary to prediction: Stoic training was associated with higher heart rate, b = 4.13, p = .038, adjusted d = 0.53, and lower heart rate variability, although the latter effect narrowly missed statistical significance, b = −0.17, p = .053, adjusted d = −0.49. Subjective distress and state-anxiety responses to the TSST did not differ significantly by condition.

Conclusions: Stoic training led to significantly greater reductions in FNE and increases in Stoic attitudes than an active control, whereas broader psychological outcomes did not differ significantly between conditions. These findings provide initial evidence that brief Stoic training may modify a cognitive vulnerability relevant to social evaluation while engaging the attitudes and behaviors it is intended to cultivate. The unexpected cardiac effects may reflect the broader training, the acute Negative Visualization exercise administered before the stressor, or their combination, highlighting the need to disentangle the cumulative and acute effects of Stoic practice and determine how the timing and context of Negative Visualization influence responses to social-evaluative stress.

articles_hidden.title: Are two words seen as one object? How age-of-acquisition affects the recognition and naming of pictorial representations of compound words
articles_hidden.authors: Mahmoud Medhat Elsherif
articles_hidden.abstract: Adults recognize objects learned in childhood (e.g., "unicorn") faster than those learned later (e.g., "taxes"). This phenomenon is known as the Age-of-Acquisition (AoA) effect. The integrated account proposes that this effect stems from higher demands on semantic processing or arbitrary input-output mappings. To investigate this, 48 British English-speaking students completed an object decision task and a spoken picture naming task using 150 compound words. Compound words were selected because their mapping to multiple morphemes requires increased semantic processing. In addition to individual task performance, we calculated a subtractive measure (naming latency minus object decision latency) for each item per participant. Results showed that early-acquired objects were identified and named more quickly than late-acquired objects. The analysis of the subtractive measure also revealed significant AoA effects. These findings suggest that the influence of AoA and semantic predictors is more pronounced in picture naming than in object decision. This supports the representation account, indicating that the AoA effect is rooted in semantic and phonological representations. Furthermore, the robust AoA effect observed in the subtractive analysis bolsters the mapping account, suggesting the effect also resides in the connections between these representations. Overall, these results align with the integrated account of the AoA effect.

articles_hidden.title: Word Frequency and Regularity in Reading and Spelling: Task and Item effects
articles_hidden.authors: Jennifer Burt
articles_hidden.abstract: Reading and spelling tasks were compared on a common word set with different groups of university students assigned to each task. In Experiment 1, words varied over 5 levels of normative frequency and each group performed speeded lexical decision (LDT), speeded spelling recognition (correct vs. incorrect classification) or (unspeeded) dictation. The results revealed frequency effects on both lexical processing and decision processes. In Experiment 2, words varied in spelling-sound regularity and each group performed LDT, speeded spelling recognition, name if a word, or dictation. Irregular pronunciation had effects on accuracy in reading and spelling tasks, whereas, when orthographic typicality was controlled, irregular spelling affected only dictation accuracy. In the two experiments there were substantial item-by-item associations in accuracy and latencies over the reading and spelling tasks. The results indicate a common effect of the quality of lexical representations over tasks, together with task-specific effects associated with decision processes and the deployment of spelling-sound connections.

articles_hidden.title: “It's my destiny.”: A Qualitative Exploration of Motivating Factors for submissives who Hold BDSM and Kink Identities
articles_hidden.authors: Briana Louise Kunstman; Jaime Derringer
articles_hidden.abstract: Although Dominant-submissive dynamics are among the most widely recognized forms of BDSM and kink, popular media often portray these relationships as inherently abusive or exploitative. Such representations contrast with growing evidence that BDSM identities and practices emerge through diverse developmental, social, and personal pathways. Building on prior research calling for greater attention to role-specific experiences within BDSM communities,the current study evaluated the themes present among 52 participants reporting submissive identities. We found that participants’ descriptions of their motivations for being a submissive consistently referred to the following themes: upbringing and past experience; submission as an identity; control and power exchange; positive mental health outcomes; and feelings of shame associated with stigma. Apart from stigma concerns, participants overwhelmingly discussed positive aspects of their experiences. This shows that there are complex motivating factors for participants to engage with or identify as submissive, opening up potential directions of exploration to understand the development of kink and BDSM identities and experiences. These findings specific to submissive motivations and BDSM identities will help work towards the destigmatization and depathologizing of kink and BDSM through increased understanding. In turn, this will allow for better mental health outcomes for community members, informed safe practice, and improved general understanding of BDSM and kink identities in our society.

articles_hidden.title: Toward a Multidimensional Operationalization of Feminist Identity: Associations with Sexism and Weight Bias
articles_hidden.authors: Daemon St-James; Annie Raymond; Annie Duchesne; Benoit Brisson
articles_hidden.abstract: Feminist identity is typically operationalized through self-identification and endorsement of select beliefs, leaving movement affiliation and competing ideologies, such as meritocracy and social dominance orientation, unaccounted for. This study explored whether a multidimensional operationalization of feminist identity reveals distinct profiles and whether these profiles relate differently to discriminatory attitudes associated with feminism: ambivalent sexism and weight bias. Adults in Quebec (N = 917; 90% women) completed the Anti-Fat Attitudes Scale, the Ambivalent Sexism Inventory, the Perceptions of Meritocracy Inventory, the Short Social Dominance Orientation Scale, a bespoke feminist movement affiliation questionnaire, and the Feminist Belief and Behavior measure. Cluster analysis yielded six profiles: four feminist-identifying profiles distinguished by movement affiliation (liberal, radical, intersectional, postmodern) and two non-identifying profiles, including Affiliated Non-Labelers, who endorsed feminist beliefs and affiliated with a feminist movement while rejecting the feminist label. They reported meritocratic and dominance-oriented scores comparable to Non-Feminists. Profiles differed on hostile sexism, benevolent sexism, and weight controllability. Compared with Zucker's (2004) two-dimensional typology, the profiles offered no clear incremental predictive value but described configurations not represented by conventional typology. Findings suggest that the combination of feminist identities a person holds alongside their beliefs shapes how feminist identity relates to discriminatory attitudes.

articles_hidden.title: Differential Effects of Types of Momentary Social Support on Mood and Anxiety in Patients with Depression
articles_hidden.authors: Annalena Jachnik; Martin Weiß; Julian Gutzeit; Fabian Rothbauer; Sebastian Walther; Grit Hein
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Social support is a multidimensional construct that includes emotional, esteem, and informational support, as well as instrumental support, referring to tangible assistance, and negative forms of support. While patients experience these types of support in their daily social interactions, the specific effects of momentary received support types on psychopathology remain understudied. Therefore, this study examined the effects of multiple types of social support on depressive mood and state social anxiety using high frequency Ecological Momentary Assessment. 
Methods: Data was collected from patients diagnosed with affective disorders and current moderate to severe depression, as well as from control participants (N = 68) using smartphone-based assessments over five consecutive days. Specifically, participants reported on social interaction characteristics, the type of received support, as well as their mood and anxiety levels based on six survey prompts per day. 
Results: Results indicated that receiving emotional support was associated with lower depressive mood, while esteem support was associated with lower depressive mood and state social anxiety. In contrast, informational support showed opposite effects. 
Conclusions: These findings underscore the potential of social support in alleviating the core symptoms of clinical depression; with specific types of support being particularly beneficial. Thus, targeted application of social support types hold promise for interventions in depression.

articles_hidden.title: Rethinking Group Differences in Psychopathology Networks: A Slow–Fast Perspective on Context and Symptom Activation
articles_hidden.authors: Kyuri Park; Denny Borsboom; Michael Lees; Leonie Elsenburg; Gabriela Lunansky; Karien Stronks; Johan Bollen; Mary Nicolaou; Vítor V. Vasconcelos
articles_hidden.abstract:
Groups differing in social and economic circumstances often differ markedly in depressive symptom levels while their estimated symptom-network structures show few clear differences. Null results in network comparisons are interpreted as if indicating that the two groups' symptom systems are the same. However, it only indicates that no difference is detected in the interactions between symptoms. How readily symptoms become present, and how that may depend on the contextual conditions under which symptoms are observed, is rarely compared. Building on a slow--fast perspective, we conceptualize depressive symptoms as a relatively fast-changing system embedded in more persistent social, economic, psychosocial, health, and lifestyle conditions that shape symptom activation.

Using a cohort of 23,689 adults from Amsterdam, we illustrate this perspective with depressive symptoms measured by the PHQ-9 and a composite index of slow-layer contextual conditions, which we call {\em Slow Risk Load} (SRL), capturing persistent socioeconomic, psychosocial, and health-related conditions. Participants with High SRL showed substantially higher depressive symptom levels than those with Low SRL. A standard Network Comparison Test did not detect an overall difference in network structure between the groups, although global strength was modestly higher in the High SRL group.

Ising models, which separate how symptoms co-occur from how readily each becomes present, indicate that activation is higher under high SRL for eight of nine symptoms, and model comparison consistently favored group-specific activation over group-specific interactions.

The slow--fast perspective reframes group network comparisons as a problem spanning multiple time scales in which symptom-network structure, symptom activation, and contextual conditions should be considered jointly. It places symptom-focused and context-focused interventions at different layers of the same coupled system rather than in competition.

articles_hidden.title: Resting-State Functional Connectivity in Antipsychotic-Naïve First-Episode Psychosis: A Systematic Review of Network Alterations and Preprocessing Heterogeneity
articles_hidden.authors: Ayla Ihsan; Ather; Joaquim Radua
articles_hidden.abstract:
Resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) abnormalities are central to characterising brain network dysfunction in first-episode psychosis (FEP), yet biomarker development remains limited by an incomplete understanding of connectivity heterogeneity. This systematic review synthesised 75 studies investigating RSFC in antipsychotic-naïve FEP across five functional network domains and one developmental subgroup. Antipsychotic-naïve FEP was consistently associated with hypoconnectivity within the default mode, salience, frontostriatal, cerebello-thalamo-cortical, and hippocampal networks. Exploratory analyses examined whether global signal regression (GSR) and motion-correction stringency were associated with differences in reported connectivity direction. Motion-control stringency showed no significant association with connectivity direction, indicating that the hypoconnectivity finding was not attributable to motion-related artefact; GSR use was strongly confounded with geographic origin, precluding independent assessment of its association with connectivity direction. Notably, no included study employed within-study preprocessing sensitivity analyses, and cross-national harmonisation efforts remain minimal. Future research should prioritise within-study GSR sensitivity analyses, establish test–retest reliability and external classifier validation for RSFC biomarkers, adopt harmonised preprocessing conventions, and systematically explore sources of directional heterogeneity across preprocessing strata to enable robust cross-national biomarker synthesis.
Keywords: Connectomics; global signal regression; motion artefact; thalamocortical dysconnectivity; salience network; default mode network.

articles_hidden.title: Advancing Global Social Science through Cross-Societal Online Behavioral Economic Games (CoBEx): Lessons Learned and A Practical Guide
articles_hidden.authors: Shuxian Jin; Vanessa Christina Clemens; Laura Carlotta Hoenig; Carsten De Dreu; Angela Rachael Dorrough; Catherine Molho; Marina Orifici; Angelo Romano; Shaul Shalvi; Ayse K. Uskul
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding human behavior across diverse cultural settings is essential for advancing theories that address pressing global social challenges. Recent advances, which use an innovative methodology—cross-societal online behavioral economic games (CoBEx)—have revealed key insights into cross-cultural differences and similarities in the mechanisms and functions of human behavior. To foster this emerging field, we discuss the key successes and lessons learned from ten years of experience in designing and conducting CoBEx studies. We illustrate the theoretical and methodological benefits of CoBEx, and offer practical recommendations on key design considerations, study materials preparation, ethics and funding, as well as analysis, interpretation, and dissemination processes. This paper aims to equip researchers around the globe with the necessary tools to conduct methodologically rigorous and culturally informed CoBEx studies, ultimately advancing the field of psychological science and beyond.

articles_hidden.title: Prediction-error tolerance: Error attribution as the hinge between inquiry and the self
articles_hidden.authors: Tomoko Sakai; Kazuhiro Hayashi; Norihiro Sadato
articles_hidden.abstract: Close to one in three early-career researchers reports elevated psychological distress, at rates varying little across disciplines, genders and career stages. The standard explanation attributes the burden to the conditions of academic work; its rival prescribes resilience. Neither says what a condition does to a researcher who cannot yet tell whether an unexpected result reflects the phenomenon, the instrument or her own competence. A prediction error has no address until a researcher gives it one: by the Duhem–Quine thesis it may belong to the object of inquiry, the method or the context of evaluation, and logic does not decide which. We define prediction-error tolerance as the capacity to keep treating discrepancies as operable questions while holding uncertainty open, and identify its core operation, error-attribution separation, as the point at which two costs are decided together. When an error is routed to the self instead of to its address, the researcher’s well-being is damaged and the error is lost to inquiry; the adaptations that follow (safe questions, discarded anomalies, work subdivided to fit the measure) are those metascience explains by incentives alone. The two costs, we propose, are effects of one regime with a shared mediating step. We distinguish the construct from ten neighbours, fix the error episode as the unit of measurement, and state six predictions with the observations that would defeat each, including one that would leave the incentive account standing and ours not. An environment that returns errors with an address protects the person and the inquiry together.

articles_hidden.title: Predicting Memberships from Memory.
articles_hidden.authors: Luigi Grisoni
articles_hidden.abstract: Neural representations are commonly described as mappings between target variables and patterns of neural activity. A central challenge is to specify not only what the brain represents, but how representational content is organised and constrained across contexts. Here, the concept of Representation of Membership (RoM) is proposed as a perspective on representational organisation. RoM assumes that cognitive representations are shaped by the elements they contain and by the membership structures linking those elements to broader semantic, functional, and contextual domains. The same element may belong to multiple structures and play different roles within them, with particular memberships becoming relevant according to context, task demands, or prior knowledge. Within RoM, prediction reflects the dynamic activation, weighting, and refinement of learned membership structures, constraining which continuations, features, interpretations, or responses become more likely. RoM thus links neural representation, memory, flexibility, and prediction through the context-sensitive organisation and updating of membership structures.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond an Ethos or Inflexible Checklist of Research Practices: Grounding Open Science in a Biomedical Research Ethics Framework
articles_hidden.authors: P. Priscilla Lui
articles_hidden.abstract: The well-documented reproducibility problem facing psychological science has driven rapid growth in open science infrastructure and practices over the past decade. Despite most researchers broadly endorsing transparency as a virtue, actual practice adoption remains uneven and lags far behind the stated support. Three issues explain the value-practice gap: (1) general ethos does not motivate and guide actual practice use within context, (2) open science is often misconceived as a one-size-fits-all, all-or-nothing mandate applied agnostic to different research questions, methods, or populations, (3) insufficient attention to relational transparency relative to procedural transparency, thus inadvertently alienating psychological researchers who use qualitative and participatory methods. Currently, researchers are left without a principled framework to decide what, when, and how to implement specific practices in any given investigation. A critical step is translating the transparency ethos into a comprehensive set of ethical principles and benchmarks that can guide eventual open science practices. Drawing on Emanuel’s biomedical research ethics framework, this article maps open science practices onto eight established ethical principles. Examples are offered on how these principles and related benchmarks motivate specific, contextually appropriate practices. The systematic ethics framework offers researchers a principled basis for building local capacity to engage with open science practices.

articles_hidden.title: An Analysis of Flavor Distribution and Consumer Perception On Color In Life Savers Neon Gummies
articles_hidden.authors: Shriyans Tiwari; Aarush Jain
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines the influence of artificial coloring, flavor naming, and  package design on consumer preference of the gummy. Although previous research has examined a product's packaging or a product's color, our study combines marketing and psychological factors to understand what appeals to the consumers. In this experiment, a survey was conducted with over one-hundred participants, asking them their preferred gummy color, flavor name, and whether or not they liked the packaging. In addition to this, the frequency and distribution of the colors was measured from eight packages of Life Savers gummies. Results revealed that Cherry Lime Splash was the most appealing flavor name, suggesting that combinations of exotic flavors appeal most to the consumers. Red emerged as the most appealing flavor color to consumers, while blue appeared most frequently in the package. These findings emphasize that both visual appeal and flavor naming significantly influence consumer decisions. Additionally, blue appearing the most was surprising, as this didn’t correlate with consumer preference. Ultimately, it is recommended that companies replace the artificial dies used to make the colors appealing, with natural alternatives such as beet juice, turmeric, and spirulina. These colors will help the gummies maintain strong visual appeal, while avoiding the usage of artificial dyes. Future research should examine whether natural colors would match or surpass artificial colors in terms of consumer preference.

articles_hidden.title: Conversation as data: Extracting features from naturalistic conversation datasets
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Templeton; Luke J. Chang
articles_hidden.abstract: In this chapter, we outline important considerations for designing and analyzing conversation studies. We first advocate for the use of representative designs to ensure that datasets adequately reflect the complexity inherent in conversation. We then focus on how behavior in conversation recordings can be quantified through a process of feature extraction, and discuss strategies to assess the validity of feature extraction pipelines. Finally, we discuss analytical considerations specific to working with conversation data. Being able to rigorously collect, operationalize, and analyze natural conversation data will lead to robust results that the entire field can build upon, advancing our understanding of exactly how conversation allows us to achieve our social goals.

articles_hidden.title: A systemic approach to self-harm in schools in Poland – a policy brief
articles_hidden.authors: Lea Satala; Daria Biechowska
articles_hidden.abstract: Self-harm among young people is a significant public health concern in Poland, while schools remain an underused setting for its early identification and prevention. Despite existing mental health initiatives and regulations, the Polish education system lacks uniform, systemic procedures for responding to self-harm, resulting in fragmented and unequal support across schools. This policy brief examines the scale and consequences of self-harm among young people, the current regulatory and institutional framework and evidence from school-based interventions in Poland and internationally. It argues that schools are particularly important for early intervention because most young people who self-harm remain in regular contact with school staff. The brief recommends a scalable, systemic intervention consisting of three complementary elements: (1) a short universal online training course for all school staff, (2) a uniform procedure for responding to self-harm and (3) a clearly defined pathway for referral to specialist support. The proposed training would strengthen staff competencies in recognising warning signs, conducting supportive conversations and directing students to appropriate services. Rather than introducing extensive new regulatory obligations, the proposal uses existing institutional mechanisms and recommends integration with the National Health Programme, professional development and staff onboarding. By establishing a common minimum standard of response, while accounting for institutional and resource constraints, the proposed approach offers a feasible first step towards a broader whole-school model of mental health support and self-harm prevention in Poland.

articles_hidden.title: A short-form decision-making task preserving value-based choices and their relationship to apathy in older adults
articles_hidden.authors: Dorothée Morand-Grondin; Madeleine Sharp
articles_hidden.abstract: Apathy, or diminished motivation, is increasingly understood as reflecting biases in value-based decision-making. The Everyday Choice Task offers an ecologically grounded setting for investigating this relationship. In this task, older adults rate everyday activities on 19 different value attributes, and then make choices between pairs of activities. Prior analyses of these value attributes recover three main value dimensions (effort, reward, and obligation) that significantly predict choice behavior, while overweighting of effort during choice is selectively associated with apathy. In this study, we tested whether a brief version of the task, inquiring about these three dimensions directly rather than using the full set of attributes, would preserve relationships between value, choice, and apathy observed using the original instrument. Older adults (n = 110) completed both the original and brief versions of the task in a randomized order, along with the Apathy Motivation Index. Ratings of effort, reward, and obligation derived from the original and brief versions of the task were strongly correlated. In both versions of the task, ratings of effort, reward, and obligation significantly predicted choice, and greater apathy severity was associated with a selective overweighting of effort. These findings support the use of the brief Everyday Choice Task as an efficient measure of value-based decision-making in future research.

articles_hidden.title: Validity, Diagnostic Accuracy, and Feasibility of Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality for Mild Cognitive Impairment
articles_hidden.authors: Panagiotis Kourtesis; Antonia Ioakeimidou; Myrto Dimakopoulou; Christina Anastasopoulou; Maria Roussou; Petros Roussos; Chrysanthi Nega; Ion Beratis
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Immersive virtual reality (VR) adaptations of neuropsychological tests change how participants respond and must be validated in each clinical population. We evaluated the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), a head-gaze version of the paper-and-pencil Trail Making Test (hereafter, TMT) that records completion times and wrong-target selections automatically, in older adults with and without mild cognitive impairment (MCI).
Methods: In this case–control evaluation, 84 adults aged 60–89 years (42 with clinically diagnosed MCI, 42 healthy comparison participants) completed the TMT-VR, the TMT and the Mini-Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination (M-ACE), with pre- and post-exposure cybersickness ratings. Planned analyses examined feasibility, convergence, group differences and diagnostic accuracy for all 26 TMT-VR scores against their TMT counterparts and the M-ACE, with demographic adjustment, multiplicity correction, bootstrap validation and education-matched sensitivity analysis.
Results: All participants completed both TMT-VR parts, and cybersickness ratings decreased over the session. Part B completion times correlated positively across formats within both groups. Participants with MCI were slower and made more wrong-target selections on TMT-VR Part B but not Part A. Score for score, the TMT-VR matched the TMT on Part B completion time and discriminated MCI more effectively on the Part B, total and B−A error scores and every Part B-specific derived score; these effects persisted after demographic adjustment and widened in the education-matched subsample. The TMT's advantage lay in Part A completion time, and its error scores carried little discriminatory information. With education equalised, the TMT-VR B−A scores gave balanced operating characteristics and approached the M-ACE, which every TMT score remained below. The M-ACE discriminated more accurately than any single trail-making score of either format.
Conclusions: The TMT-VR is a feasible, well-tolerated adaptation with convergent validity against the TMT and known-groups validity for MCI. Because it discriminated MCI more effectively on the Part B-specific and error-based scores that carry the test's executive demand, it emerges as the preferable Trail Making Test format within neuropsychological batteries for MCI; whether it adds diagnostic information beyond global screens such as the M-ACE must be established in consecutive clinical referrals, together with age- and education-stratified normative cut-offs.

articles_hidden.title: From Population–Case Mismatch to Cumulative Homogenisation in AI-Assisted Cognition
articles_hidden.authors: Fangxing Bai
articles_hidden.abstract: A growing literature reports homogenisation under generative AI assistance and offers diverse explanations, yet a unified account grounded in AI’s statistical foundations remains underdeveloped. Through a parallel thought experiment, this Perspective derives how population–case mismatch creates differences between model-based and independent human trajectories, and how AI intervention can turn these differences into cumulative homogenisation. The degree and rate of homogenisation vary with the stage of intervention. The same mechanism also explains why AI can support scientific research under conditions that limit mismatch and support independent judgement.

articles_hidden.title: Structural Equation Modeling with Causal Discipline: A Practical Tutorial from Regression and Mediation to Latent Variables and Growth Models in R and Mplus
articles_hidden.authors: Subir Hait
articles_hidden.abstract: Structural equation modeling (SEM) makes it easy to draw paths, estimate latent-variable models, and decompose associations, but those conveniences can blur three distinct questions: what statistical parameter is being estimated, what construct is being measured, and what additional assumptions would justify a causal interpretation. This tutorial organizes SEM around that three-layer distinction. Using one synthetic educational dataset, it moves from regression and path analysis through mediation, confirmatory factor analysis, latent-variable SEM, measurement invariance, longitudinal measurement models, and latent growth curves. Parallel examples in R using lavaan and Mplus show how the same model is represented across software. The mediation section makes the statistical-versus-causal distinction concrete: it derives the linear product-of-coefficients decomposition, shows when it can identify a natural indirect effect under stronger assumptions, and uses a residual-correlation sensitivity analysis with a known-truth simulation. Measurement-error attenuation, partial invariance, longitudinal latent means, and conditional growth models show why better statistical fit or richer latent-variable structure does not by itself create causal identification. A frozen reproducibility bundle supplies the data-generating process, truth files, software syntax, benchmark estimates, and independent numerical checks. The intended audience is graduate students and applied researchers who know regression and want a practical route into SEM without treating an arrow in a fitted model as evidence of causation.

articles_hidden.title: Working Memory and the Effectiveness of Written Corrective Feedback on Production Accuracy of the English Definite Article
articles_hidden.authors: Mohammad Nowbakht; Thierry Olive
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigated the role of working memory (WM) in the effectiveness of direct, indirect, and metalinguistic written corrective feedback (WCF) on the production accuracy of the English definite article among pre-intermediate EFL learners. One hundred and thirty-five learners (72 female, 63 male) performed four picture-composition tasks and one argumentative essay transfer task, received WCF on their definite article errors, and rewrote their compositions accordingly. WM was measured using a first-language Operation Span Task (OSPAN). Results showed that WM predicted the effectiveness of metalinguistic and direct WCF at both immediate and delayed post-tests but did not predict the effectiveness of indirect WCF. Metalinguistic WCF produced the highest accuracy gains, which were maintained at the delayed and transfer assessments; direct WCF also outperformed indirect WCF. The findings are discussed in relation to cognitive load theory (Sweller, 1988; Sweller et al., 1998)—which accounts for how WM constraints shape learners' differential responses to instructional feedback of varying explicitness—and Schmidt's (1990) Noticing Hypothesis and cognitive models of writing (Hayes, 1996; Kellogg, 1996; Olive, 2004).

articles_hidden.title: Large Language Models for Test-Enhanced Learning: A Tutorial and Proof of Concept
articles_hidden.authors: Ariana Modirrousta-Galian; Daryl Yu Heng Lee; Frederic Dick; Eva Lash; David Shanks
articles_hidden.abstract: Practice tests improve retention of studied information and enhance learning and retrieval of new information (test-enhanced learning; TEL). In five preregistered studies (total N = 623)—four online randomized experiments and one correlational classroom study with final-year psychology undergraduates—we examined whether large language models (LLMs; Gemini and ChatGPT) can generate practice tests that promote TEL and whether this use of LLMs can be feasibly incorporated into a classroom setting. LLM-generated multiple-choice tests with fixed feedback did not improve 2-day recall of a TED Talk relative to a control (Studies 1 and 2). In contrast, LLM-generated short-answer tests with personalized feedback significantly improved 7-day recall of an educational video relative to rewatching it (Studies 3 and 4), regardless of whether final test format matched that of the practice test. In the classroom study, participation in fortnightly LLM-generated short-answer tests (with personalized feedback) on lecture content was positively associated with graded assessment performance, and students’ attitudes towards this use of LLMs were generally favorable. Overall, we demonstrate that LLMs can substantially reduce the practical burden of implementing TEL, while maintaining sufficiently good question quality and enabling automated personalized feedback, and that this approach can be feasibly deployed in an undergraduate psychology class.

articles_hidden.title: Causal Inference in Mediation Studies When Using Psychological States as Mediators
articles_hidden.authors: Guangyu Zhu; Yiyun Shou; Michael Smithson
articles_hidden.abstract:
The growing interest in the underlying causal mechanisms of phenomena has led to the widespread application of mediation models in social science research. Researchers usually employ regression-based approaches (such as Baron and Kenny’s criteria, Sobel test and SEM) to explore causal relationships. However, the effectiveness of regression-based approaches in establishing causal relationships relies on two key assumptions: temporal order between variables and the elimination of confounders.
Previous literature has cautioned researchers about these restrictions, but misuses of regression-based approaches persist when the assumptions are not satisfied or not testable. In addition, researchers may encounter various challenges in assessing the causal relationship between variables, especially when using psychological states as mediators. These challenges include but are not limited to: (1) Psychological states are latent variables; (2) Discrepancy between measurement lag and causal lag; (3) Potential unknown or uncontrolled confounders; and (4) Bad control problem.
This article discusses the limitations of regression-based approaches and the challenges in assessing causal mediation relationships when using psychological states as mediators. It then elaborates several advanced approaches to address these challenges.

articles_hidden.title: No evidence that positive outcomes elicit a stronger sense of agency once correcting for publication bias: a commentary on, and re-analysis of, Mariano et al. (2025)
articles_hidden.authors: Robrecht van der Wel; Shaheed Azaad; Pernille Hemmer; John Michael
articles_hidden.abstract: In a recent meta-analysis, Mariano et al. (2025) conclude that people experience a stronger sense of agency over positive than negative outcomes, indexed by temporal compression. In this commentary, we evaluate that claim and identify several concerns about its validity. First, we argue that temporal compression effects should be standardized before being combined, because values in milliseconds are not necessarily comparable across different paradigms. When we analyzed standardized effects, evidence for a valence effect was absent once adjusting for publication bias. Second, we identified data integrity issues, identifying several studies that were included but either (1) did not manipulate outcome valence at all, or (2) contained only a positive or negative condition compared to a neutral condition. Excluding these studies meant that even unstandardized effects did not support Mariano et al.’s headline finding.

articles_hidden.title: “Who Will Marry a Mad Doctor?”: A Qualitative Study of Associative Stigma Among Mental Health Professionals in India
articles_hidden.authors: Deepti Dilip Moar; Rajat Kanti Mitra; Sunil Mittal
articles_hidden.abstract: Mental health professionals (MHPs) can experience stigma through their professional association with mental illness and mental healthcare. Existing studies have often focused on particular professions, service populations, or specific aspects of associative stigma, making it difficult to identify recurring patterns across professions and beyond the workplace. This study explored associative stigma among MHPs in India across professional, family, and wider social contexts. Semi-structured interviews with 22 MHPs, including psychiatrists, clinical psychologists, counsellors, psychiatric social workers, and psychiatric nurses, were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis within a constructivist framework. Eight themes were developed, spanning misconceptions about MHP roles and abilities, mistrust of expertise and motives, concerns about how mental health work might affect them, devaluation of mental health work, exclusion involving social distancing and concealment, role expectations extending beyond work, ambivalent responses in which admiration or reliance coexisted with misunderstanding, avoidance, or devaluation, and differences in professional standing. Across the analysis, experiences that might otherwise appear separate were connected by recurring meanings attached to mental illness and mental healthcare. The study broadens understanding of the social and professional reach of stigma surrounding mental illness. Through professional association, these meanings can shape how MHPs, their expertise, and mental health work are understood and valued.

articles_hidden.title: Can Large Language Models Code Reality Criteria in Autobiographical Statements? Reliability and Validity of an Artificial Intelligence–Based Tool for Criteria-Based Content Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Elsa Gewehr; Laureen Gräflich; Johannes Zimmermann; Renate Volbert
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Coding for Criteria-Based Content Analysis (CBCA) to differentiate fabricated from experience-based autobiographical statements is slow and depends on trained coders whose agreement is imperfect. We developed the large language model (LLM) based system CBC-AID and evaluate its reliability and validity in coding CBCA. Hypotheses: As preregistered, AI–human consistency is non-inferior to the interrater reliability of trained coders (H1: total score; H2: each criterion), and AI-based scores discriminate between experience-based and fabricated statements at least as well as human scores (H3: total score; H4: each criterion). Method: Two versions of an LLM-based coding tool (CBC-AID), a single-prompt and a multi-agent system, coded 957 transcripts from 399 persons in nine laboratory studies with human CBCA codings and known truth status. Bivariate Bayesian multilevel models estimated within-study correlations and standardized truth effects under global rating and weighted frequency. Results: AI–human correlations of the total scores (ρ = .53–.67) fell short of the benchmark of .66 in all four combinations of version and scoring scheme; Version 1 under global rating came closest (ρ = .67, 95% CrI [.62, .72]). The AI assigned higher scores than human coders (0.7–2.7 SD). Truth effects were similar for AI-based (δ = 0.17–0.32) and human coding (0.16–0.24; Δδ = −0.06 to 0.12); non-inferiority was supported for one of four combinations, and human coding itself discriminated weakly. Conclusions: LLM-based coding approximated but did not reach the consistency of trained coders and preserved their modest discriminative validity. It may serve as a traceable supplement to human coding in research; forensic use requires field validation and human oversight.

articles_hidden.title: Intentional Forgetting of Autobiographical Memories: Current Neuroimaging Evidence and Moving Towards an Integrationist EEG-fMRI Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Dhruv Aggarwal; Palmer Smith
articles_hidden.abstract:
Intentional Forgetting (INF) is one of many human memory processes which has gathered academic intrigue in emergent literature. Understood as a conscious and voluntary cognitive effort to suppress the recall of, or remove certain memories, INF has been extensively studied in associative paradigms. However, its application to autobiographical memory (AM) remains under-investigated, especially within neuroimaging studies. First, we summarize existing neuroimaging literature on intentional forgetting of autobiographical memories (INF-AM). Upon reviewing, we found evidence to be fragmented, providing no clear consensus around the neural bases of INF-AM. We argue this fragmentation is, in part, a result of a reliance on single-modality applications of electroencephalograph (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) methodology. 
EEG and fMRI, however, are complementary in their respective temporal and spatial superiority. Subsequently, we propose the application of an EEG-fMRI integrationist approach to INF-AM. We discuss how its application may help address conceptual, paradigm-level, and methodological concerns. Since human AM and the process of forgetting are inherently longitudinal, we contrast the popular cross-sectional design with a longitudinal alternative. We then present the application of the integrationist approach to longitudinal INF-AM designs. Though cognizant of the limitations that may accompany such an approach, we present the integrationist approach as a much needed and promising way forward in decoding the neuroscience of INF-AM.

Keywords: intentional forgetting, autobiographical memory, neuroimaging, EEG-fMRI, integrationist

articles_hidden.title: Neural representations and adaptive states in human action control
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Beste
articles_hidden.abstract: Adaptive behaviour requires goals to remain effective while actions are revised when circumstances change. This chapter integrates a collaborative research programme with wider theories and findings on cognitive control, episodic memory, neural dynamics, and clinical variation. It develops a selective narrative synthesis centred on the content, stability, retrieval, and reconfiguration of perception–action representations. Established accounts of goal maintenance, conflict monitoring, proactive and reactive control, and the expected value of control provide complementary explanations of how control is recruited. Event coding and binding–retrieval frameworks specify the representations on which these adjustments operate. EEG decomposition and multivariate analyses help distinguish representational contents and their temporal organisation, while oscillatory and connectivity findings identify candidate processes for coordinating their use. Aperiodic activity offers a further perspective on task-dependent processing biases, but pharmacological and biophysical evidence limits its interpretation as a unique measure of excitation–inhibition balance or metacontrol. Intervention studies connect neural dynamics with neurochemical modulation, while demonstrating dependence on baseline state, experience, and the operation targeted. Developmental and clinical evidence reveals both shared constraints and dissociable routes to similar behavioural outcomes. The proposed integration links representational operations, neural coordination, and control policy through testable predictions. It retains distinctions between descriptive markers, computational explanations, causal influences, and clinical benefit. Progress depends on separating competing accounts experimentally, establishing measurement reliability, and testing generalisation across tasks, samples, and settings.

articles_hidden.title: THE EVOLUTION OF DYSLEXIA AS A MEDICAL, EDUCATIONAL, AND SOCIAL CONCEPT: A CONCEPTUAL ANALYSIS OF DYSLEXIA
articles_hidden.authors: Tyler Ogata
articles_hidden.abstract: Phenomena relating to reading difficulties assume many names but none more controversial than dyslexia. Previous historical accounts of the so-called “dyslexia debates” (Elliott & Grigorenko, 2024b; Kirby, 2020) focus on definitions of dyslexia that incorporate the assumption that dyslexia results from some specific, albeit not completely understood, neurobiological etiology of specific reading challenges. Similar disagreements appear presently in the form of competing conceptualizations of dyslexia (Elliott, 2020; Odegard et al., 2024) and their influence on the International Dyslexia Association’s 2025 definition of dyslexia. The ensuing conceptual analysis examines dyslexia according to its past, present, and possible future conceptualizations by highlighting the varied contexts in which dyslexia evolved, namely the fields of medicine, education, and disability. The analysis reveals that the concept of dyslexia has become entangled in paradigmatic differences between these contexts. It is suspected that these differences will continue to subject dyslexia to the same old debates and limit the translation of developing thought on dyslexia into meaningful service delivery systems. A sketch of an integrative framework is proposed to guide dyslexia’s future.

articles_hidden.title: Historical Trends in Associations of Caregiver Knowledge of Whereabouts and Perceived Cannabis Use Among Friends With Cannabis Use Frequency Among Chilean Adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Mauro P. Olivera; Diego Manríquez-Robles; Luis Sáenz-Herrera
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescent cannabis use is associated with family and peer contexts, but whether these associations vary across historical periods is uncertain. We analyzed 12 repeated cross-sectional waves of the Chilean National School Population Survey on Drug Use (2001-2023; 636,008 records). Wave-specific Spearman correlations were estimated using complete cases, with sampling variances and within-wave covariance matrices obtained from 5,000 stratified course-cluster bootstrap replicates. Random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression used Hartung-Knapp small-sample inference; subgroup interactions used wave-delete jackknife tests. Complete-series unweighted estimates were primary because final expansion weights were unavailable for three waves; supported-wave weighted analyses were sensitivity checks. Caregiver knowledge of whereabouts was inversely associated with cannabis use frequency (pooled ρ = -.200, 95% CI [-.212, -.189]), while perceived regular cannabis use among friends was more strongly and positively associated (pooled ρ = .427, 95% CI [.408, .445]). Neither overall historical trend was significant under small-sample inference (knowledge: β = .0014, p = .065; friends: β = -.0027, p = .109). Weighted sensitivity supported attenuation for knowledge (β = .0027, p = .007). Peer-use trends differed by sex and family structure, whereas knowledge trends did not. These repeated cross-sectional findings indicate strong, persistent associations but limited evidence for a uniform historical change. The subgroup variation and sensitivity dependence emphasize cautious interpretation.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable prospective effects between shame, loneliness, and non-suicidal self-injury among Chinese adolescents: A reassessment of Chen et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Chen et al. argued that shame and loneliness play a role in the longitudinal emergence of non-suicidal self-injury among adolescents. However, significant cross-lagged parameters do not by themselves establish genuine prospective influence because similar estimates may arise through alternative statistical processes. Using simulated data that reproduced the sample size and correlation matrix reported by Chen et al., we examined whether their conclusions were robust across several defensible analytic specifications. The pattern of results depended strongly on analytic choice: some models suggested positive prospective associations, whereas others indicated negative or null effects. When estimates from all specifications were combined using meta-analytic methods, no overall effect reached statistical significance. Accordingly, the available evidence does not provide a firm basis for concluding that shame, loneliness, and non-suicidal self-injury exert reciprocal prospective influences on one another. In line with multiverse-analysis recommendations, conclusions should be drawn from the collective pattern across reasonable analytical alternatives rather than from a single model.

articles_hidden.title: When does cortical coherence carry shared content? Compatibility and self-reconstruction as testable conditions
articles_hidden.authors: Sebastian Bobadilla-Suarez
articles_hidden.abstract: Synchrony accounts treat collective phase order as the mechanism that integrates distributed cortical activity. We show formally that shared content and a self-model each need a condition beyond phase order, and state it. Three conditions are separated: coherence (collective phase order), compatibility (agreement of independently decoded local descriptions where regions overlap) and self-reconstruction (accurate recovery of the global state from an internal encoding). Compatible local descriptions determine a unique global state. Coherence bounds disagreement between overlapping descriptions only through shared encoders of bounded sensitivity, and the bound grows as the square root of the population read: on one simulated cortical sheet it constrains at most 10 sites, chaining through overlapping patches extends it to 0.312 mm, and across distant regions the link from coherence to content is an assumption. A contracting self-map fixes one state but reconstructs accurately only states within a diameter set by its error and contraction factor. Lean 4 verifies these implications; one model satisfies all connecting hypotheses at once, showing consistency, not cortical realization. The conditions yield a disconfirmable comparison: at matched phase coherence and single-region decoding accuracy, decoders fitted independently on two regions should agree more, beyond their separate accuracies, on perceived than on unperceived stimuli classified by a no-report marker. Choosing the overlapping regions by what each decodes makes the unity correlate operational relative to a pre-registered decoder and criterion. An exploratory EEG analysis is a measurement check only. Unity and a minimal self remain interpretations that need an independent experiential endpoint.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Dementia
articles_hidden.authors: William Goette
articles_hidden.abstract: Dementia is a progressive syndrome characterized by neurodegeneration across distributed brain networks that results in cognitive, behavioral, and functional declines. Conventional psychoeducation provides disease facts and resources but often lacks the mechanistic grounding needed to translate knowledge into durable caregiver skills. Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) extends traditional approaches by offering brain-based explanations of symptoms and caregiving challenges, paired with learning principles optimized for stressed learners. This chapter proposes a dementia-specific NIPE framework grounded in network-level neuroscience and cognitive reserve, specifying core content domains across the disease course, delivery structures, and mechanism of efficacy. The chapter synthesizes evidence for effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, cultural adaptation, clinician training, and outcome measurement, presenting NIPE as a pragmatic approach to strengthening person-centered dementia care.

articles_hidden.title: Children’s Behavior to Response-Independent Stimuli: A Replica of Wagner and Morris’ (1987) Superstition Experiment
articles_hidden.authors: Karen Henao; Erika Garcia; Alvaro Arturo Clavijo-Alvarez; Mónica Arias-Higuera; Camilo Hurtado-Parrado
articles_hidden.abstract: Skinner (1948) dubbed the idiosyncratic responses of pigeons exposed to noncontingent accidental or adventitious reinforcement “superstitious”. According to Skinner’s interpretation, the rate of these responses is expected to be higher under richer, non-contingent schedules (e.g., FT15s) than under leaner schedules (e.g., FT30s). However, children’s response rate in replications of Skinner’s superstition experiment did not show a clear difference between FT15s and FT30s schedules. This study evaluated whether the response rate was higher during an FT15s or an FT45s schedule by replicating Wagner and Morris’ (1987) methodology. Five-year-old children played with a tablet application in which they received virtual balls independently of their behavior. We expected that the response rate of idiosyncratic responses displayed during the game should have been higher under the FT15s schedule than under the FT45s, as accidental reinforcement frequency is higher. Our findings did not conform to Skinner’s interpretation. An approach based on stimulus control and behavioral systems better accounts for our results.

articles_hidden.title: STORM: Study of Open Research Methods in Undergraduate Psychology Students
articles_hidden.authors: Marta Topor; Charlotte Bradley; Kait Clark; Emily Kate Farran; Adele Lindsay; Su Morris; Bertil Wegmann; Ashley Yvette Williams; Priya Silverstein; Katie Anne Gilligan-Lee
articles_hidden.abstract: The open research movement reflects an ongoing research culture change that aims to tackle issues of research replicability, reduce the use of questionable research practices, and improve the quality of research. We argue that a cornerstone of changing research culture in the psychological sciences and increasing the use and implementation of open research practices is through the training and development of junior researchers, i.e., undergraduate/bachelor students. In this paper, we present findings from the Study of Open Research Methods (STORM), which investigated understanding (contextual and situational perceptions, awareness, and experience) of the replication crisis and open research in undergraduate psychology students in the UK for the first time. Cross-sectional data were collected over three waves (2020-2022) with a total of 2,063 student responses. Our findings provide benchmarks of psychology student understanding of the replication crisis and open research across the UK. The most consistent predictor was students’ year of study, reflecting increasing open research knowledge and experience over the course of their psychology programmes. In Wave 1, this predictor showed evidence of an effect only for universities with a local UKRN lead, whilst in Wave 2 evidence of an effect was present for the other universities on some of the outcome measures. Our exploratory findings reflect a likely increase in open research teaching between 2020 and 2022 in universities with a local UKRN lead. This paper highlights areas for student improvement in open research understanding and teaching gaps in undergraduate research methods training.

articles_hidden.title: The Impact of Effectiveness of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) on Mindfulness and Perceived Stress in Healthy Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Ampere A. Tseng
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper reviews and examines the effectiveness of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) interventions in enhancing mindfulness and mitigating stress-related symptoms. Drawing on trial data from 13 selected studies involving 574 generally healthy adults, this research seeks to establish a robust correlation between heightened mindfulness and reduced perceived stress. We assessed mindfulness using the Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MAAS) and measured stress reductions through self-reported questionnaires. Normalized effectiveness scores, calculated as percentages from pre-intervention baselines, enabled linear regression analyses. To ensure the integrity of our findings, we rigorously controlled for external influences by isolating MBSR as the exclusive intervention and MAAS as the sole mindfulness measurement. Aggregate data confirm positive outcomes: mindfulness improvements ranged from 3.77% to 26.80%, and stress reductions varied from 8.41% to 49.05%. Linear regression trendlines reveal a strong positive correlation between increased mindfulness and decreased perceived stress. This highlights the profound benefits of MBSR interventions in enhancing mental well-being and suggests their potential for widespread integration into mental health initiatives. Ultimately, this article not only underscores MBSR's role in promoting mental well-being but also offers a quantitative framework for predicting health outcomes based on mindfulness levels.

articles_hidden.title: Approach-avoidance contingencies shape expression memory and valence evaluation
articles_hidden.authors: Arijit De; Kinkini; Jeeviga Yasokaran; Ashvit Varaganti; William A. Cunningham; Adrian Nestor
articles_hidden.abstract: Facial expressions guide approach and avoidance, but actions toward a person may also change how that person is later represented. We tested whether learned action-category relations shape the accuracy of later expression-memory reports and affective evaluation. Across three online experiments, participants (N = 629 in primary analyses) learned either a congruent mapping (approach Happy, avoid Disgust) or the reversed mapping. Experiment 1 implemented approach and avoidance as looming and receding faces; Experiments 2-3 used stationary faces and response-contingent monetary progress, and Experiment 3 changed both identities and target-expression intensity. After training, participants reported previously encountered expressions using an identity-cued continuous-report wheel built from neural-network-generated expression continua and rated faces for valence and arousal. Reversing the mapping produced a crossover interaction: each expression category was reported more accurately when assigned to approach than to avoidance. This crossover persisted after exact chance adjustment and controls for face-recognition ability and final rule sensitivity. Further, each category was rated more positively when approached; this evaluative effect extended to once-exposed identities in Experiments 1–2 and never-trained identities in Experiment 3. No corresponding arousal interaction was detected. These findings identify learned action-category relations as a source of structure in subsequent expression-memory accuracy and evaluation, linking action learning to the reporting of remembered emotional content and the evaluation of new category members.

articles_hidden.title: Predicting the Sustainability of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) Effects: The Influence of Baseline Mindfulness on Longitudinal Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Ampere A. Tseng
articles_hidden.abstract: This article examines the influence of baseline mindfulness on the effectiveness of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) interventions. Data from twelve MBSR studies (568 participants) were analyzed to assess changes in mindfulness and stress over an eight-week intervention and a subsequent two-month follow-up. The findings show that MBSR significantly enhances mindfulness and reduces stress (17–28%), with individuals exhibiting lower baseline mindfulness experiencing the greatest gains in both outcomes. However, evidence for sustained mindfulness enhancement beyond the intervention period is weak, suggesting that while baseline mindfulness may represent a stable trait, mindfulness cultivated during MBSR functions more as a transient state. Concluding remarks summarize the main findings and outline directions for future research on the durability of mindfulness-based intervention effects during follow-up periods.

articles_hidden.title: Nonconscious Threat Extinction Using Mid-Level Visual Features
articles_hidden.authors: Jamie Greer; Annika Inampudi; Patrick Mair; Joseph E. Dunsmoor; Talia Konkle; Elizabeth A. Phelps
articles_hidden.abstract: Exposure therapy is an effective treatment for emotional memory-related disorders, but it can be aversive because it requires repeated confrontation with feared stimuli. We explored an alternative using “texforms,” unrecognizable stimuli derived from images of animals and objects that preserve mid-level visual features and evoke similar ventral visual stream brain activation patterns. Participants underwent threat Acquisition using recognizable images of animals and objects, with exemplars from one category intermittently paired with shock (CS+) and exemplars from the other never paired with shock (CS-). During Extinction, participants viewed new images of animals and objects (conventional extinction), texform versions of those images (texform extinction), or a neutral video (no extinction), all without shock. At Test, participants viewed novel recognizable images of animals and objects. Only the no extinction group exhibited higher skin conductance responses to CS+ than CS- exemplars beyond the first few Test trials. These findings suggest that exposure to the mid-level visual features of learned aversive stimuli can attenuate learned threat responses through nonconscious extinction.

articles_hidden.title: Unjust World Theory: A Tripartite Model of Justice Worldviews and the Moralization of Inequality
articles_hidden.authors: Gabrielle Ibasco; Azim Shariff
