articles_hidden.title: Bodily Rhythms Bias Temporal Decisions Through Dissociable Neural Processes
articles_hidden.authors: Amir Jahanian Najafabadi; Srishti Mittal; Kayser Christoph
articles_hidden.abstract: Being able to judge time accurately is central to behavior. Yet, judgements of time are shaped by factors such as attention and arousal, and hence our physiology. We studied the relation between cardiac and respiratory states and categorical judgements of sub-second intervals in humans. We asked whether these states relate to specific biases in time judgements and how they reflect in neurophysiological (EEG) signals. Thirty participants categorized tones of 450 to 600 ms duration as short or long, while we recorded 128-channel EEG, ECG, and respiration. Participants' reaction times were linked to cardiac and respiratory rates as well as respiratory phase. Systematic biases in interval categorization were predicted by heart rate and respiration rate. The physiological variables were not predictive of response accuracy, hence reflecting biases in time judgments rather than being tied to sensory precision. We then used multivariate EEG analysis to dissect neurophysiological signals related to interval duration and participants’ choice and modelled the influence of the physiological states on these. The respiration phase was linked to multiple EEG signals during a trial, while heart rate was predictive of choice-related signals carried by EEG components shortly before the response. This shows that cardiorespiratory states are systematically associated with the transformation of temporal information into categorical decisions, supporting an embodied account of time perception in which time perception fluctuates with ongoing physiological states.

articles_hidden.title: Toward a Validity Argument for Automated Assessment from Transcript and Video Data
articles_hidden.authors: James Soland
articles_hidden.abstract: Automated assessment of psychological constructs from interview transcripts and video data has seen rapid technical development, yet the field lacks a systematic psychometric validity framework for interpreting scores from such measures. This paper applies Kane's interpretive/use argument structure alongside the five sources of validity evidence specified in the \textit{Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing} to automated transcript- and video-based assessment, using clinical assessment of depression as the primary illustrative case. We distinguish two design approaches --- item-based scoring, in which large language models (LLMs) rate explicit, theoretically derived items, and end-to-end embedding or classification approaches --- and examine how one could accrue validity evidence for each across the five sources. We argue that the field has concentrated almost exclusively on evidence based on relations to other variables (convergent validity against self-report criteria) while leaving response process and consequential evidence largely unaddressed. Further, we argue that construct validity evidence is often dismissed too quickly, especially for end-to-end approaches. Both evidence sources require fundamental reconceptualization for automated behavioral measures, and we propose reinterpretations suited to this context. Although the analysis centers on depression, the framework applies broadly to any construct assessed from passively collected video or transcript data. Implications for the design of future validation studies are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: No convincing evidence for a mediated effect of childhood trauma on alexithymia among patients with depression: A reevaluation of Zhou et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Using the covariance matrix reported by Zhou et al., we reexamined the evidence underlying their proposed mediation model linking childhood trauma and alexithymia in individuals with depression. Our analyses show that the same covariance structure is equally compatible with a conceptually distinct latent-variable framework that does not require the directional pathway advanced in the original study. In this competing model, self-reported childhood trauma, sleep disturbances, anhedonia, and alexithymia are viewed as manifestations of a broader latent factor, core self-evaluation. The findings highlight a general challenge in the interpretation of observational data: the same pattern of associations may often be accounted for by multiple theoretically plausible models. Consequently, correlational evidence alone offers limited justification for privileging one explanatory account over others. Consideration of alternative models should therefore constitute a standard component of efforts to infer psychological mechanisms from observational findings.

articles_hidden.title: AI Mindset – An Empirically Tested Theoretical Framework on the Psychological Factors Shaping AI Competence and AI Use
articles_hidden.authors: Shuyan Feng; Martin J. Koch; Astrid Carolus
articles_hidden.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful tool in the educational sector. Research
examining the factors that facilitate its practical application by teachers has increased
substantially. Although empirical studies highlight the importance of psychological factors in
shaping engagement with AI technologies, the systematic integration of cognitive, emotional,
and motivational variables into AI use research remains fragmented. To advance the
psychological foundation, the present study proposed and empirically tested a model for AI
Mindset, conceptualised based on prior psychological and social-cognitive theories. The AI
Mindset framework posits a triadic structure, comprising dispositional factors, contextual and
situational characteristics, and technology-related appraisals, to explain teachers’ use of AI.
Structural equation modelling of 224 teachers revealed that AI Mindset variables significantly
predict pedagogical AI competence and AI use. Specifically, dispositional factors of openness
and need for relatedness associated with AI use indirectly through pedagogical AI
competence. Contextual and social facilitations of habit demonstrated the strongest direct
effect on AI use and indirect effect via competence. In terms of technology-related appraisals,
fear showed a complex pattern, with a positive direct effect on AI use but a negative indirect
effect through AI competence. The effect of effort expectancy was fully mediated by
competence, whereas hedonic motivation exerted a direct positive effect on AI use. In sum, by
introducing and empirically testing the AI Mindset framework, the present study integrates a
psychological perspective into the AI use research, provides a foundation for understanding
AI-related use patterns, and informs professional development and AI technology design.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Rules of Thumb: Empirical Sample Size Requirements for Detecting Institutional Effects in the context of Therapist Effects
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Segundo Pena Loray; Björn S. Siepe; Miriam Ina Hehlmann; Anne-Katharina Deisenhofer; Robin Anno Wester; Julian Rubel
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Multilevel modelling of therapist effects (TE) and institutional effects (IE) is standard in psychotherapy research, yet empirical sample-size guidance is scarce for TE and virtually absent for IE. Existing recommendations rely on rules of thumb from two-level designs that vary widely across sources and do not extend to three-level structures. We aimed to provide empirically derived design recommendations for reliably detecting TE and IE in three-level psychotherapy studies. Methods: We conducted a fully factorial Monte Carlo simulation crossing six design factors: true TE, true IE, patient allocation (balanced vs. unbalanced), patients per therapist, therapists per institution, and number of institutions. This yielded 52,488 unique conditions, each with 1,000 replications. For every condition we fitted a three-level random-intercept model and derived parametric bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for both intraclass correlations, evaluating bias, RMSE, coverage, and statistical power at three pre-registered thresholds. Results: Detecting TE was feasible across a wide range of realistic designs, requiring as few as 10 to 40 total therapists for moderate effects (TE ≥ 0.05). Detecting IE, in contrast, was strongly constrained by the number of institutions: no design with fewer than four institutions reached 80% power at the primary threshold, and adequate detection of small to moderate IE (≤ 0.20) required at least five institutions with substantial within-institution sampling. Conclusion: Reliably detecting IE imposes qualitatively different design requirements than TE, particularly regarding the minimum number of institutions. We provide cutoff tables and a Shiny application to support empirically informed sample-size decisions.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding Creativity in Human–AI Collaboration:  How Cognitive Strategies and Student Profiles Relate to Students’ Creativity
articles_hidden.authors: Kim van Broekhoven; Marian Hickendorff
articles_hidden.abstract: Creativity is widely recognized as a critical competency for addressing the complex challenges of the twenty-first century. At the same time, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming how students learn, think, and solve problems in higher education. In human-AI collaboration, this study first identified students’ cognitive strategies in GenAI-supported contexts, and examined the relationship between the cognitive strategy used and the creativity (i.e., originality and quality) of each idea. Second, this study identified latent profiles of students’ cognitive strategy use, and their relationship with creativity. Using a novel process-oriented theoretical framework and a combination of deductive and inductive analyses, six cognitive strategies were identified: repeat, unmediated, experiential, conceptual combination, semantic, and assumption reversal. A laboratory-based observational study involving 146 undergraduate students showed that constructive cognitive strategies (conceptual combination and semantic) were more frequently associated with highly original ideas than active cognitive strategies (unmediated and experiential), whereas no differences were found for idea quality. Furthermore, latent profile analysis identified four distinct profiles of human–AI collaboration: Largely Independent Thinkers, AI-Constructive Combiners, AI-Balanced Thinkers, and AI-Reliant Reproducers. Although the profiles did not differ in their average originality, they differed significantly in their average quality. Students classified as AI-Constructive Combiners, AI-Balanced Thinkers, and AI-Reliant Reproducers produced ideas of higher quality than the Largely Independent Thinkers. These findings demonstrate that the way students cognitively engage with GenAI shapes their creativity and provide insights for fostering effective human–AI collaboration in higher education.

articles_hidden.title: An optimal parameter range for tactile symbol recognition using a Haptic Mesh
articles_hidden.authors: Yu Cheng; Kenji Yamaguchi; Daniel Zymelka; Toshihiro Takeshita; Tatsuhiro Nakamura; Hiroki Togo; Kenji Yoshinaga; Takashi Hanakawa
articles_hidden.abstract: Tactile stimulation offers a potential means of conveying symbolic information when visual or auditory communication is unavailable or impractical. However, the temporal conditions required for reliable recognition of complex tactile symbols remain unclear. We systematically examined how stimulus duration (Duration) and interstimulus interval (ISI) jointly shape the recognition of digit-like tactile trajectories presented to the palm. Ten healthy adults received nine digit-like trajectories presented through a 3 × 3 vibrotactile actuator array under 30 Duration × ISI combinations and rated recognizability, perceived continuity, and stimulus intensity. We defined an Optimal Parameter Region (OPR) a priori as the largest 4-neighbor contiguous set of conditions with group-mean recognition accuracy of at least 0.60. We identified a cluster of 11 adjacent conditions, primarily at Durations of 200–300 ms and ISIs of 100–250 ms, corresponding to apparent motion speeds of approximately 28–58 mm s⁻¹. Within the OPR, recognition was more stable, and misclassification entropy was lower than outside it. Recognition also varied among conditions with the identical apparent motion speeds, prompting us to examine time allocation between Duration and ISI. Apparent motion speed accounted for 39% of the variance in recognition performance; relative time allocation explained an additional 13%. Subjective recognizability was higher within the OPR and closely tracked objective accuracy, whereas perceived continuity and stimulus intensity did not consistently explain recognition performance. These findings indicate that tactile-symbol recognition is optimal within a range of Duration–ISI combinations whose effects cannot be reduced to apparent motion speed alone, while trajectory geometry imposes an additional constraint on robust tactile-symbol design.

articles_hidden.title: Packaging Psychological Theory: A New Standard for Reusable Computational Models
articles_hidden.authors: Kyra Evers; Lourens Waldorp; Eiko I Fried; Fred Hasselman; Denny Borsboom
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychological theories are increasingly expressed as computational models to improve their rigour, robustness, and testability. Yet in the absence of shared standards for distributing such models, researchers often rely on idiosyncratic code formats. This creates large heterogeneity in the accessibility, quality, and intelligibility of models, making implementations difficult to reproduce, interpret, or extend. As a consequence, computational models are rarely reused, creating a vast space of isolated models with little effort towards theoretical integration. To address this challenge, we propose a new standard: computational models representing psychological theory should be distributed as software packages (e.g., in R, Python, or Julia). Packaged models should be openly available and licensed for reuse, documented and tested, checked by automated workflows, and preserved with a persistent identifier. Unlike static code archives, packages are tools made for users, with a familiar and engaging interface. Their format accommodates different programming languages, modelling frameworks, and stages of model development, giving authors substantial flexibility in how models are formalized and implemented. We illustrate the packaging standard with affectOU, an example R package implementing a psychological theory of affect dynamics. Our proposed standard draws on established infrastructure and best practices from software engineering to improve model quality and reproducibility. Adopting this standard would lower the cost of verifying and reusing computational models for authors, reviewers, and readers alike. In our view, improving model reusability is not optional but essential for cumulative progress in psychological theory.

articles_hidden.title: Crossmodal Congruency Affects Sensitivity but not Speed in Auditory–Tactile Go/NoGo Tasks
articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Andonovska; Ben Godde
articles_hidden.abstract: Crossmodal congruency and interference influence perception and action depending on modality, congruency, and task constraints. This study investigated auditory–tactile interactions using a Go/NoGo paradigm to dissociate effects on response speed (reaction time, RT) and perceptual sensitivity (d’). Participants performed a frequency discrimination task in which high- and low-frequency auditory tones (1000 vs. 500 Hz) and tactile vibrations (100 vs. 70 Hz) served as Go and NoGo signals across five conditions: unimodal auditory (A0), unimodal tactile (T0), auditory targets with tactile distractors (At), tactile targets with auditory distractors (Ta), and a combined condition (AT). In the crossmodal conditions, participants attended one modality while ignoring the other, and distractors were either response-congruent (both stimuli signaled the same response) or response-incongruent (the two modalities signaled different responses). Modality significantly affected performance, yielding particularly slow RTs and reduced d’ in the tactile-target condition containing auditory distractors (Ta). Crossmodal congruency robustly altered sensitivity, showing higher d’ for congruent than incongruent trials, particularly for tactile targets, but did not reliably influence RT. No evidence for multisensory facilitation emerged in the combined condition. These findings reveal a dissociation between speed and sensitivity in auditory–tactile processing, consistent with accounts where crossmodal congruency primarily limits or enhances the quality of perceptual evidence.

articles_hidden.title: Complex coordination through partner choice in baboons (Papio papio)
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolas Claidière; Constantin Montel; Tatsuya Kameda; Yohsuke Ohtsubo; Joel Fagot
articles_hidden.abstract:
Coordination is a cornerstone of social life, enabling individuals to achieve collective goals and maintain group cohesion. In non-human primates, coordination can rely on flexible partner-dependent strategies, but the interplay between these strategies and partner choice remains poorly understood. Here, we introduced a complex anti-matching coordination task to a group of Guinea baboons (Papio papio), requiring individuals to select a different stimulus from their partner to be rewarded. We compared their performance with a previously studied matching task, where selecting the same stimulus as their partner was rewarded. While baboons adapted to both tasks, increasing their success rate over time, we found little evidence of partner-dependent strategies. Instead, they primarily relied on partner choice: individuals reorganized their social interactions to engage with compatible partners, avoiding those with conflicting strategies. This reorganization was particularly pronounced in the anti-matching phase, where partner choice was critical to maintain high performance.
Our results demonstrate that, when possible, baboons prefer partner choice over partner dependent strategies to solve coordination problems. This highlights the importance of social flexibility and individual differences in shaping coordination outcomes, offering new insights into the cognitive and social mechanisms underpinning flexible cooperation in non-human primates.

articles_hidden.title: Capturing the Hostile Attribution Bias through Conditional Reasoning Tasks: The Hostile Reasoning Test as an Indirect Measure of Aggressiveness
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Bacher; Manuel Becker; Fabian Hölzenbein; Hannes Krahl; Karl Christoph Klauer; Sarah Teige-Mocigemba
articles_hidden.abstract: The Hostile Attribution Bias is considered a central component of aggressiveness. It is thought to be a rather impulsive mechanism which justifies (reactive) aggressive behavior as logical and reasonable. Therefore, reasoning tasks may provide an unobtrusive means to make the hostile attribution bias accessible to measurement. In this manuscript, we developed such a task, the Hostile Reasoning Test (HRT), and assessed its psychometric properties. In three studies, we found that the HRT is reliable, shows convergent and discriminant validity for a male (Study 1, N=206) and female (Study 3, N=207) sample, and demonstrates incremental validity beyond self-reported aggressiveness in predicting reactive aggressive behavior (Study 2, N=78). The present results indicate that reasoning tasks such as the HRT are a promising complement to self-report measures, in particular if the more reactive and impulsive aspects of aggressiveness are of interest.

articles_hidden.title: From Epic to Applied Psychology: A Conceptual Mapping of Sanskrit Psychological Constructs and Their Contemporary Relevance
articles_hidden.authors: Manoj Kumar Mallick
articles_hidden.abstract: This conceptual paper examines whether four Sanskrit epic constructs hold structural resonance with four established areas of psychological science. It responds to a growing interest in integrating Indian Knowledge Systems with psychological theory, extending that integration into underexplored epic material. Sanskrit's own literary and grammatical heritage has long been recognised in linguistics and aesthetics; this paper asks whether its psychological vocabulary deserves comparable recognition. Following a conceptual-article design (Theory Synthesis), the paper pairs dharma saṅkaṭa with moral cognition, tapas-nirvṛtti with self-regulation, rasa with affective science, and karma yoga with motivation theory. Four criteria—definitional precision, scope-matching, textual traceability, and precision over popularity—guided construct selection. Constructs were drawn from named episodes in the Mahābhārata, Kumārasambhava, and Buddhacarita, rather than from Sanskrit thought treated generally. Each pairing shows meaningful structural alignment without collapsing into a single unifying model. Applied implications extend to education, therapy, policy, and Gen-Z digital burnout, illustrating the pairings' contemporary relevance. Each pairing was illustrated through a textual episode and a contemporary vignette, grounding abstract resonance in concrete cases. The paper offers four testable propositions for future empirical validation. It also proposes a shared vocabulary bridging Sanskrit psychological thought and contemporary science, without claiming either tradition anticipated or exhausts the other.

articles_hidden.title: Stronger together? Examining the buffering effects of same-ethnicity partners on experiences of discrimination among sexual minority men of color
articles_hidden.authors: Paolo Aldrin Palma; Shayna Skakoon-Sparling; Joel Michel Le Forestier; Terri Haochuan Zhang; Jane Cao; Aki Gormezano; Tin D. Vo; Milada Dvorakova; Joseph Cox; Nathan Lachowsky
articles_hidden.abstract: Group membership and social connections play important roles in protecting people from stigmatized groups against the effects of discrimination on mental health. However, because people can belong to many groups, they may find themselves in situations where they experience stigmatization from others with whom they also share a stigmatized identity. We examine these intersectional experiences with a subsample of sexual minority men of color from a larger cohort study focused on sexual minority men’s health and wellbeing in Canada’s three largest cities (N = 314, nvisits = 725). We examine (i) whether experiences of racism from other sexual minority men and homophobia from other people of color affects the types of partners people seek out and (ii) whether having partners from a similar ethnoracial background protects against the effects of discrimination on mental health. We found that neither racism from other sexual minority men (including sexual racism) nor homophobia from people of color affected whom participants sought out as sexual partners. Having more partners of the same ethnoracial background had mixed protective effects. The effects of racism from sexual minority men (but not sexual racism) on mental health were attenuated among participants who reported more ethnoracial ingroup partners. However,  having more partners exacerbated the effects of homophobia from other people of color. These effects were limited to partners of the same race or ethnicity, and not to partners of color in general. These findings highlight the importance of attending to intraminority intersectional experiences and nuances of the effects of group membership across different forms of stigma.

articles_hidden.title: How Meaning Shapes a Rule: Neural Signatures of Morphological Learning and Generalization
articles_hidden.authors: Marianne Azar; Alec Marantz
articles_hidden.abstract: Rule generalization is one of the most useful tools our mind uses to facilitate learning. In language, we apply it to connect what words mean to what they are made of, such as their suffixes. This is a morphosemantic relation, and it helps us process words we already know and easily acquire new words by composing their meaning. How is this relation acquired, and how does it manifest into generalization for understanding new words? In this study, we investigated the brain basis of these questions through an English-based artificial language study, where learners read sentences to learn a suffix-meaning relation of new words like “thinkle”. Words were either meaningful (places or things) or had no clear meaning. Each suffix family had majority and minority meaning words that participants had to keep track of for testing. For meaningful words in training, we found that higher performance scores predicted higher selective engagement in the left inferior frontal gyrus, specifically the pars triangularis and pars opercularis. In testing, both learned and generalized words, both increased lateral prefrontal cortex engagement. Meanwhile, words with no clear meaning had a much more diffuse brain engagement, recruiting bilateral temporoparietal regions. This resembles the processing of abstract words from previous literature. We found no difference between majority and minority meaning words, especially with the variance in participants’ performance strategies, but found differences in what predicted significant brain activity based on strategy difference. This study grounds itself in the reality of word and affixal semantics with previous research on language learning and universals. Ultimately, it lends a learning paradigm that resembles natural language learning across many languages to carefully investigate its brain basis, while addressing an understudied aspect of rule generalization: ambiguity.

articles_hidden.title: Word Learning Seasons: Climate Effects on Early Vocabulary in Monolingual and Bilingual Children
articles_hidden.authors: Laia Fibla; Krista Byers-Heinlein
articles_hidden.abstract: Children’s vocabularies reflect the dynamic worlds they inhabit, yet traditional models of language acquisition treat environmental influences as static. This study reveals how seasonal variations in weather systematically influence early vocabulary composition. Three studies involving 16–30 months old monolinguals and bilinguals (total N = 1294), examine how climate conditions affect word learning using parent-reported vocabulary checklists. Children in cold-weather regions (Wisconsin, Montreal) produced significantly more winter-related words compared to peers in milder climates (Texas, Florida), while seasonal analyses showed that within populations, winter word acquisition and knowledge peaked in the coldest months and declined during the warmest months. This pattern was most pronounced in older children, and in bilinguals with greater language exposure. Our research shows how children’s language systems adapt to environmental variations, advancing our understanding of language acquisition as a responsive process shaped by continuous interactions between cognitive development, language exposure, and the changing environmental landscape children navigate.

articles_hidden.title: The Emergence of a Distinction between Things and Stuff
articles_hidden.authors: Vivian C. Paulun; Sanghee Song; Elizabeth Spelke
articles_hidden.abstract: Solid objects typically move as cohesive, bounded bodies; they do not split apart, spread, or divide. Yet, non-solid substances, like sand, do. Adults hold distinct expectations for solid objects and non-solid substances, or things and stuff. But when does this distinction emerge in development? Here, we asked whether infants expect sand to be non-cohesive. We familiarized 4-to-6- and 13-to-15-month-old infants with videos of a solid object or non-solid sand. Subsequent test events showed the object or sand falling onto a wedge and either splitting into two pieces or piles or moving cohesively on one side of the wedge. Infants in both age groups looked longer when the solid object unexpectedly split apart, confirming robust cohesion expectations. Yet, for granular substances, infants showed no equivalent preference—neither expecting stuff to be cohesive nor to be non-cohesive. These findings suggest that cohesion expectations develop along different trajectories for things and stuff.

articles_hidden.title: Does internalized homonegativity lower sexual satisfaction? A longitudinal assessment among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM) in Canada's three largest cities
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Meora Kowall; Paolo Aldrin Palma; Shayna Skakoon-Sparling; Terri Haochuan Zhang; Aki Gormezano; Jérémy Lelièvre; Darell H.S. Tan; Daniel Grace; Trevor Adam Hart
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: Internalized homonegativity is associated with lower sexual satisfaction among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM). Though internalized homonegativity is commonly seen as an antecedent to lower sexual satisfaction, existing research tends to be cross-sectional, limiting our ability to make causal inferences. This has important implications for GBM sexual health and clinical interventions. The goal of this study is to examine the longitudinal associations between internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction.

Methods: We analyzed data from a longitudinal study of GBM in Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal, Canada (N = 1307). Using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM), we analyzed data from baseline up to two years of follow-up to model the within-person changes in internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction. The RI-CLPM allowed us to account for the stable differences between individuals that may inflate correlations, thus allowing for a stronger estimate of within-person variation over time.

Results: There were no cross-lagged associations between internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction, but there were significant random-intercept associations such that participants who scored higher on internalized homonegativity tended to score lower on sexual satisfaction.

Conclusion: Our findings suggest that cross-sectional associations in past research  are likely due to stable between-person differences and that internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction may be independent processes. From a clinical perspective, internalized homonegativity may be useful in identifying potential issues with sexual (dis)satisfaction, but reducing internalized homonegativity may not be sufficient in alleviating these challenges.

articles_hidden.title: In-Person Contemplative Dyad Meditation to Increase Mindfulness, Connection, and Well-Being in Young Adults:  A Small Randomized Controlled Trial
articles_hidden.authors: Vera U. Ludwig; Jenny Wey; Mahir Sudad; Boris Bornemann; Elaina Lin; Scott Rennie; Mironel de Wilde; Michael Platt
articles_hidden.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: This study tested whether in-person Contemplative Dyad Meditation (CDM) can help young adults connect and improve well-being. In CDM, two individuals take turns sharing present-moment experiences while the other listens non-judgmentally. CDM was compared to an active social comparison condition, Fast Friends (FF), and a no-intervention group (NI).
METHODS: This preregistered, randomized controlled trial enrolled 119 participants aged 18–35 (82% women, 1% non-binary, 17% men). Participants were assigned to CDM, FF, or NI. CDM participants received a meditation training followed by up to six in-person practice sessions over two weeks, whereas FF participants completed up to six structured in-person conversations. Primary intervention-level outcomes—assessed before and after the entire intervention—included self-reported mindfulness, thriving, and loneliness. The primary session-level outcome—assessed before and after each exercise—was closeness. Secondary and exploratory outcomes included intervention-level measures of affect, depression, anxiety, social anxiety, self-compassion, and empathy, as well as session-level measures of affect and heart rate. Analyses were per-protocol, supplemented by a conservative, complete-case intention-to-treat analysis. 
RESULTS: CDM significantly increased mindfulness compared to both FF and NI, but no effects were found for thriving or loneliness. Lower baseline mindfulness was associated with greater increases in mindfulness following CDM. Both CDM and FF increased momentary closeness from before to after the respective practices. Regarding secondary intervention-level outcomes, CDM increased overall positive affect after the intervention period, whereas no effects emerged for the remaining measures or for FF. However, modest statistical power warrants caution in interpreting null findings. At the session-level, both CDM and FF increased momentary positive affect after the practices, while FF additionally reduced momentary negative affect. Exploratory analyses indicated that CDM, but not FF, was associated with reduced heart rate following the exercises, consistent with reduced emotional arousal. Intention-to-treat analyses showed broadly similar patterns of results, although mindfulness effects no longer survived correction for multiple comparisons.
CONCLUSIONS: We provide initial evidence that CDM can increase mindfulness, positive affect, and social connection in young adults, whereas FF showed benefits primarily for social connection. Exploratory analyses suggested distinct physiological correlates across conditions. CDM involved a higher time investment due to the initial meditation training, potentially affecting comparability. Both CDM and FF may be beneficial for improving social connection, while operating through partly different mechanisms. Given the small sample size and lack of long-term follow-up, further research is needed.

articles_hidden.title: Associations between dark triad traits and affective and cognitive theory of mind
articles_hidden.authors: Lucy Hampson; Caitlin Hill; Kacie Hoyles; Ellie Hunstone; Gareth Richards
articles_hidden.abstract: The dark triad comprises three socially aversive personality traits: Machiavellianism, subclinical psychopathy, and subclinical narcissism. Theory of Mind (ToM) involves ability to infer thoughts and beliefs (socio-cognitive component) and attribute emotional states to others (socio-perceptual component). With conflicting findings in the literature, we utilised a cross-sectional online survey to examine correlations between dark triad traits and ToM. Zero-order correlations revealed negative associations between narcissism and socio- cognitive ToM, and between psychopathy and socio-perceptual ToM. Although follow-up multiple regression models were not statistically significant, psychopathy remained a significant predictor of socio-perceptual ToM once age and sex had been controlled for. Conclusion drawn from these data should consider the relatively small and unrepresentative sample, and low internal consistency observed for the ToM measures.

articles_hidden.title: The Emotional Approach Coping Scales in Hebrew: Validation of Structure and Psychometric Properties
articles_hidden.authors: Chen Erez; Roy Aloni; Nathaniel Laor
articles_hidden.abstract: The Emotional Approach Coping (EAC) scale assesses coping processes related to emotions and emotional experiences during stress. Most prevalent emotion-focused coping scales do not differentiate between engaging with and avoiding emotional experiences, and present and conflate emotional coping with negative appraisal or distress. This study aimed to provide a validated measure for assessing individuals' orientation to emotions and emotional coping in Hebrew-speaking populations. Following backwards-forward translation, the translated version was administered to two Hebrew-speaking samples (Ns = 421 and 309). We focused on the scale's structure via confirmatory factor analyses and on correlation trends with related constructs - emotion regulation, coping mechanisms, anxiety, depression, perceived stress, and self-esteem - examined using Pearson correlations. The results indicated good fit and internal consistency and potential for additional inquiry into active vs passive coping. The scale demonstrated positive associations with approach-oriented coping mechanisms and favorable outcomes such as self-esteem. It also showed negative associations with psychopathology and maladaptive emotion regulation. While this Hebrew version of the EAC can provide a valuable tool for clinicians and researchers interested in individual differences in coping styles, we hope that future studies could recommend cutoffs and test psychometrics within clinical populations.

articles_hidden.title: Cooperative care as a candidate mechanism linking prolonged childhood and brain expansion in human evolution
articles_hidden.authors: Tobias Grossmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Two traits distinguish modern humans from all other primates: an exceptionally large brain and an exceptionally prolonged childhood. What mechanism produced this combination, and why are the two traits dissociated in other hominins? Standard models predict that brain size and developmental duration should co-vary tightly, yet the fossil record reveals that they do not: small-brained hominins at Dikika, Dmanisi, and Rising Star show slow development, while large-brained Neanderthals matured fast. Evolutionary simulations show that cooperative care can offer a coherent account of these dissociations. In Experiment 1, cooperative care extends childhood and, as an emergent consequence, enhances social learning independent of brain size (+32.5% childhood extension with no change in brain size), creating a knowledge–storage mismatch that generates selection pressure for brain expansion. In Experiment 2, when the metabolic ceiling is lifted through allomaternal provisioning, cooperative care populations show significant brain expansion (+34%) co-occurring with further childhood extension and enhanced social learning. In Experiment 3, when populations lacking cooperative care achieve equivalent brain expansion through dietary improvement alone, they instead mature faster, producing brain expansion decoupled from developmental prolongation. The simulation thereby identifies two emergent routes to large brains: a cooperative-care route producing coupled brain–childhood expansion, and a nutrition-only route producing brain expansion without developmental prolongation—a dissociation that parallels the comparison between modern humans and Neanderthals. These results suggest that the distinctly human developmental package may reflect not brain expansion per se, but the cooperative care system within which that expansion occurred.

articles_hidden.title: Continuous-Time Subgrouping of Heterogeneous Time-Series
articles_hidden.authors: Jonathan JaeHong Park; Nathan Xin Mills; Harriette Riese; Omid V. Ebrahimi
articles_hidden.abstract: The clinical and behavioral sciences have increasingly focused on the treatment and modeling of individuals as complex, dynamical systems. This rise in idiographic theories and applications has led to concerns regarding the generalizability of results based on person-specific analyses. Several methodological techniques have been developed to address these concerns via the identification of subgroups. Many of these approaches are based in the discrete-time framework and inherit the limitations of that framework such as sensitivity to sampling rates. As such, clustering methods based on discrete-time dynamic parameters may suffer from what we refer to as, “illusory homogeneity”. We present a subgrouping extension to continuous-time Group Iterative Multiple Model Estimation (cts-gimme) framework which enables researchers to identify homogeneous subgroups of individuals in multivariate time-series. Simulation results indicated that cts-gimme maintained consistent classification of individuals across sampling rates, whereas the discrete-time methods were comparatively more dependent on sampling intervals.

articles_hidden.title: Low-dose cannabigerol (CBG) has different effects on sustained and divided attention in rats
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Joseph McLaughlin; Lily M Bement; Laney R. Burns; Gemma M. DeSanzo; Katarina L. Lords; Amber McKay; Shali A. Slater
articles_hidden.abstract:
Rationale: Cannabigerol (CBG), a non-intoxicating cannabinoid with high affinity for alpha-2 adrenergic receptors and antagonist activity at 5-HT1A receptors, has been suggested to enhance certain cognitive domains. Better-known alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine and guanfacine treat attention deficits, and CBG should produce similar effects to these.
Objectives: This study examined whether low doses of CBG, clonidine, and guanfacine could improve performance on rodent models of sustained and divided attention, while assessing sedation as a potential confound.
Methods: Twenty-four adult female and male Long-Evans rats were trained on a signal-detection task assessing sustained attention, combined with an auditory distractor task to assess divided attention. In three experiments, rats received systemic injections of clonidine (0.005–0.08 mg/kg), CBG (0.3–10.0 mg/kg), or guanfacine (0.1–0.4 mg/kg).
Results: Clonidine impaired both sustained and divided attention at higher doses, accompanied by sedation and reduced responding. CBG produced a significant dose X task interaction: divided attention was enhanced at 0.3 and 3.0 mg/kg, while sustained attention was mildly impaired, an effect limited to the shortest (100 ms) stimulus duration. Guanfacine did not affect sustained attention but impaired divided attention starting at 0.2 mg/kg. Neither CBG nor guanfacine produced sedation.
Conclusions: Low-dose CBG selectively enhances divided attention while mildly impairing sustained attention, a dissociation not explained by sedation or overt motor effects, and distinct from the alpha-2 agonists tested. These findings support continued investigation of CBG's therapeutic potential for attention deficit.

articles_hidden.title: Adolescent Mental Healthcare as a Public Utility: A Multi-Sectoral Economic Case for Proactive Investment
articles_hidden.authors: Mackenzie Swirbul; Emily Peake; Anne Bischops; Marie-Laure Charpignon; Maimuna S. Majumder; Aarthi Padmanabhan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Adolescence is a critical developmental period marked by substantial neuroplasticity and the onset of most psychiatric disorders. Despite this epidemiologic reality, the current US mental healthcare landscape remains largely reactive rather than proactive, leaving nearly half of symptomatic youth untreated and generating a considerable economic burden through lost productivity and increased healthcare expenditures. While clinical outcomes are well-documented, the multi-sectoral fiscal consequences and potential returns on investment of such proactive youth mental healthcare remain poorly integrated into US policy frameworks. 

This narrative review synthesizes evidence from econometric analyses and longitudinal studies across four key sectors: education, legal and correctional, labor market (caregiver productivity), and healthcare. We describe how untreated mental health conditions contribute to high-cost, crisis-driven care, chronic school absenteeism, and increased involvement with the juvenile correctional system, while also quantifying their effects on caregiver workforce participation and productivity. Furthermore, we highlight emerging public financing models that conceptualize mental healthcare as an essential public good. 

Current evidence suggests that proactive investment in accessible adolescent mental healthcare yields meaningful socioeconomic returns. Strategic investment in youth mental healthcare should therefore be regarded as both a public health imperative and a fiscal priority.

articles_hidden.title: Credible Signaling through Sound – the Role of Timbre in Music Recognition in Young BaYaka Foragers
articles_hidden.authors: Matthias Melchior Chanan van der Vlist; Jiaxin Li; Frans T. M. van Schaik; Roger Mundry; Henkjan Honing; Karline R. L. Janmaat
articles_hidden.abstract: This study explored perceptual sensitivity to spectral and temporal acoustic features in music recognition among BaYaka hunter-gatherer children. Using an interactive, non-competitive game (Move to Match), we tested song recognition under various forms of audio degradation to identify which musical dimensions are crucial for recognizing familiar songs. BaYaka children demonstrated robust recognition of songs across unaltered, spectrally degraded, and temporally degraded versions, highlighting sensitivity to multiple acoustic dimensions. We suggest that songs may be recognized despite degradations because of spectral contour processing, rather than pitch and rhythm cues alone. Moreover, recognition performance decreased for duration-degraded songs (“plinks”), as the brevity constrains the cues available to listeners. However, song identification of (spectrally degraded) plinks far exceeded chance levels and outperformed Western adults performing similar tasks. This suggests that onset-transients and spectral shape, contributing to timbre perception, might serve as reliable markers for identifying musical sounds. We discuss the possibility that music cognition evolved for reasons beyond social bonding to support identification of personal contributions within musical exchanges through timbre, which may hold importance in cooperative contexts. As one of the first experimental studies of music perception in hunter-gatherers, this work demonstrates the potential of culturally adapted methods for future cross-cultural research.

articles_hidden.title: Detecting Abrupt Changes in Developmental Trajectories with Continuous-Time State-Space Models
articles_hidden.authors: Marcos Romero-Suárez; Sy-Miin Chow; Pablo Fernández Cáncer; Eduardo Estrada
articles_hidden.abstract:
Developmental trajectories are typically characterized by gradual, monotonic change. But what happens when a trajectory shows an abrupt shift? A child's reading ability may suddenly drop following the onset of anxiety or peer victimization, or accelerate after a sustained reading habit takes hold. When such shifts go undetected, they are absorbed into background noise, obscuring who is affected, when the disruption occurred, and why.
This article addresses that gap, focusing on identifying which individuals experience abrupt changes and when. We extend an existing outlier detection framework to continuous-time state-space models and propose a combined detection criterion (ρ² & SOI) that improves the balance between sensitivity and false-positive control relative to existing alternatives. A Monte Carlo simulation (3 × 3 × 3 × 2 = 54 conditions, 1,000 replications each) compared two model specifications and two existing statistics against the proposed criterion. Detection is sharpest under a deterministic model with process noise fixed to zero, which outperforms the correctly specified alternative and prevents abrupt changes from being absorbed into background variability. Once shocks are identified, a corrected re-estimation with them explicitly incorporated improves recovery of the process noise variance, which is otherwise systematically overestimated.
Knowing which individuals experienced abrupt changes, and when, transforms outlier detection into a practical scientific tool, linking disruptions to their causes and informing targeted prevention and intervention. To support adoption, we provide a step-by-step tutorial, annotated R functions ready to be sourced, and an example dataset that reproduces the full pipeline, applicable to any developmental domain.

articles_hidden.title: A Standardized Protocol for Fear Extinction Enhancement Research
articles_hidden.authors: Xandra Kredlow; Meghan Whalen; Patrick Laing; Lingwei Ouyang; August C. Morgan; Samuel Emerson Cooper; Bram Vervliet; Joseph E. Dunsmoor
articles_hidden.abstract: For over a century, fear conditioning and extinction have served as a foundational model and laboratory protocol for studying how fear is learned and regulated in health and disorder. Several recent innovations in exposure treatments for anxiety-related psychopathology follow advances in fear extinction research. However, the field lacks a standardized protocol—critical given the many consequential parameters in conditioning protocols—that provides a benchmark standard for systematic research on how to improve exposure via enhanced extinction. Here, we present a standardized differential fear conditioning protocol based on international expert input via survey and initial multi-site validation data (n=196; 65% female). The protocol demonstrates expected patterns of fear acquisition and sufficient extinction and return of fear response needed for tests of enhanced extinction. The protocol is simple to implement and amenable to modification, providing an accessible tool for both field-domain experts and allied fields with interest in fear and anxiety.

articles_hidden.title: Unpacking cognitive variability: Dynamic systems modeling to understand daily cognitive change in healthy aging and mild cognitive impairment
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew J. Aschenbrenner; Joshua James Jackson
articles_hidden.abstract: It is increasingly accepted that single scores are insufficient to fully capture the complexities of cognition as it relates to daily life. Many studies now employ repeated cognitive assessments to measure variability in scores across the testing sessions. Exploration of additional characteristics of participant’s time series may provide more explanatory power in understanding cognitive health in aging and early neurodegenerative disease. We administered a standard attention test daily for 3 weeks to healthy younger adults, healthy older adults and participants diagnosed with cognitive impairment. Participants self-rated the frequency of their cognitive failures in daily life. We used an established cognitive model to decompose participant scores into two latent parameters, mean inputs and “dissipation” which reflects the speed with which one returns to baseline performance after a deviation in scores. More traditional summary statistics, including mean performance and variability, were also calculated. Linear regression was used to compare group differences on each outcome and their association with real-world cognitive failures. Results indicate that variability in scores followed a U-shaped pattern across groups. Variability changes in cognitive impairment were due exclusively to changes in the dissipation parameter and this parameter was uniquely related to self-rated cognitive failures. Our findings indicate dissipation may reflect high levels of cognitive reserve, which protects against the manifestation of functional symptoms in daily life. More generally, our results underscore the importance of using repeated cognitive assessments in studies of healthy and pathological aging, as traditional measures of performance did not evince relationships with cognitive failures.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Robin Aupperle; Dalia El-Shafie; Claire A. Lavalley
articles_hidden.abstract: Over the past several decades, substantial progress has been made in elucidating the neurobiological mechanisms underlying trauma exposure and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), including alterations in large-scale brain networks involved in threat detection, emotional regulation, and cognitive control. Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) represents a compelling approach for translating neuroscientific research to impact real-world clinical care. In this Chapter, we first summarize current neurobiological models of PTSD and the growing literature supporting how evidence-based treatments for PTSD, such as prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, or medication-based approaches, at least partially target these neurobiological mechanisms thought to be maintaining symptoms. Next, we review the variable use of NIPE within evidence-based psychotherapies, including first-line treatments such as prolonged exposure (PE) and cognitive processing therapy (CPT) as well as second-line and emerging treatments. We also discuss the availability and limitations of stand-alone NIPE materials relevant to PTSD for clinicians, patients, and the public. Finally, we emphasize considerations and future directions for the field. This includes the need for (a) development of standardized, evidence-based NIPE materials that are grounded in sound neuroscientific evidence, emphasize neuroplasticity, are available in accessible and engaging formats, and are adaptable to diverse populations and contexts and (b) randomized controlled trials comparing NIPE materials to standard psychoeducation approaches. NIPE holds considerable potential to enhance treatment outcomes and reshape public understanding of trauma-related disorders, with its continued evolution requiring further research and development to fully realize these benefits.

articles_hidden.title: Cultivating Flourishing through Yoga Nidra Practice in Students: A Longitudinal Randomised Waitlist-Controlled Study
articles_hidden.authors: Vicky Kachera; Neha Shekhawat; Saurabh Mishra; Alka Mishra; James Gomes; Rahul Garg
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: University students globally face an escalating mental health crisis (Paiva et
al., 2025), yet interventions often overlook the active cultivation of complete well-being
(flourishing). Objective: This randomized, waitlist-controlled study evaluated the impact of a
14-week Yoga Nidra Practice (YNP) module on mental distress and complete well-being at a
premier technical institute in India. Methods: One hundred and forty students (N=140) were
randomized 1:1 to either a structured YNP intervention or a waitlist control (WC) group.
Primary outcomes included depression, anxiety, perceived stress, sleep quality, flourishing, life
satisfaction, mood and peace of mind. Secondary outcomes assessed cognitive flexibility,
visual scanning, processing speed and academic performance. Results: The YNP group
demonstrated significantly greater improvements than the WC group across six primary
outcomes: depression (p < .001, r = -0.35), anxiety (p < .001, r = -0.34), life satisfaction (p <
.001, r = 0.34), perceived stress (p = .003, r = -0.29), flourishing (p = .004, r = 0.28), and peace
of mind (p = .001, r = 0.32). Furthermore, while sleep quality significantly deteriorated in the
WC group compared to baseline (p = .003), it remained same in the YNP group (p = .817)
resulting in a significant between-group difference (p = .010, r = -0.25). YNP group also
achieved significantly greater gains in cognitive flexibility compared to the WC group (TMTB: p = .001, r = -0.32). Reflexive thematic analysis revealed that effective coping practices
facilitated a foundational shift from reactivity to response, cultivating an inner calm that drove
holistic restoration. This central mechanism resulted in significant physical restoration,
cognitive enhancement, and the integration of mindful living into students' daily academic
routines. Conclusion: This YNP module is a potent, scalable intervention that reduces
psychological distress, and educators may consider including it in their curriculum to support
students' holistic well-being, particularly those in high-stress environments.
Keywords: Yoga Nidra, Psychological Distress, Sleep Quality, Cognitive Flexibility, Mental
Well-being, Students.

articles_hidden.title: The development and psychometric evaluation  of the brief Compulsive Pornography Use Scale  (CPUS-4)
articles_hidden.authors: Terezie Babilonová; Halley M. Pontes; Helena Pipova; Táňa Reháková; Štěpán Komrska; Jaroslava Suchá
articles_hidden.abstract: Online pornography use has increased worldwide in recent decades, with problematic use being associated with negative mental health outcomes. However, no brief instrument is currently available to specifically assess Problematic Pornography Use (PPU) by operationalizing the behavioral manifestations of Compulsive Sexual Behavior Disorder (CSBD) as defined in the 11th International Statistical Classification of Diseases (ICD-11). This study aimed to develop the Compulsive Pornography Use Scale (CPUS-4). The sample consisted of 1,023 Czech adults that completed an online survey assessing pornography use behaviors, Pornography Addiction Screening Tool (PAST), Depression, Anxiety, Stress Scales-21 (DASS-21), and Three-Item Loneliness Scale (UCLA-3). Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses indicated a single-factor structure of the CPUS-4, supporting its factorial validity. The scale demonstrated high internal consistency and significant associations with theoretically related constructs, supporting both convergent and concurrent validity. Overall, the CPUS-4 appears to be a valid and reliable brief instrument for assessing pornography-related behavioral manifestations within the ICD-11 framework for CSBD.

articles_hidden.title: Self-Generated Goals in the Age of Foundation Models: Artificial Autotelic Agents and Their Implications for Cognitive Science
articles_hidden.authors: Gaia Molinaro; Anne Collins; Pierre-Yves Oudeyer; Cédric Colas
articles_hidden.abstract: Goals have traditionally been treated as inputs to intelligent systems, biological and artificial, rather than as products of intelligence itself. A growing body of work in cognitive science and artificial intelligence (AI) challenges this framing through autotelic agents — self-improving systems motivated to represent, generate, select, and pursue their own goals. Recent advances in foundation models (large-scale generative AI models trained on broad datasets) expand this research program by extending the languages and tools through which artificial agents can express, evaluate, and pursue goals. By operating over formats such as natural language and code, foundation models allow agents to generate more abstract and compositional goals, approximate human judgments of interestingness and learnability, and support richer loops of problem generation and problem solving. These advances create new opportunities for cognitive science to model human goal dynamics, for AI to build more adaptive autotelic systems, and for human–AI systems to support shared goal exploration without narrowing human agency.

articles_hidden.title: Predicting Across Classifier Systems: Homographic Interference in Mandarin Learners of Japanese
articles_hidden.authors: Chuyu Huang; Yuki Hirose; Takeshi Kishiyama; Itsuki Minemi; Saki Tsumura; Xilai Zang; Theres Grüter
articles_hidden.abstract: Numeral classifiers in languages such as Japanese and Mandarin Chinese provide semantic information that can constrain upcoming nouns. Although listeners have been shown to use classifier information predictively, little is known about how speakers of one classifier language process classifiers in another, particularly when formally corresponding classifiers differ in their semantic mappings. We investigated this question using a visual-world eye-tracking paradigm with 37 L1-Mandarin learners of Japanese and 40 L1-Japanese listeners. Participants heard sentences in which a classifier preceded the target noun and selected a referent from a three-picture display. We manipulated whether the Japanese classifier uniquely identified the target and whether a competitor was compatible with the semantic category associated with the homographic Mandarin classifier. Cluster-based permutation and divergence-point analyses of target-to-competitor fixation ratios showed that both groups used classifier information predictively, with earlier target preference when the classifier uniquely constrained the referent. Crucially, only the L1-Mandarin group showed slower target convergence when the competitor matched the Mandarin classifier category. These findings indicate that advanced L2 learners can use classifiers predictively while remaining susceptible to cross-linguistic competition from the L1 classifier system, consistent with models in which lexical-semantic representations are interconnected across languages.

articles_hidden.title: “For me, it is like a tide: it is always there...”: a qualitative exploration of dynamic suicidal thoughts in autistic adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Mirabel Pelton; Lilian Clark; Xinxin Zhu; Ed Flexney; Martha Enticott; Rachael Adams; Olivia King; Maria Gardani; Rachel L Moseley-Braund; Tanya L Procyshyn
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Autistic young people are twice as likely to die by suicide than their non-autistic peers, but mechanisms driving this remain undefined.  This study explored factors contributing to suicidal thoughts in adolescence (aged 11-15), alongside processes of coping and recovery.  

Methods
We conducted reflexive thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with nine autistic young people (mean age=21.1) to produce conceptual models of: (i) suicide risk; and (ii) recovery. 

Findings
An over-arching theme described adolescent suicidal thoughts as omnipresent, fluctuating, and unpredictably building to crisis. Self-exploration uncovered multiple meanings and functions of suicidal thoughts. Nested sub-theme 1 described the development of autistic identity. Early experiences of rejection and de-humanisation resulted in existential questioning; self-discovery, neuroaffirming resources, and neurodivergent communities enabled agency and a protective autistic identity. Nested sub-theme 2 described marginalisation and social identity. Harmful school environments, pressure to mask autistic traits and invalidation in health services resulted in suicidal distress and crisis. Critical consciousness and leaving education enabled autonomy, purposeful coping and pursuit of life goals. Living well as an autistic person offered greatest protection, but recurrent setbacks and others’ lack of understanding hindered progress. 

Interpretation
Suicidal thoughts and feelings were shaped by interactions between autistic young people and their environment and marked by epistemic injustice.  Findings resonate with the Integrated Motivational-Volitional model’s emphasis on defeat and entrapment; however, defeat was experienced early, and was pervasive and entrenched, while fluctuations in risk were shaped by harmful environments and neuronormative pressures. Findings further support the COURAGE model of suicide recovery, particularly domains for optimising identity, self-understanding, and meaning in life; however, domains dependent on social acceptance and empowerment were less well-supported, suggesting that opportunities were constrained by broader social and structural barriers. Across both models’ structural factors increased risk and constrained the conditions necessary for autistic people to live meaningful and sustainable lives. Clinicians should prioritise neuroaffirming approaches and resources, but lasting reductions in suicide risk in autistic young people will require structural change, including greater equality of opportunity and an urgent action to reduce the distress of educational environments.

articles_hidden.title: Amotivated Solitude: Naming the Space Between Vairagya and Escapism
articles_hidden.authors: Pooja Tyagi; Baljeet Kaur
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent global data indicate that roughly one in six people worldwide experience loneliness, prompting the World Health Organization to name social disconnection a public health priority. Yet not everyone who prefers solitude over social engagement is lonely, distressed, or withdrawing from life. A growing body of solitude research documents this distinction, but the specific combination addressed here, a preference for solitude that is neither reactively avoidant nor autonomously growth-seeking, remains unnamed. This preference is neither the growth-oriented non-attachment described by the Indian philosophical concept of Vairagya, nor the reactive, affect-driven retreat captured by passive escapism, nor the impairment associated with loneliness or clinical depression, nor the positively-valenced enjoyment described by affinity for aloneness. This paper proposes Amotivated Solitude (Preference) to name this gap: a dispositional or situational preference for solitude that is low in both autonomous, growth-seeking motivation and reactive, anxiety-driven avoidance. Drawing on self-determination theory's amotivation continuum, the solitude-motivation literature, and the developmental construct of unsociability, this paper differentiates the proposed construct from eight neighbouring constructs, addresses the risk of construct proliferation (the jingle-jangle problem) directly, and presents a conceptual map locating the construct along a volition-outcome spectrum. It outlines a research program for construct validation, including qualitative grounding, item development, and psychometric testing against existing non-attachment measures, and closes with limitations and open questions for discussion regarding naming, boundary conditions, and trait versus state framing.

articles_hidden.title: An Experience-Sampling Study of Daily Affect and Global Life Satisfaction in the United States and Japan
articles_hidden.authors: Hiroki Hirano
articles_hidden.abstract: Evidence for cultural differences in affect–life satisfaction associations has largely come from retrospective measures, and whether these variations also emerge when emotional experiences are captured in daily life remains less clear. Therefore, the present study analyzed experience-sampling data collected over a two-week period to examine associations of momentary positive and negative affect with global life satisfaction among U.S. and Japanese adults. In both groups, higher positive affect and lower negative affect were each uniquely associated with greater life satisfaction. The primary analysis also indicated a stronger relationship between positive affect and life satisfaction among Japanese than U.S. participants, although this cultural contrast was not consistently statistically significant across sensitivity analyses. Meanwhile, the strength of the link between negative affect and life satisfaction did not differ significantly between the two groups. Considered alongside prior research using retrospective reports, the current findings highlight the importance of both cultural context and assessment methods in understanding the emotional correlates of life satisfaction.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting Cross-Modal Matching in the Light of Luce’s Global Psychophysical Theory
articles_hidden.authors: Katharina Naumann; Jürgen Heller
articles_hidden.abstract: This study presents a replication of the classical cross-modal matching experiment by J. C. Stevens and Marks (1965, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA, 54, 407-411), which examined loudness-to-brightness and brightness-to-loudness mappings.  We extend prior work by complementing traditional group-level analysis with an individual-level examination and by applying the theory of global psychophysics with internal references. This mathematical framework formalizes the underlying mechanisms of cross-modal matching behavior. In matching tasks, the well-documented phenomenon termed the regression effect emerges, wherein the adjusted stimuli gravitate toward mid-level intensities. To model this effect, we implement a novel Bayesian estimation of the global psychophysical model for cross-modal matching. In a sample of seven subjects, including many repetitions at the subject level, the regression effect is observed at both the aggregated and individual levels. The model effectively captures the prevalent nonlinearity in individual matching curves. We discuss the theoretical and methodological implications of these findings and outline directions for future research.

articles_hidden.title: Brain–Environment Rhythmic Coupling: An Interdisciplinary Review of Rhythm Synchronization between the brain and the environment
articles_hidden.authors: Farzaneh Behzadi; Amir Kalantarifard; Dylan Chau Huynh; Lars Brorson Fich; Aja Khalid Hussein; Zakaria Djebbara
articles_hidden.abstract: Rhythm is a fundamental aspect of both architectural design and brain–body dynamics, yet research across these domains remains fragmented and largely descriptive. The absence of a shared conceptual framework limits systematic investigation of how architectural rhythms interact with human brain–body dynamics and may influence cognition and behavior. Drawing on enactivism and the concept of natural attunement, we propose that movement through patterned spaces may convert spatial organization, such as repeated forms, geometric intervals, and variations in light, into temporally structured sensory input. Neuroscience studies have shown that sub-second, strictly periodic sensory stimulation can produce phase-consistent neural responses under restricted laboratory conditions. However, it remains unknown whether repeated, aperiodic, or movement-dependent architectural structures generate comparable temporal organization in neural activity during active navigation. We therefore hypothesize that temporally structured environmental input may align with ongoing neural and bodily activity, a process we refer to as brain–environment rhythmic coupling. To better understand this hypothesis, we first propose a structured vocabulary that classifies architectural rhythms according to their structural complexity, spatiotemporal arrangement, and constituent visual elements, with particular emphasis on visuomotor rhythms. We then consider candidate mechanisms that may support this coupling, including magnocellular processing, stimulus-locked responses, phase resetting, and, under restricted conditions, neural entrainment. By integrating insights from architecture, neuroscience, and cognitive science, this paper proposes a conceptual framework that positions rhythm as a bridge between built environments and brain–body dynamics, while providing a basis for future empirical research on design, action, cognition, and well-being.

articles_hidden.title: Adaptive search promotes asymmetrical learning
articles_hidden.authors: Samuel David Jones; Paul Rauwolf
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent theoretical work has argued that learning trajectories are shaped by adaptive search and satisficing. The central idea of this work is that the value of an information source (i.e., its utility or valence) modulates engagement, sampling density, and encoding fidelity, providing a behavioural pathway to variation in learning outcomes. The current manuscript reports the first explicit empirical test of this idea in adults using a modified version of a multi-step decision-making paradigm known as 'Mouselab'. Across two experiments and six sub-tasks, N=101 participants searched a decision tree at a cost until settling on and executing a high-value policy. While Experiment 1 involved a non-symbolic decision space, Experiment 2 incorporated symbolic cues that allowed us to determine the extent to which associative learning is sensitive to underlying value structure. We found that value-sensitive adaptive search promoted rank-dependent learning asymmetries at test – estimates for the value of the best symbol were near veridical, while those for low-value symbols were at chance. In addition, we found that (i) informative symbolic cues shifted search from balanced exploration (breadth ≈ depth) towards depth-first exploitation; (ii) cue-guided search developed rapidly, with high-value symbol exploitation emerging within a handful of trials; (iii) search evidenced a win-stay tendency and was sensitive to cue valence, with individuals quickly pruning negatively valued branches; (iv) raising cost constrained search volume but preserved its depth-first, cue-sensitive character; and (v) observed individual differences in search behaviour were not predicted by common measures of cognitive function. These results provide new insight into how adaptive search and satisficing shape learning, supporting an emerging theory of the behavioural origins of individual differences in human development.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of task-switch proportion and strategy instructions on cognitive stability and flexibility
articles_hidden.authors: Lara Sophie Knaup; Marcus Möschl; John Dylan Haynes; Marie Therese Bartossek; Thomas Goschke
articles_hidden.abstract: To meet the challenges of daily life, we must continuously adapt to optimize the balance between cognitive stability and flexibility depending on the current task demands. The control dilemma theory posits that cognitive stability and flexibility are polar opposites on the same dimension incurring opposing costs and benefits, resulting in a trade-off. Accordingly, a shift towards flexibility (i.e., reducing costs of task-switching) incurs costs in stability (i.e., increasing interference costs), and vice versa. Here, we manipulated the list-wide proportion of task-switches between a flexibility (75% task-repeats) and a stability (25% task-switches) condition. We interspersed coveted trial sequences with balanced task transitions between strongly biased sequences while retaining the list-wide 75:25 ratios. Additionally, we asked participants to adapt to the prevalent transition type by behaving more flexible or stable. We hypothesized that switch costs would be reduced within the flexibility condition, that simultaneously reduced interference in the stability condition would be indicative of a trade-off, and that both control adaptations would persist within the balanced trial sequences. In a within-subjects design, participants (N = 96) completed two online sessions of a classic cued task-switching paradigm. While we did not observe the hypothesized trade-off in either of the two sequence types, the level of flexibility was adapted within the biased sequences, but this effect decayed within the balanced sequences. Taken together, these results highlight that individuals are able to adapt cognitive control modes supporting cognitive flexibility remarkably fast in response to dynamic changes in the likelihood of local trial transitions.

articles_hidden.title: Rates and covariates of suicidal behaviour and mental ill-health in young Australians: findings from wave one of the Right Here, Right Now national survey
articles_hidden.authors: Jo Robinson; Bridget Kenny; Elise Carrotte; Shu Mei Teo; Caroline X. Gao; Eleanor Bailey; India Bellairs-Walsh; Gowri Rajaram; Deanna DeCicco; Alex Dalton
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: To examine the rates of suicidal ideation, self-harm, and symptoms of depression and anxiety among Australians aged 12 to 25 years, and covariates.
Design: A multi-wave national cross-sectional survey.
Setting and participants: Participants were recruited online from research panels, boosted through convenience sampling. Data were weighted by age, gender, and location.
Main outcomes: Rates of suicidal ideation, self-harm, depressive and anxiety symptoms. Population-weighted descriptive statistics were used to examine prevalence; logistic and linear regressions identified demographic, clinical and social covariates.
Results: N=2,863 participants were included in analysis. Mean age was 18.6; 50.7% (1439/2840) were cisgender men/boys; 4.5% (127/2840) were trans and/or gender diverse. One in three (32.1%, 859/2680) reported lifetime suicidal ideation, 26.8% (748/2787) lifetime self-harm and 8.0% (210/2631) lifetime suicide attempt. Twelve-month prevalence rates were 14.6% (387/2655) for suicidal ideation and 12.5% (347/2779) for self-harm. 38.9% (1107/2847) reported at least moderate depression symptoms, and 34.6% (988/2857) reported at least moderate anxiety symptoms. Rates of suicide-related behaviour, depression and anxiety were highest in trans and/or gender diverse young people followed by cisgender women/girls. Covariates for suicidal ideation and self-harm included loneliness, younger age, depressive symptoms, >2 adverse childhood experiences, and suicide bereavement. Covariates associated with depression and anxiety outcomes also included social exclusion/withdrawal, sleep problems, and alcohol or other drug problems.
Conclusions: Suicidal ideation, self-harm and mental ill-health in young Australians appear higher than previous estimates, and are particularly high among young women/girls and trans and/or gender diverse youth. Findings highlight the need for urgent responses that extend beyond individual-level intervention to address the broader social conditions shaping young people’s mental health. The study also points to the need for timely and robust data that can inform practice and policy and help evaluate new initiatives. Future waves of this survey will help these efforts.

articles_hidden.title: The relation between math anxiety and math self-concept to math performance varies across study math load
articles_hidden.authors: Krzysztof Cipora; Maristella Lunardon; Ida von Lehsten; Gabriella Daroczy; Klaus Willmes; Hans-Christoph Nuerk; Christina Artemenko
articles_hidden.abstract: Arithmetic skills are important to navigate everyday tasks and to successfully engage in the fields of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). Among the factors supporting these skills, lower math anxiety and higher math self-concept show consistent associations with better performance. However, the effect size of these associations is heterogeneous, and the factors that contribute to this variability are still not fully understood. Most of the studies on adults were conducted among psychology students, who may not be representative of the whole population and do not consider the different importance that mathematics plays for individuals’ careers. Therefore, the present study investigated whether the relation of arithmetic performance to math anxiety and math self-concept varies between university programs with different levels of math load. 836 German university students were included in the present online study. They completed self-report questionnaires to assess math anxiety and math self-concept and a timed arithmetic task. We found that arithmetic performance is negatively associated with math anxiety and positively with math self-concept overall, but the size of this association is different across math loads of the individuals’ study programs. Specifically, these associations were considerably stronger among students in university programs with low math load compared to students in programs with high math load. We conclude that the math load of the university program is a factor to take into account, as results from students of a particular subject (e.g., psychology) are not representative of the relationship of math anxiety and math self-concept with math performance and should not be overgeneralized. Specifically, those individuals whose negative attitudes do not translate to lower performance are the ones likely to be enrolled in math intense programs.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring links between type- and timing-specific characteristics of childhood maltreatment and epigenetic aging in formerly out-of-home placed young adults
