articles_hidden.authors: Maria Meier; Eva Unternaehrer; Danielle Otten; Inga Schalinski; Laura Gurri; Marc Schmid; David Bürgin; Vera Clemens
articles_hidden.abstract:
Childhood maltreatment (CM) is a key risk factor for psychopathology, physical morbidity and premature mortality, potentially mediated by epigenetic processes like DNA methylation. While differential links between type and timing of CM and psychopathology are increasingly acknowledged, it remains unclear how type- and timing-specific characteristics of CM are associated with epigenetic measures of biological aging, including age acceleration, mortality risk, and the pace of aging. We thus aimed to explore these links in an at-risk sample of formerly out-of-home placed adults who often report significant exposure to CM and high rates of adverse health outcomes. 
One-hundred-sixteen young adults previously placed in youth residential care (33% women, age M = 26.3 years, SD = 3.6) completed the Maltreatment and Abuse Chronology of Exposure (MACE-X) and provided blood samples to estimate DNA methylation using the Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC BeadChip Microarray. In preregistered analyses, conditional random forest regressions were used to estimate the importance of CM types (abuse, neglect, peer victimization, sexual abuse), timing (ages 3-18), and global measures (severity, multiplicity, duration) for the prediction of markers of epigenetic aging (Hannum’s and Pheno’s age acceleration and DunedinPACE). 
Abuse from age 9 until late adolescence predicted Hannum’s age acceleration more strongly than global CM measures and was consistently and negatively associated with it. BMI was positively linked to Hannum’s age acceleration. We found no association between CM and newer epigenetic clocks (i.e., Pheno’s age acceleration and DunedinPACE). 
In an at-risk sample of formerly out-of-home-placed young adults with high rates of CM, we provide first evidence that parental abuse from mid childhood until late adolescence – a potential sensitive period – was linked to decelerated epigenetic aging. CM should therefore be assessed dimensionally, rather than as a single, undifferentiated cumulative exposure.

articles_hidden.title: Autobiographical Recollective Style in Grapheme–Color Synesthesia: Overlap with Fantasy Proneness and Multisensory Imagery
articles_hidden.authors: Eiko Matsuda; Eiko Matsuda
articles_hidden.abstract:
Although more vivid mental imagery and subjectively richer individual autobiographical memories have been reported in
synesthetes, whether synesthesia is associated with a trait-like autobiographical recollective style governing how individuals
typically recollect their personal past remains unclear. We compared 27 participants operationally classified into a grapheme–
color synesthesia group through large-scale screening with 30 controls selected through individual matching on age and sex.
Autobiographical recollective style was assessed using the Japanese version of the Autobiographical Recollection Test (ART-
J), and we examined the extent to which group differences overlapped with Big Five personality traits, fantasy proneness,
and multisensory imagery vividness. The synesthesia group scored higher than the control group on the ART-J total score
and all seven subscales. The group coefficient was not substantially attenuated in a model that included the five Big Five
traits. By contrast, adding fantasy proneness and multisensory imagery significantly increased the explained variance and
substantially attenuated the point estimate of the group coefficient. These findings suggest that the characteristics of the
grapheme–color synesthesia group extend beyond visual imagery to a broad subjective autobiographical recollective style
encompassing scene construction, reliving, rehearsal, and integration into a life story, and that this group difference partly
overlaps with broader characteristics of inner experience.

articles_hidden.title: Empirically derived phenotypes can reduce diagnostic heterogeneity
articles_hidden.authors: Miriam K. Forbes; John F. Buss; Daniel P. Moriarity; Eiko I Fried; Holly Frances Levin-Aspenson; Lorenzo Lorenzo-Luaces; Kasey Stanton; Ashley L. Watts; Gregory W. Forbes
articles_hidden.abstract: Diagnostic heterogeneity is a longstanding challenge for the classification of mental illness because people who receive the same diagnosis can differ markedly in their symptom presentations as well as in the mechanisms underlying those symptoms. High heterogeneity undermines both the clinical utility of diagnostic labels and the scientific accuracy of research that treats disorders as coherent constructs. In this study, we examined heterogeneity across six internalizing disorders (specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia, generalized anxiety disorder [GAD], major depressive disorder [MDD], and posttraumatic stress disorder [PTSD]) using three complementary approaches to quantifying heterogeneity: 1) descriptive heterogeneity (how many symptom profiles can theoretically satisfy the diagnostic criteria, and how many are observed in practice), 2) person-focused heterogeneity (whether diagnostic labels capture people with similar symptom presentations), and 3) construct-focused heterogeneity (whether diagnostic labels group symptoms with similar patterns of association with external validators). Analyses drew on subsamples from a large convenience sample with elevated psychopathology, predominantly from Australia and the USA (n = 14,762, mean [SD] age = 38.0 [18.0]; 55% women). Results showed that specific phobia was consistently the least heterogeneous; social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia, and GAD had mixed results; and MDD and PTSD were highly heterogeneous across all metrics. Notably, empirically derived phenotypes nested within each disorder substantively reduced heterogeneity relative to the DSM diagnoses. The study provides both a systematic multi-method approach to characterising different types of diagnostic heterogeneity, and a practical path toward more precise and informative constructs that can be implemented by rescoring existing data.

articles_hidden.title: Increasing Youth Engagement with Community Arts through a Youth-led, AI-supported pathway
articles_hidden.authors: Nikki Rickard; Simone Minett; Simon D'Alfonso; Kejian Cui; Thomas Whitford
articles_hidden.abstract: Young adults experience high rates of loneliness, yet existing interventions are often poorly suited to this population. Social prescribing offers a promising, non-clinical alternative, but uptake among young people is low, and pathways remain largely designed for older adults. The aim in this two part study was to co design a youth friendly digital tool that supports engagement with community-based arts activities, and to pilot the acceptance of this tool for diverse young adults.  A participatory co-design approach was employed (Study 1), comprising exploratory youth workshops (n = 24) and interviews with community leaders (n = 6), complemented by a larger scale youth survey (n=269), to understand the needs, barriers and enablers to participation in community-based arts activities for young adults (18-30 years). In Study 2, we used a strengths-based, positive youth development approach to translate the co-design and survey outcomes from Study 1 into an AI-powered conversational platform l, consulting three youth co researchers throughout. The platform prototype (‘Connie’) was pilot evaluated for usability by a sample of diverse young adults (n=22). Survey respondents showed strong interest in a digital discovery tool (84%), with preferences for personalisation and ease of use. Five themes were identified across youth and community leaders’ qualitative data: trust and authenticity, reducing uncertainty, belonging and social confidence, inclusive participation, and lowering barriers to engagement. Connie was rated highly by trial users across all usability domains, with an average of 80% satisfaction. The findings provide support for the viability of a digital tool to support youth social prescribing. Findings suggest that personalised activity discovery can help reduce the uncertainty that prevents many young people from engaging with community-based activities. Effectiveness was also supported by transparency about how AI was used, sensitivity to different levels of user social readiness, and inclusion of diverse stakeholders in the tool’s design.

articles_hidden.title: The three biggest obstacles to solving motivated behavior, and how to overcome them
articles_hidden.authors: Amitai Shenhav
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans and other animals have a wide repertoire of actions they can engage in at any given moment, ranging from moving their limbs to generating utterances to controlling the flow of information from perception to action. What motivates them to engage some of these actions and not others at any given moment? To answer this question, motivation scientists have historically leveraged three kinds of explanatory variables: goals (what directs action), value (what determines a good or bad action), and affect (what it feels like if an action is or isn’t taken). I will argue that each of these variables faces significant challenges in explaining motivated behavior: Goals can explain how actions are directed, but not what directs goals; value can be assigned to an action, but it is a mystery how these values are assigned and how they are shaped by both “cold” and “hot” systems; and affect can explain what actions will make you feel best, but under most definitions affect is neither specific nor reliable enough to guide action selection. My Affective Gradient Hypothesis (AGH) proposes a way out of this entanglement, by re-centering motivation on two sets of processes: prediction and optimization. AGH suggests that motivated behavior arises from the continual representation of potential future states and their affective value, and the dynamic adjustment of available actions and control states to achieve states that are anticipated to be most positive and/or least negative. This account revises traditional definitions of goals, value, and affect to overcome existing obstacles and to provide a complete, coherent, empirically grounded, and generalizable account of what drives motivated behavior.

articles_hidden.title: From Unstructured Text to Causal Inference: Addressing Proxy Measurement Error and Omitted Variable Bias
articles_hidden.authors: Soojin Park; Luke Rabelhofer; Su Yeon Kim; Chioun Lee
articles_hidden.abstract: Unstructured text offers a rich source of nuanced information that is often difficult to capture with structured survey measures. However, Natural Language Processing (NLP) tools result in labels prone to measurement error, which can cause significant bias and invalid statistical inference. Although several studies have proposed methods to address measurement error in text-extracted measures, these solutions often rely on the ``no omitted confounders'' assumption, which is rarely met in observational settings. Addressing measurement error in isolation from omitted variable bias is often insufficient for valid causal conclusions. Therefore, this study aims to provide a rigorous and credible foundation for drawing causal conclusions from unstructured text in observational settings. To do this, we derive nonparametric and parametric bias formulas for cases in which 1) we ignore both omitted confounders and measurement error and 2) we correct measurement error in a treatment proxy while ignoring omitted confounders. Based on these bias formulas, we develop a framework for estimating Average Treatment Effects using a text-derived treatment that addresses the dual challenges of measurement error and omitted confounders. We illustrate our proposed methods using unstructured data from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study to examine the effect of social interaction on cardiovascular health.

articles_hidden.title: Normative Data for PID-5 Items, Facets, and Domains in a Large American Sample
articles_hidden.authors: Ian Shryock; Sara J Weston; Maureen Zalewski; David M Condon
articles_hidden.abstract: In the alternative model of personality disorders (AMPD), the criteria for personality disorder diagnosis are bifurcated into the assessment of self and interpersonal function (Criterion A) and the presence of maladaptive personality traits (Criterion B).  While the Personality Inventory for the Diagnostic and Statistics Manual, Fifth Edition (PID-5) (R. F. Krueger et al., 2012) enables the assessment of these traits, a remaining challenge to implementing Criterion B is the question of what constitutes the presence of a maladaptive trait. In the present study of over 190,000 Americans, we report descriptive norms of the PID-5 items, and facets, domains, and personality disorder composites for a normative sample, as well as for 14 sub-samples that are grouped by age and gender, and we provide item response parameters for each of the subscales. We also include facet and domain descriptive norms for the 100- and 25-item versions of the PID-5. These data provide resources for researchers and clinicians alike enabling the further study of personality disorders and implementing the AMPD in clinical practice.

articles_hidden.title: Occupational Sex Segregation is Strongly Predicted by Psychological Sex Differences
articles_hidden.authors: Joakim Karl Erik Frostegård; Björn Persson; Kimmo Sorjonen; Kåre Hedebrant; Mikael Lundqvist; Agneta Herlitz
articles_hidden.abstract: If traits of individuals are associated with occupational choice, sex differences in those traits should be associated with sex differences in occupational choice, and consequently, with occupational sex segregation. In this cross-sectional study, we assessed the extent to which this is the case for spatial ability, verbal ability, agreeableness, emotional stability, interest in people and interest in things, across 429 occupations. Participants (N = 2,576, aged 35-45) completed online tests and questionnaires, while students rated occupational requirements. For each occupation, the population sex composition of people with traits in line with requirements was estimated, using trait sex differences and occupational requirement profiles. Estimates were highly predictive of actual population sex ratios, with the model assessing interest and cognition in conjunction explaining the most variance (R2 = .49), followed by the interest model (R2 = .46) and the cognition model (R2 = .18). Among individual traits, sex differences in interest in things were by far the most predictive (R2 = .42). Notably, sex differences in cognition were more predictive of high proportions of men in occupations than high proportions of women. Given lifespan trait stability, these results suggest that cognition and interests matter in occupational choice, with sex differences consequently contributing substantially to occupational sex segregation.

articles_hidden.title: Structural Stigma and LGBTQ+ Youth Mental Health
articles_hidden.authors: Erica Szkody; Steven Hobaica; Laura Jans; Tyra Bergstrom; Ya-Wen Chang; Arielle C. Smith; Jessica L. Schleider
articles_hidden.abstract: Structural stigma has been shown to have negative consequences on LGBTQ+ youth's mental health. Most research has focused on stigma at the national or state level, limiting understanding of how local institutions and environments influence mental health. In the current study, we sought to examine the association of multiple layers of structural stigma (e.g., at the county and state levels) on depression and anxiety severity, substance use, and mental healthcare access, for LGBTQ+ youth in the United States. Thus, we recruited 609 LGBTQ+ youth (Mage = 15.6, SDage = 1.17; 71.9% White) to complete survey measures about their mental health and access to care. Further, we extracted 2023 data from Project Implicit and the Human Rights Campaign to create factors of structural stigma at the county and state levels. Consistent with existing literature, our results demonstrate that structural stigma, particularly when examined at the county level (as opposed to the state level), may exert significant impacts on mental health outcomes such as depression, anxiety, and substance use severity for LGBTQ+ youth.

articles_hidden.title: Test-retest reliability of multiple-target search: Eye movements and performance metrics
articles_hidden.authors: Kayley Birch-Hurst; Jamie Cooper; Isabella Foot; Oli Muckleston; Kait Clark
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual search plays a critical role in life-saving careers such as radiology and airport security. Professional searches often contain multiple-targets and while some work has explored factors that affect search performance in this context (e.g., personality, search strategy), paradigms and measures with low test-retest reliability are inappropriate for investigating individual differences. Understanding variability in multiple-target search is an important endeavour, but the test-retest reliability of multiple-target search performance and eye movement metrics remain unknown. Seventy-three undergraduate participants completed a multiple-target search task (0, 1, or 2 target ‘T’ shapes, presented at high or low salience, amongst distractor ‘L’ shapes) across two sessions separated by 1-3 weeks. We measured accuracy, response time, and eye movements, and assessed performance across single-, dual-, and no-target trials. Analyses revealed varying test-retest reliabilities: Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) for accuracy measures ranged from poor (.25 ≤ ICC < .4) to moderate (.4 ≤ ICC < .6), with low-salience (difficult) targets producing higher reliabilities than high-salience (easy) targets. Response time measures were more reliable than accuracy measures, ranging from moderate (.4 ≤ ICC < .6) to good (.6 ≤ ICC < .8). Eye-tracking measures (number of fixations, fixation duration, initiation time, saccade rate, saccade amplitude, saccade duration) had the best reliabilities, ranging from good (.6 ≤ ICC < .8) to excellent (ICC ≥ .8). These results indicate that only some multiple-target search metrics are suitable for assessing individual differences. Future work should integrate performance and eye-tracking measures when considering individual differences in visual search with multiple targets.

articles_hidden.title: Covariance Estimation Matters for Multidimensional Normative Modeling: A Demonstration with Obsessive–Compulsive Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Brian Zaboski; Christopher Pittenger
articles_hidden.abstract: Normative models characterize individuals relative to a reference distribution, but choices used to estimate that distribution may change who appears most atypical. We examined how covariance estimation affects Mahalanobis-based deviation scores when reference measures concentrate at their minimum. Study 1 compared minimum covariance determinant (MCD), Ledoit–Wolf shrinkage, and sample covariance across 11 simulated conditions varying distributional shape, floor prevalence, and contamination, with reference samples of 62–5,000. Estimates and distances were evaluated against benchmarks derived from the generating distributions. All three estimators approached the target covariance under multivariate normality. MCD had the lowest covariance bias in the Gaussian contamination conditions. In uncontaminated floor conditions, its bias persisted at the examined prevalences of .25 or greater, while both alternatives approached the target. Study 2 examined 263 adults with obsessive–compulsive disorder and 62 screened controls. MCD excluded 24 controls whose profiles were consistent with ordinary reference variation. Ledoit–Wolf deviation scores correlated with quality of life (r = −.53). Across five scoring specifications, however, deviation added little explained variance beyond depression and obsessive–compulsive severity (ΔR² ≤ .003). Default MCD and Ledoit–Wolf shared only 17 of the 27 patients in their respective highest-deviation deciles. These findings show that stability of a group-level conclusion does not establish stability of individual characterization. Covariance estimation should be evaluated in relation to the reference distribution and intended use, including sensitivity of individual scores and rankings.

articles_hidden.title: A Strength‑Based Neurodiversity‑Affirming Investigation of Digital Interventions for  Autistic Children in China: Multi‑Perspective Thematic Analysis With Parents and  Therapists
articles_hidden.authors: Vicky Yiran Zhao; Ling Li; Gang Zeng; Zhaona Cai; Huali Song
articles_hidden.abstract:
Autistic children in China often experience disparities in access to high-quality autism 
support. Digital tablet‑based interventions offer scalable potential, yet its real‑world 
performance is inconsistent. This qualitative study intends to understand why and how digital 
interventions can be more effective for autistic children in China using a 
neurodiversity‑affirming framework. Reflexive thematic analysis is conducted using 
semi‑structured interview data from seventeen parents and five therapists after trialling a 
tablet‑based digital cognitive intervention over two months. Participants reported tangible 
benefits including fine‑motor skill gains. However, digital tools required design adjustments 
to accommodate autistic children’s strengths, namely pattern‑seeking reasoning, perceptual 
acuity, and deep‑focus capacities. Effective personalisation relied on alignment between 
digital content and offline therapeutic practice alongside reliable skill‑level calibration. 
Findings indicate digital interventions work best as complementary practice to adult 
emotional co-regulation and scaffolding.

articles_hidden.title: Targeting Emotion Intolerance Beliefs in Young Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial of An Online Single-Session Intervention
articles_hidden.authors: Riley McDanal; Hein Kim; Pau Ortells-Faci; Nicholas R Eaton; Jessica L. Schleider
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Traditional psychological interventions pose various access barriers related to time, geography, provider availability, and cost. Online, self-directed single-session interventions (SSIs) can mitigate such access barriers. However, SSI effect sizes are highly heterogenous. Targeting core transdiagnostic processes may improve SSI consistency. This randomized controlled trial (registration NCT07034027 via clinicaltrials.gov) evaluated a novel SSI targeting the transdiagnostic construct of emotion intolerance beliefs. Method: Participants aged 18-29 reporting deficits in emotional nonreactivity abilities (N = 550) were randomized to the SSI condition or the control and completed questionnaires assessing emotion intolerance beliefs and related constructs at baseline, post-activity, and two-week follow-up. Multilevel modeling was used to assess differential proximal and distal change in emotion intolerance beliefs. Participants in the SSI condition also provided ratings of perceived intervention teaching effectiveness. Results: The first hypothesis — that proximal reductions in emotional intolerance beliefs would be greater for SSI participants than for control participants — was supported at p < 0.001, with a near-medium Cohen’s d effect size derived from a standard regression. This differential benefit was not sustained at follow-up. The second hypothesis — that participants would self-report the activity “somewhat” helped them learn to be nonreactive — was not sufficiently supported, as the mean rating was slightly below the preregistered cutoff. However, participants provided positive views of the intervention. Conclusions: The SSI is a strong candidate for future testing as an on-demand intervention during states of acute distress. Future efforts should examine the conditions under which acute benefits might be sustained.

articles_hidden.title: Nonsuicidal self-injury and approach behavior toward aversive images:  A MouseView.js study
articles_hidden.authors: Sarina Rain; Lily Wanlu Martin; Edwin S. Dalmaijer; Thomas Armstrong; Jeremy Gordon Stewart
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI) is associated with altered responses to self-injury-related cues. However, extant behavioral measures do not capture intentional engagement with stimuli, which may be most clinically relevant to understanding persistent NSSI. 

Methods: We created a novel task in MouseView.js to measure voluntary engagement with NSSI-relevant stimuli using cursor movements. Young adults (N=143) with self-injurious thoughts and/or behaviors histories completed the task and questionnaires assessing NSSI and suicidal ideation (SI) at baseline and 2-, 4- and 6-month follow-ups.

Results: More frequent NSSI and greater SI severity were associated with increased engagement with suicide images (i.e., staged suicide attempts), but not general gore images, across the 10-second viewing period. Greater average engagement with both image types was associated with the presence (versus absence) of past-month NSSI. Greater baseline engagement with both image types prospectively predicted NSSI frequency over follow-ups; however, effects were non-significant when controlling for baseline symptoms.

Conclusion: We provide preliminary evidence that engagement with NSSI-relevant stimuli – measured using cursor movements – may be a concurrent behavioral correlate of NSSI. Effects were most consistent for images depicting self-injury, compared to general gore, suggesting that individuals with NSSI may be especially prone to engaging with content depicting intentional self-directed harm.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Psychotherapy: Understanding How Therapy Supports Brain-Based Change
articles_hidden.authors: Marc L. Copersino; Jamie Berry
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychotherapy can be conceptualized as a structured, experience-dependent process of learning supported by neuroplasticity. Although psychotherapies differ in theory, technique, and therapeutic entry points, they may engage overlapping functional domains of therapeutic learning and change. This chapter presents a transdiagnostic, domain-based framework in which neuroplasticity provides the biological capacity for change and learning serves as the overarching therapeutic process. Five interacting domains organize the framework: emotion regulation and threat learning; cognitive control and belief updating; memory updating and integration; motivation, reinforcement, and habit learning; and social and relational learning and co-regulation. These domains are conceptual organizers rather than discrete mechanisms common to all psychotherapies. Repeated and emotionally meaningful experiences may support changes in expectations, emotional responses, memories, behavior, self-understanding, and interpersonal functioning. The framework also provides a practical structure for neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE). Connecting therapeutic activities with accessible explanations of relevant neuroscience may clarify the treatment rationale, reduce self-blame, support engagement, and foster realistic expectations about change. Consistent with a biopsychosocial perspective, the framework integrates neurobiological processes with meaning, agency, relationships, and environmental context rather than treating them as competing explanations. Domain-based NIPE may help bridge neuroscience and psychotherapy, although its effects on treatment engagement, therapeutic alliance, persistence, and clinical outcomes require empirical evaluation.

articles_hidden.title: Emotion Mindsets at Work: Emotion Malleability Beliefs, Emotion Regulation, and Employee Well-Being in Two National Studies
articles_hidden.authors: Peihao Luo; James Floman; Marc A. Brackett; Annette Ponnock
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotion beliefs are well-studied in clinical and social psychology, yet they remain relatively underexamined in applied psychology despite substantial interest in related topics, such as emotional labor and burnout. Across two large-scale national studies (Ntotal = 3,282), we integrated the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model with emotion mindset (EM) research to examine whether beliefs about emotions as malleable versus fixed functioned as personal resources associated with employee well-being (EWB) for workers in emotionally demanding jobs. We also tested whether emotion regulation (ER) strategy use mediated, and individual differences in ER ability moderated, these relationships. In Study 1, a malleable EM (T1) prospectively predicted more reappraisal and less rumination and disengagement (T2), and higher subsequent EWB (T2), accounting for baseline EWB (e.g., lower emotional exhaustion, greater job satisfaction). ER strategy use, especially less rumination, in part explained the relationship between EM and EWB, as rumination disrupts post-work recovery periods. In Study 2, conceptually replicating Study 1, a malleable EM was also related to healthier ER strategy use and higher EWB. Indirect effects varied by ER strategy, with rumination again showing the most consistent pattern. ER strategy use also mediated the association between EM and EWB more strongly for employees with higher ER ability test performance, primarily with rumination and partially with reappraisal as mediators. These findings suggest that EMs matter for EWB because they may factor into how employees regulate emotions. A malleable EM may be especially beneficial when employees have the ER ability to translate this belief into effective emotion management.

articles_hidden.title: Maternal Emotional Experiences During Everyday Infant Soothing: Within- and Between-Person Predictors from an Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles_hidden.authors: Sarvenaz Oloomi; Alexis Hernandez; Alexa Monachino; Irene Tung; Lauren C Shuffrey; Santiago Morales
articles_hidden.abstract: Infant crying and mothers’ efforts to soothe their infants are highly emotional experiences that shape parent–infant co-regulation and bonding. Despite the importance of this process, relatively little research has examined how mothers feel when they soothe their infants, especially with real-time, ecologically-relevant measures. In this study, we collected ecological momentary assessment (EMA) in a geographically representative sample between September 2022 and September 2025 for up to 14 days to capture mothers’ (N = 250; Mage = 33.2 years, range = 19–45, 51.5% Hispanic/Latinx) emotional experiences during soothing interactions with their infants (Mage = 9.4 months, range = 3–23 months; 52.8% female; 57% Hispanic/Latinx). Mothers also completed questionnaires about their distress (anxiety, depression, and stress) symptoms and their infant’s temperamental negative affectivity. Within-person analyses revealed that maternal positive affect decreased and negative affect increased as soothing became longer and more difficult. Between-person analyses indicated that higher infant negative affectivity and greater maternal distress were associated with mothers reporting more negative emotions while soothing, whereas more positive maternal emotions were related to less maternal distress. Results were present while accounting for mothers’ mood while completing the survey, soothing difficulty and duration, infant age and sex, and socioeconomic factors. These findings highlight that soothing can be a particularly challenging and emotional experience for mothers high in distress symptoms and those with infants high in temperamental negative affectivity, pointing to the need for targeted interventions within this population that support maternal emotion regulation and parent-infant interaction quality.

articles_hidden.title: More effort, more variability, but greater relative precision: Distributional modeling of effort-performance coupling
articles_hidden.authors: Lukas Hack; Katja Rewitz; Silas Wagner; Wanja Wolff
articles_hidden.abstract: Ratings of perceived exertion (RPE) are widely used to prescribe exercise intensities. When used this way, researchers and practitioners may implicitly or explicitly rely on assumptions about the coupling between perceived effort and performance. These assumptions refer to two dimensions: the average shape of how effort translates to performance and the variability of performance across effort levels. Straightforwardly, effort-performance coupling can be thought of as linear, with constant variability across the intensity spectrum. However, classic psychophysical scaling laws (e.g., Fechner’s law) and motor control research (e.g., signal-dependent noise) predict that such coupling is non-linear, with intensity-contingent increases in variability. These assumptions are rarely made explicit and have not been jointly tested. To address this, we fitted and compared theory-driven Bayesian multilevel models reflecting distinct assumptions about the mean and the variability structure, using leave-one-out cross-validation for model selection. Data were collected from 101 climbers performing an isometric handgrip task with effort prescribed using a RPE 1-10 scale. We found robust evidence for a heteroscedastic variability structure, with a systematic increase in absolute force variability with prescribed RPE. Additionally, we found modest evidence favoring an exponential mean shape over a linear mean shape, suggesting that force increases disproportionately with effort. These effects were gender unspecific and are broadly consistent with Fechner’s psychophysical law and signal-dependent noise theory. Together, these findings suggest that a direct translation from effort to performance systematically misrepresents the actual relationship. Instead, practitioners and researchers should expect a disproportionate increase in performance with increasing absolute performance variability.

articles_hidden.title: A School-Based Intergenerational Engagement Program to Improve Older Adults’ Cognitive, Health and Social Outcomes: A Pilot Randomised Controlled Trial.
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Krzeczkowska; William J. McGeown; Alan J. Gow; Louise A. Brown Nicholls
articles_hidden.abstract: High quality evidence on the potential health benefits of intergenerational engagement (IE) for older adults, particularly using relatively moderate exposure, is limited. This pilot randomised controlled trial (RCT) evaluated the impact of a school-based IE intervention designed to engage healthy older adults in real-world activities and provide multimodal (cognitive, social, physical) engagement. Additionally, feasibility of the program was evaluated. The sample comprised 36 participants (29 females, 7 males), aged 60-80 years, who had been randomised to the intervention or a wait-list control group. Intervention participants assisted primary (elementary) school teachers in supporting children’s (4-8 yrs) reading, writing, and numeracy for 8 hours per week over six months, with data collected at baseline and 3- and 6-month follow-up sessions. The intervention was found to be generally feasible and was associated with significant improvements in: cognition (working memory, episodic memory, auditory verbal learning); daytime functioning (staying awake/alert); attitudes towards children; and sense of generative achievement (helping the younger generation). Benefits were typically observed at 3 months and maintained at 6 months. Moderate intensity participation in this school-based IE intervention therefore shows preliminary efficacy as a multimodal health promotion initiative for older adults. Minor intervention modification and full-scale assessment is now warranted.

articles_hidden.title: Preregistration Publication Consistency – A Study of Psychological Research Published by Authors from German-Speaking Institutions
articles_hidden.authors: Lena Hahn; Kai Sassenberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Preregistrations aim at reducing researchers' degrees of freedom. This goal is only reached if researchers adhere to them or at least transparently report deviations. The popularity of preregistration in psychology has increased, and so has research on preregistration publication consistency. However, previous research investigated preregistered publications in specific samples (e.g., a single journal, a restricted research area). Thus, generalizability of previous results is limited. To avoid this limitation, we scrutinize preregistration publication consistency in psychology by coding a diverse sample of journal publications and preregistrations from 2021 to 2024 drawn from a database of all empirical publications by psychologists with affiliations to institutions in German-speaking countries. We analyzed three aspects critical to researchers’ degrees of freedom in confirmatory research: the preregistered hypotheses, the sample size, and the exclusion criteria. Consistent with previous research, our results show that deviations are common, with roughly half of the sample having inconsistencies in at least two of the aforementioned aspects. Additionally, preregistration publication consistency was neither related to journal reputation (i.e., Journal Impact Factor and Transparency and Openness Promotion Factor) nor time (i.e., preregistration and publication year). We discuss implications of our findings for reporting preregistration deviations.

articles_hidden.title: Attachment-Informed Leadership (AIL):  A New Leadership Framework based on Attachment Theory and Social Neuroscience
articles_hidden.authors: Pascal Vrticka; Jonathan Wolf-Phillips
articles_hidden.abstract: Leadership research has catalogued many styles, among them transformational, authentic and servant leadership, but has offered few accounts of the regulatory mechanisms through which leader-follower relationships operate. We propose that attachment, understood through social neuroscience, supplies one such mechanism. Humans regulate environmental demands relationally, and attachment organises this social regulation of a finite bioenergetic budget under challenge. When followers face threat, dependence or uncertainty, this relationship can come to serve attachment functions, and the leader's reliability as a security provider bears on how much of followers' regulatory resources remains available for work. Building on the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment (SoNeAt), we develop an attachment-informed leadership (AIL) framework spanning social allostasis, attachment and caregiving, predictive regulation and biobehavioural synchrony. We position AIL relative to evolutionary accounts of leadership and derive nine propositions that distinguish attachment processes from exchange, trust and identification, measurable from self-report to physiology and brain activity.

articles_hidden.title: Improving Brain-Behaviour Causality with Neurofeedback
articles_hidden.authors: Theo Ferreira Marins; Michal Ramot; Aurelio Cortese; Ranganatha Sitaram; Guilherme Wood
articles_hidden.abstract: A robust and reliable causal mapping of human brain function requires ruling out multiple sources of bias and confounding. New standards for causal inference suggest that the causal evidence provided by traditional methods, such as lesion mapping and non-invasive brain stimulation, may have critical gaps. Based on recent evidence, we discuss how brain-behaviour causality has been assessed in humans with well-established tools, and the extent to which emerging techniques, such as neurofeedback, provide additional insights. Finally, we introduce the Causal-Neurofeedback, a unifying framework based on functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) that dictates experimental and analytical choices designed to address new standards for causality with high granularity. This framework consists of manipulating fine-grained neural signatures and adopting key experimental and analytical control strategies to improve causal robustness. We conclude by discussing the potential of neurofeedback, through this framework, to provide robust causal evidence across diverse experimental contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Pluralism within limits: How to make the idea of multiple NCC kinds useful
articles_hidden.authors: Lukas Kob; Tomas Marvan
articles_hidden.abstract: Recently, several authors have argued that the current impasse in consciousness science supports a pluralistic interpretation: the view that seemingly contradictory findings may both be valid because consciousness can be brought about in different ways, each sufficient to generate conscious experience. We analyze different versions of pluralism to determine under what conditions it offers a viable interpretation of consciousness science. We argue that viable pluralism requires a two-factor framework distinguishing general consciousness factors (mechanisms rendering contents conscious) from content encoding itself. Moreover, NCC kinds must be finite in number and systematically ordered to enable a unified scientific model. While pluralism enables testable hypotheses, significant ontological tensions arise: how can consciousness constitute a unified natural kind if realized by fundamentally distinct NCC kinds? Drawing on philosophy of science, we propose an alternative interpretation in terms of scientific rather than natural kinds. Our goal is not to advocate for pluralism, but rather, to critically examine its viability and implications. Based on this, we urge the field to engage more explicitly with the foundational assumptions that shape consciousness research.

articles_hidden.title: From Morality to the Plate: Moral Foundations, Food Neophobia, and Sustainability Preferences
articles_hidden.authors: Giovanni Telesca; Marika Rullo; Carol Coricelli
articles_hidden.abstract: The present study examined whether moral foundations and food neophobia are associated with sustainable food choices and support for food-related sustainability policies in a sample of 296 Italian adults. Food neophobia (FN), a stable psychological tendency to refuse new foods, has been associated with reduced dietary variety and lower consumption of plant-based alternatives. Moral foundations (MFs) shape individuals' pre-reflective sensitivities to different moral orientations and have been linked to pro-environmental attitudes and food-related behaviors. Drawing on Moral Foundations Theory (MFT), we hypothesized that binding and individualizing foundations would differentially predict FN and, through it, sustainable food outcomes. Binding MFs (i.e., oriented toward purity and ingroup preservation) may function as dispositional antecedents of FN, as individuals who strongly endorse these concerns are likely to perceive novel foods as potential sources of contamination or threats to cultural and group identity. Conversely, individualizing MFs (i.e., oriented toward care and fairness) may reduce such avoidance by fostering openness toward foods associated with reduced harm and environmental benefit. Results showed that binding MFs were associated with higher FN, whereas individualizing MFs were negatively associated with it. FN was negatively associated with liking for plant-based foods and consumption frequency, as well as with policy support. FN fully mediated the associations between moral foundations and affective and behavioral indicators of sustainable food consumption and partially mediated the effects of MFs on policy support. These findings suggest that FN may be a key psychological pathway through which moral sensitivities translate into sustainable dietary choices and policy preferences.

articles_hidden.title: A Crucial Source of Psychological Certainty in Human Cognition: The Certainty Signature of Central Form
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Haward
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans often exhibit more certainty than is justified. Drawing on recent work in Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure, the present paper proposes and tests a novel hypothesis about one important source of psychological certainty. On Form Theory, concepts have a central form: a core structure within each concept that stores a subset of its information, gives that information default influence in cognition, and activates a distinctive set of strong form-generated beliefs. The present paper tests the proposal that psychological certainty is one such form-generated belief. In Experiment 1, participants judged which properties would be present in newly encountered instances of familiar concepts. While they generalized both form and non-form properties to new instances, they reported being certain only for form properties. In Experiment 2, participants showed the same pattern for newly learned concepts. As soon as a property had been encoded as part of a concept’s central form, participants were much more likely to report being certain of its presence in a new instance than when the same property had been introduced in a generic sentence, but not as part of the concept’s central form. These findings help reveal a deep connection between psychological certainty and the structure of human concepts. Further, they suggest that conceptual structure is one important source of psychological certainty and provide a framework for investigating whether strongly held beliefs documented in research on stereotyping, memory, clinical depression, and conflict may sometimes derive from how concepts have been structured.

articles_hidden.title: Using natural language processing analysis to investigate daily-life positive autobiographical memories
articles_hidden.authors: Christina Haag; Lynn Alison Bueeler; David Bürgin; Michel Philipp; Birgit Kleim
articles_hidden.abstract: Recalling positive autobiographical memories (AMs) can improve wellbeing, yet few studies capture these memories as they naturally occur or examine their detailed content. In a sample of 70 community adults, we used ecological momentary assessment to assess naturally occurring positive AMs in daily life. Using the large language model-based Python library BERTopic, we identified eight underlying topics: ‘Friends, partner, family’ (68.42%), ‘Work, study’ (8.33%), ‘Being in nature or the moment, pets’ (5.60%), ‘Family & social events’ (3.69%), ‘Exam success’ (3.96%), ‘Success in sports – self or as a fan’ (3.28%), ‘Outdoor activities and sports’ (3.14%), and ‘School days, studies’ (2.19%). Participants reported vivid, sensory AMs accompanied by positive emotions. Greater AM vividness was systematically associated with greater immediate AM-related happiness, underscoring vividness as a potential amplifier in everyday remembering. By sharing our detailed methodology, code, and anonymized examples, we lay the groundwork for large-scale computational analysis of AMs assessed under the noisy and unstructured conditions of everyday life.

articles_hidden.title: Structure and function of corpus callosum modified by common variation in the ROBO1 gene
articles_hidden.authors: Nea Rinne; Elisa Sahari; Tuija Tolonen; Elísabet Einarsdóttir; Juha Salmitaival; Kimmo Alho; Juha Kere; Patrik Wikman
articles_hidden.abstract: The corpus callosum (CC) connects the cerebral hemispheres and enables interhemispheric communication that supports numerous cognitive functions, including reading. ROBO1, a dyslexia susceptibility gene involved in axonal midline crossing, has previously been associated with CC structure, but its relationship with the functional organisation of cerebral reading networks remains unclear. Here, we examined associations between ROBO1 variation, CC structure, reading-related brain function, and reading performance in 178 typically reading adolescents and young adults. Variation across five ROBO1 single nucleotide polymorphisms was summarised using principal component analysis. The resulting PC1 score was examined in relation to fractional anisotropy (FA) and tract count across five CC subdivisions, as well as reading-related activation and functional connectivity in cortical regions connected by these pathways. A greater number of rare alleles across the examined variants was associated with lower FA in the central, middle posterior, and posterior CC. ROBO1 variation was also associated with activation in cortical regions corresponding to the endpoints of the CC tracts, as well as with reading-related functional connectivity between these endpoint regions and clusters in the left temporoparietal cortex and right temporal pole. However, neither ROBO1 variation nor CC structure explained reading performance, suggesting that ROBO1 may contribute to individual differences in the structure and function of interhemispheric language networks even in the absence of measurable behavioural differences.

articles_hidden.title: Environmental and social context are associated with emotional states and their dynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Florencia Altschuler; Christophe Gauld; Enric Vilajosana; Cecilia González Campo; Pamela Chavarría-Elizondo; Víctor De la Peña-Arteaga; Asier Juaneda-Seguí; Ignacio Martínez-Zalacaín; VIktor Jirsa; Pierpaolo Sorrentino
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotional states fluctuate with everyday context, but contextual influences can operate at markedly different temporal scales and magnitudes. We examined the longitudinal effects of two naturalistic contextual exposures - daily weather (precipitation and temperature) and the COVID-19 lockdown-  on emotional states assessed using ecological momentary assessment (EMA) in a university-based cohort in Barcelona, Spain, comprising up to 25,724 observations from 156 participants. Lockdown analyses were restricted to the subset of participants with observations both during and outside the lockdown period (n=45). Participants completed daily smartphone-based assessments of happiness, anxiety, muscular tension, worry, and avoidance over six months. Within-participant fixed-effects models showed that greater precipitation was associated with lower happiness and higher anxiety, muscular tension, and avoidance, whereas temperature showed no significant associations with any of these outcomes. In contrast, lockdown was associated with a broad shift toward lower happiness and higher negative emotional states and with greater day-to-day variability in happiness, anxiety, muscular tension, and avoidance. These findings illustrate how low-magnitude environmental variation and large-scale social disruption can be detected within the same real-world EMA framework, with the latter affecting both emotional states and short-term dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: Differential Effects of Task-Context and Stimulus-Category Changes on Recognition Memory: A Replication and Extension of Morse et al. (2023)
articles_hidden.authors: Raju Pooja; Pritha Ghosh; Vishnu Sreekumar
articles_hidden.abstract: Event segmentation is the process by which ongoing experience is organized into discrete events, with event boundaries marking transitions between successive events. Although contextual changes are thought to trigger event segmentation, different types of contextual change may vary in their effectiveness and their consequences for subsequent memory. In the present study, which is a replication of Morse et al. (2023), albeit with some methodological improvements, we examined whether stimulus-category shifts and task-context shifts produce differential consequences for recognition memory and mnemonic discrimination. Across three experiments using the Mnemonic Similarity Task (MST), event boundaries were instantiated by changes in image category (Experiment 1), encoding task (Experiment 2) or both simultaneously (Experiment 3). Task-context shifts produced reliable behavioral signatures of event segmentation, reflected by an increase in post-boundary encoding response times, and also led to impaired recognition memory for items encountered immediately after a boundary. In contrast, stimulus-category shifts alone produced neither time processing costs nor memory impairments. Critically, combining stimulus-category and task-context changes did not increase recognition-memory impairment beyond those observed for task-context shifts alone. Across all experiments, participants’ ability to discriminate similar lure items from studied targets (lure discrimination) was unaffected by whether the items were experienced close to event boundaries. Our findings suggest that event boundaries capable of impacting memory depend more strongly on changes that require updating of task-goals and control states than on changes in perceptual input alone. Broadly, our results indicate that not all contextual changes are functionally equivalent for event segmentation.

articles_hidden.title: Business-size bias in consumer dishonesty: Consumers are less likely to cheat small businesses than big ones
articles_hidden.authors: Jareef Martuza; Hallgeir Sjåstad; Helge Thorbjørnsen
articles_hidden.abstract: Consumer dishonest behavior—such as return fraud, insurance overclaiming, and retail theft—costs businesses billions of dollars every year. Yet the potential role of organizational features in shaping consumer dishonesty remains unclear. This research examines whether consumers are less likely to cheat small businesses than big ones, and why they might do so. While certain normative theories in philosophy contend that moral transgressions—like dishonesty—are equally wrong regardless of victim identity, we suggest that consumers perceive small businesses as more victim-like than big businesses, which increases the moral cost of cheating small businesses. Supporting this hypothesis, a preliminary study (N = 13,239 businesses) and seven main and seven supplemental studies (N = 10,436) reveal that consumers are less likely to cheat small businesses than big ones, across economic crime surveys, scenario-based, conjoint, and incentive-compatible experiments. Further, consumers perceive small businesses as more vulnerable and moral than big businesses, which mediates lower dishonesty toward small businesses, and increasing perceived vulnerability and morality can causally reduce dishonesty toward big businesses. Thus, beyond incentives, consumer dishonesty is also shaped by victim characteristics. Managers could benefit from pre-empting such victim-based biases by considering business size perceptions when considering policies to deter consumer dishonesty.

articles_hidden.title: Does the Creature of Habit Scale capture general habit tendencies? Lessons from anorexia nervosa.
articles_hidden.authors: Caroline Monica Harbison; Sanne de Wit; Joseph Wonderlich; Caroline Touzeau; Alexandra Muratore; Hilde Geurts; Joanna Steinglass; Karin Foerde
articles_hidden.abstract: The Creature of Habit Scale (COHS) was designed to assess general habit tendencies, with Automaticity and Routine subscales assessing distinct features of habits. However, the Automaticity subscale is composed predominantly of eating-related items, raising questions about the scale’s construct and content validity. To evaluate this, COHS scores were compared between individuals with anorexia nervosa, restricting subtype (ANr; n = 35) and controls (n = 26), and associations with eating disorder habit strength (Self-Report Habit Index) and psychopathology (Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire; Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire) were examined. Automaticity scores were significantly lower in ANr than controls (W = 192, p < .001). Within ANr, Automaticity was negatively associated with eating disorder severity (B = -2.74, p < .001) and eating-related habits (B = −4.18, p < .001). Automaticity was positively associated with TFEQ Disinhibition across groups (B = 0.39, p < .001) and, within ANr, negatively associated with TFEQ Restraint (B = -0.21, p = .012). The Automaticity subscale of the COHS may primarily reflect disinhibited eating rather than general habitual tendencies, challenging its construct and content validity and suggesting caution in its use as a general habit measure in eating disorders and across populations.

articles_hidden.title: The Case Against the Design Hierarchy in Psychological Network Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Adela-Maria Isvoranu
articles_hidden.abstract: The network perspective conceptualizes psychological phenomena as systems of interacting components, placing dynamics at the center of explanation. This has justified criticism of studies that use cross-sectional networks to claim within-person dynamics, uniquely identified causal mechanisms, or effective intervention targets. In the current methodological climate, however, an implicit design hierarchy has emerged in which cross-sectional design is itself treated as the objection. In an audit of 157 papers across three journals, 65% of 127 eligible papers named cross-sectional design as a limitation and 68% recommended longitudinal research as a remedy. Such a hierarchy mischaracterizes designs operating at different temporal scales: they estimate different structures rather than progressively better answers to one question. Cross-sectional networks can distinguish conditional from marginal associations, characterize the conditional-association structure, support measurement development, identify patterns for replication, and generate constrained hypotheses, particularly when measures represent characteristic tendencies or experiences over a defined period. Longitudinal and intensive longitudinal designs are not automatic upgrades over cross-sectional designs; their evidential value depends on temporal resolution, lag selection, measurement quality, model assumptions, and the distinction between group-average and person-specific inference. Designs should therefore be judged by alignment of question, measurement, model, and claims—not by position in an assumed hierarchy.

articles_hidden.title: Examining the Relations Between Self-Construal, Culture, and Cognitive Dissonance Using the Induced-Compliance Paradigm
articles_hidden.authors: Tim Figureau; Daniel Priolo; Willem W. A. Sleegers; Kenneth G DeMarree; Omid Ghasemi; Amélie Gourdon-Kanhukamwe; Maxime Mauduy; Asil Ali Özdoğru; Robert M Ross; Bjørn Sætrevik
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive dissonance, traditionally conceptualized as a fundamental psychological process involving discomfort from inconsistent cognitions, may vary across cultures. These variations could be attributed to self-construal, or how individuals define themselves in relation to others. Although previous cross-cultural research has predominantly used the free-choice paradigm, significant concerns have been raised regarding its procedural validity and the robustness of its findings. To address this issue, this registered report presents secondary analyses of a large-scale international dataset. We investigated the moderating role of cultural variables on dissonance effects within the induced-compliance paradigm across 18 countries (N = 3,804). We hypothesized that dissonance effects would be stronger for participants with higher individual-level self-construal scores (H1), in more individualistic countries (H2), and in countries with higher country-level self-construal scores (H3). Our results did not support these hypotheses, suggesting that cultural moderation may not generalize to the induced-compliance paradigm. We discuss the necessity of reassessing the procedure’s reliability and clarifying the theoretical role of choice.

articles_hidden.title: Chronometric Normalization for BYOD Digital Assessments: Separating Hardware Latency from Cognitive Fluency
articles_hidden.authors: Eudald Correig Fraga; Carlos García Sancho; Marc Colomer Canyelles; Brian Butterworth
articles_hidden.abstract:
The transition to digital, Bring-Your-Own-Device (BYOD) environments has vastly expanded the scale and accessibility of psychological and educational testing. However, unstandardized
hardware introduces systematic mechanical latencies that contaminate timed cognitive performance, leading to measurement error and possible diagnostic misclassification. Furthermore, naive device-specific normalization strategies are inadequate, as they inadvertently suppress meaningful sociodemographic variance that inherently correlates with device ownership. To address this methodological gap, we introduce a chronometric normalization framework designed to isolate and remove hardware-driven latency without altering underlying cognitive capacity. The model leverages a brief motor task to estimate individual mechanical delay and calibrates this correction against a device-minimal, untimed cognitive task that is substantially less sensitive to hardware speed. This anchors the calibration so that real between-group differences in ability are retained. We demonstrate the framework’s practical utility using data from COSMOS, a large-scale dyscalculia screening battery administered to 54,538 students across 910 schools using the hardware available at each school. Results indicate that while trackpad users initially exhibited severe, artifactual underperformance on timed fluency tasks, the chronometric correction successfully neutralized this hardware penalty. By realigning score distributions while preserving structural
demographic differences, this open-source method ensures that subsequent norming and diagnostic decisions reflect true cognitive architecture rather than the mechanical limitations of the user’s interface.

articles_hidden.title: Mathematical modelling of interactive tapping reveals tap intervals as strongest predictor of subsequent tap timing
articles_hidden.authors: Shane Mannion; Ivana Konvalinka
articles_hidden.abstract:
Successful interpersonal rhythmic coordination requires people to continuously adapt both the
timing and tempo of their actions to one another. Classical error-correction models distinguish these
processes as phase and period correction, typically modeling them as responses to instantaneous and
cumulative asynchrony, respectively. These models were developed mostly for sensorimotor synchro-
nisation to an external pacing signal, rather than interactive interpersonal coordination where both
partners adapt. It thus remains unknown which temporal information people actually use to adapt
their behaviour to one another. We show, using a bounded generalised least-squares framework and
joint finger-tapping data obtained from both bidirectional (reciprocal) and unidirectional (leader-
follower) interactions, that the previous inter-tap interval (ITI) of a partner is a better predictor for
an individual’s next ITI than either cumulative or instantaneous asynchrony. We argue that this
predictor is not only the strongest from a modelling perspective, but also the most parsimonious
from a theoretical point of view. Our results support these claims and show that the partner’s
previous ITI provides a less endogenous predictor of adaptation, addressing a long-standing issue in
models of tapping behaviour.

articles_hidden.title: Emotion Recognition From AI-Generated and Human Faces: Performance, Mental Health, and Demographic Diversity
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew J Vowels; Laura Marika Vowels
articles_hidden.abstract:
Facial emotion-recognition tasks are widely used to investigate social-cognitive differences across mental health conditions, but their
scientific value depends on the faces used to measure performance. Established photographic databases are difficult and expensive to
expand, and many provide little ethnic diversity. AI-generated faces offer a more representative, flexible, and scalable alternative,
provided they capture the same clinically relevant individual differences as photographs of human faces. We compared 161
photorealistic AI-generated faces with 72 images from FACES, an established human-photograph set. Prolific participants contributed
83,206 valid trials; 77,238 trials covering the six shared emotions entered the primary comparison (accuracy \textit{n} = 1,047; response
time \textit{n} = 1,046). AI-diverse expressions were recognised more accurately (89.12\% vs.\ 81.72\%) and faster (2.29 vs.\ 2.64 s) than
FACES expressions, while AI-diverse and AI-White performance did not differ significantly. The AI task retained the individual differences needed for research: lower accuracy on both sources was associated most consistently with psychotic-like experiences and obsessive-compulsive symptoms, with magnitudes aligned with previous literature. AI-diverse and FACES accuracy correlated at \textit{r} = .56, and corrected split-half reliability was .70 and .60, respectively. Women were more accurate than men; participant ethnicity was unrelated to performance. Higher AI accuracy indicates that the expressions were clear; it does not show general psychometric superiority, possibly because very easy items can compress differences among high performers. The combination of clear expressions, comparable symptom sensitivity, and broader representation shows that generative AI can modernise a core social-cognition research tool while making stimulus design more controllable, expandable, and shareable.

articles_hidden.title: How Researchers’ Analytical Decisions Impact Brand Price Elasticity Estimates: Insights from A Many-Analyst Study
articles_hidden.authors: Oliver Koll; Hannes Datta; Karin Teichmann; koen pauwels; Vahideh Abedi; Joop Adema; Anirban Adhikary; Hamed Aghakhani; Gwen Ahn; Simo Alami Chehboune
articles_hidden.abstract: Price elasticities are central empirical measures in marketing, informing pricing, promotion planning, or evaluations of consumer responsiveness. Yet estimates may depend not only on brands, categories, and markets but also on the analytical decisions researchers make in transforming raw purchase data into elasticities. We use a many-analyst design in which 156 independent research teams (RTs) estimate brand price elasticities for 68 meat-substitute country-brand combinations from the same dataset. Each team retained discretion over its analytical approach, including choices concerning modeling, aggregation, fixed effects, control variables, and endogeneity correction. Results show substantial heterogeneity in both choices and estimates. Across 10,415 brand price elasticity estimates, the average is -0.61. However, the variation across the 156 RTs is considerable: the average brand price elasticity per RT ranges from -7.3 to +3.1, with a standard deviation of 0.84. Choices related to time aggregation, fixed effects, time controls, and marketing-mix covariates explain the largest share of variation in reported estimates. Because analytical choices occur in configurations rather than in isolation, we cluster RTs and reveal distinct analytical pathways associated with different patterns of estimates. Our findings contribute to elasticity research by identifying modeling decisions that warrant particular scrutiny and to the open science debate by supporting the call for greater transparency about analytical decisions.

articles_hidden.title: Tone Timing: An Eye-Tracking Study of Dynamic F0 Integration in Spoken Word Recognition
articles_hidden.authors: Xin Wang; Bob McMurray
articles_hidden.abstract: To recognize words, listeners must map a temporally unfolding auditory input to representations at multiple levels.  Typical accounts argue for immediate and incremental integration of asynchronous acoustic cues, such that each cue is used to partially update phonemic or lexical representations as soon as it arrives, with later cues further modulating those decisions. However, recent studies suggest that incrementality is not universal and fricatives follow a different principle in which early cues are stored in a memory buffer and listeners wait to identify the phoneme until all cues have arrived.  It is unknown why different speech sounds show these differences.  Here, we extend this paradigm to lexical tone, an acoustic/phonetic dimension which extends over a syllable and tracks the dynamics of F0.  In a visual world experiment, we index the relative activation of minimal pairs only differing in Mandarin tones as they change over time to ask whether lexical tone is incrementally integrated or processed in a buffered manner. Our findings first show lexical activation patterns are closely coupled to the timing of pitch contours, supporting the immediate integration of lexical tone.  Therefore, with respect to temporal integration of asynchronous cues, tone is like most segments, though different from fricatives.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive Probe Framework: From Passive Reading to Active Probing
articles_hidden.authors: YUTing Sun; Zewei Yu
articles_hidden.abstract:
Natural language processing systems are strong readers. Given text, they can classify, extract, and generate. Yet a fraud investigator assessing a suspicious borrower, an AI tutor helping a student who answers incorrectly, and a brand manager studying consumer perceptions face a different problem. The central question is not what a text says, but what the system should ask to reveal how a person thinks. NLP has spent decades improving the ability to answer questions, while the systematic design of questions remains underdeveloped.
This paper introduces the Cognitive Probe Framework (CPF), a general computational framework that actively presents structured semantic stimuli, or probes, to elicit responses from a human cognitive subject. CPF represents the responses as structured cognitive vectors and uses those representations to generate steering options. The framework supports the probing, interpretation, and bounded intervention of cognitive states through a closed-loop process with three stages: Probing, Modeling, and Steering.
CPF is organized as a four-level family. CPF serves as the general framework at L0. Eight specialized branches occupy L1: the Adversarial, Heuristic, Linking, Stress, Consensus, Foresight, Elicitation, and Metacognitive Cognitive Probe Frameworks, abbreviated ACPF, HCPF, LCPF, SCPF, CCPF, FCPF, ECPF, and MCPF. Each branch contains specialized probe tools at L2 and can support applications at L3. The family spans individual, organizational, market, and societal levels. MCPF is the only inward-facing branch: it uses reflective questions to examine a person's awareness of their own cognitive processes, addressing a structural blind spot left by the seven outward-facing branches.
Beyond its technical architecture, CPF describes a dual mechanism for cognitive augmentation. Expertise augmentation externalizes memory, amplifies weak cues, and directs attention, reducing cognitive load and unstable judgment under pressure. Learning scaffolding makes expert reasoning visible, traceable, and reproducible, accelerating skill acquisition by novices. Grounded in situation awareness, distributed cognition, and cognitive apprenticeship, CPF is positioned not only as a framework that uses NLP but also as a paradigm for bridging limits in human cognition and the complexity of real-world decisions.
The paper also introduces Probe Ethics as a meta-layer constraining the entire framework. It establishes transparency, reversibility, and human judgment as three governing principles and addresses risks that arise when AI is used in social settings, including cognitive manipulation, power asymmetry, cultural bias, and automation bias.
As a vision and position paper, this work defines the scope, family structure, core concepts, design principles, and research roadmap of CPF. It does not claim that all branches are empirically validated. Its aim is to move NLP from passive text reading toward active, accountable cognitive probing.

articles_hidden.title: When do intentions predict action? The temporal dynamics of the intention–action gap
articles_hidden.authors: Peiyuan Zhang; Luisa Leonelli; Yijun Lin; Wei Ji Ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Procrastination is defined as voluntarily delaying an intended course of action, yet the gap between intention and action is rarely measured directly, and little is known about how it unfolds over time. We gave 127 adults seven days to complete 180 units of a self-paced online reading task and recorded the timestamp of every completed unit. Before the task began, 67 of them reported how many units they intended to complete on each of the seven days, so that intended and actual work were expressed in the same units on the same days. Among those who finished, work was concentrated 0.59 days later than intended, although the day people finished did not differ from the day they had planned. The gap widened through Day 4, stopped growing on Day 5, and narrowed over the final two days. Intentions predicted when people started but not when they finished, and their influence faded after the first half of the task. Trait procrastination showed the opposite pattern, predicting actual but not intended work and shaping the timing of work throughout the task, most strongly in the middle.

articles_hidden.title: Development of the Alcohol-Linked Typical Experienced Responses Scale
articles_hidden.authors: Kohsuke Yamamoto; Mami Kato; Ryo Eguchi
articles_hidden.abstract: Alcohol-related subjective experiences are associated with drinking behavior and alcohol use disorders (AUD) risk. However, existing measures access limited domains, such as alcohol expectancies, emotional reactions, or physiological effects, hindering multidimensional assessment of subjective alcohol experiences. This study developed and validated the Alcohol-Linked Typical Experienced Responses (ALTER) Scale, positive/negative and psychological/physiological responses to alcohol consumption among Japanese adults. Habitual drinkers provided free descriptions of alcohol-related experiences, which, together with findings from previous studies, informed the development of candidate items. Study 1’s exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a five-factor structure: Communication Facilitation, Negative Emotional Arousal, Cognitive Decline, Relaxation Responses, and Physiological Responses. The scale demonstrated acceptable internal consistency and one-month test–retest reliability (Study 2). Study 3 supported construct validity through associations with drinking motives, personality, interoceptive awareness, and problematic drinking, assessed using the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test. Individuals with higher problematic drinking tendencies reported stronger rewarding and aversive psychological responses, whereas physiological responses did not differ significantly. These findings provide initial evidence for the reliability and construct validity of the ALTER Scale as a multidimensional measure of recalled subjective alcohol experiences, providing a framework for examining individual differences in alcohol responses and AUD-related risk.

articles.title: Organising the Social Layer: How Organisational Paradoxes Shape Engagement in Cryptocurrency Communities
articles.authors: Annika Aebli; Fabienne Silberstein-Bamford; Joshua Silberstein Bamford
articles.abstract: Cryptocurrencies (crypto) and their underlying blockchain technologies are designed around the promise of collective organising without reliance on centralised authority, intermediaries, and hierarchical coordination. Yet sustaining collective participation in decentralised networks without conventional forms of coordination remains an organisational challenge. This study demonstrates that keeping participants engaged in crypto communities depends on continuous work within crypto’s social layer. Drawing on the organisational paradox lens and 26 semi-structured interviews with developers, team members, and regular users across four crypto communities, we show that sustained engagement depends on balancing organisational paradoxes rooted in communication, decision-making, and community development: technical discourse versus social-media-style interaction, decentralised participation versus centralised guidance, and scaling versus a sense of authentic community. Our findings suggest that continually balancing, rather than resolving these tensions is essential for engagement and community cohesion. This research contributes to the theoretical understanding of decentralised organising by showing how collective participation can be maintained in organisational arrangements that seek to reduce reliance on conventional centralised structures. More broadly, we show that decentralisation does not eliminate the need for organising but relocates much of this work to the social layer of interaction, coordination, and community building, where contradictory demands must be continually negotiated to keep participation workable and sustainable.

articles.title: The Electoral Costs of Exclusion: Women’s Candidate Placement and Party Performance
articles.authors: Iris E. Acquarone; Alba Huidobro
articles.abstract: Political elites continue to behave as if including women in electable positions is electorally risky, despite growing evidence of voter support for gender-inclusive representation. This paper advances a theory of the electoral costs of exclusion, arguing that continued exclusion can become electorally costly when parties fail to adapt to changing electoral responses to women's representation. Using data from Spanish local elections (2003-2019) and a difference-in-differences design, we show that parties increasing women's representation in electable list positions gain votes and seats relative to parties that do not; this divergence coincides with gains among parties increasing women's representation and losses among those maintaining or reducing it. These consequences grow over time and are strongest where inclusion is voluntary rather than quota-mandated. Our findings challenge the idea that underrepresentation persists because inclusion fails electorally, pointing instead to a changing electoral constraint some elites may fail to recognize: exclusion has become costly.

articles.title: Rethinking methods for studying online information and health decision-making: a participant-centred approach
articles.authors: NIHR Policy Research Unit in Reproductive Health; Elena Proffitt; Nicola Merrett; Lois Harvey-Pescott; Jennifer Hall; Abigail McNiven; Abimbola Ayorinde; Kamilla Abdullayev; Rebecca French; Kelly Dickson
articles.abstract:
Online information, accessed through social media, websites, apps and artificial intelligence, is frequently described as shaping health attitudes and decision-making.  Many methodological approaches to understanding how online information influences decisions provide important insights into online content, information exposure, or user perspectives, but often struggle to capture the personalised and algorithmically curated digital environments people encounter, how they engage with information as it appears in their everyday lives, and how such encounters intersect with wider social, cultural and personal contexts to shape decision making. New methodological approaches are needed that can generate meaningful evidence about the varied realities of navigating online health information and the role it plays in decision-making.  

Drawing on reproductive justice and feminist principles that privilege participant expertise and lived experience and informed by literature and collaboration with lived and learnt experts, we co-designed a participant-centred longitudinal content-oriented study exploring the influence of online information on contraceptive decision-making. Inspired by Photovoice approaches, participants documented in real time the online information they encountered over a one-month period, capturing content presented through their own tailored digital environments.
