Interviews conducted before and after the collection period explored contraceptive experiences, attitudes, decision-making and reflections on the role of online information. By combining real-time documentation with in-depth interviews, this approach enabled interpretations of participants lived encounters with online information, including algorithmic changes, emerging trends, current events, and the types of content that resonated with them. Collaborators with lived experience were involved throughout the methodological development and interpretation and analysis of findings.  

This participant-selected content-oriented longitudinal design demonstrates the value of methodologies that capture and generate evidence on lived digital and offline realities as they unfold in real time. Understanding how online information shapes health decision-making requires moving beyond approaches that treat the internet as an isolated and static influence on behaviours. Online information is not a singular, stable object of inquiry but dynamic, personalised, algorithmically mediated and embedded within broader social, cultural, and political contexts. Methodologies that recognise this complexity are essential for generating evidence capable of informing empathetic and meaningful health care and support and care for people prioritising their needs and navigating complex health decisions.

articles.title: Detecting Inequality in Noisy Communication: Promises and Pitfalls of Large Language Models
articles.authors: Susanne Reinhardt; Jonathan J.B. Mijs; David Schieferdecker; Michael Vaughan
articles.abstract: How inequality is communicated shapes how it is explained, understood, and legitimated or contested. Yet studying these communicative processes at scale is challenging because inequality is multidimensional, often expressed implicitly and relationally, and context dependent. We argue that large language models (LLMs) shift, but do not eliminate, these methodological challenges. We trace the development from manual content analysis to rule-based computational approaches and machine learning to LLMs and assess how these methods combine conceptual alignment, semantic sensitivity, contextual sensitivity, and scalability. LLMs help relax some longstanding trade-offs between semantic sensitivity to meaning and scalability, thus promising more comprehensive analyses of established research questions and opening possibilities for comparative research across contexts. Yet untapping their full potential for research on inequality communication depends on addressing problems concerning conceptual validity, representation, comparative measurement, and substantive inference. We conclude by outlining a research agenda for rigorous LLM-based inequality communication research.

articles.title: The Vanishing Mutual Citation
articles.authors: Maayan Matsliah
articles.abstract: Mutual citation – a pair of publications that cite each other – provides a simple measure of reciprocation linkage within scientific literature. Such pairs arise because papers are not published in strict sequence: authors often cite each other's preprints and working papers, add citations during revision, and sometimes publish related papers together. Using OpenAlex citation data from 1975 to 2023, we ask two questions: how has the rate at which papers reciprocate citations changed over five decades, and are interdisciplinary papers reciprocated less often than non-interdisciplinary papers? Contrary to both expectations, reciprocation declined sharply rather than rising with improved discoverability of scholarly work, and interdisciplinary papers did not reciprocate less than non-interdisciplinary papers. Mean mutual citations per paper fell by ~88% and the pooled mutual-citation rate fell by ~95% between 1975 and 2023. Papers citing three or more fields (interdisciplinary) exceeded the reciprocation rates of papers citing one or two fields (non-interdisciplinary) across a central band of six reference-count deciles (10-46 references, accounting for approximately 58% of the corpus), reciprocating up to 17% more. The two groups converged at 47-64 references (a 0.6% gap, non-interdisciplinary papers slightly ahead), and non-interdisciplinary papers reciprocated up to 28% more at the shortest and longest reference lists (3-9 and 65-5,000 references).

articles.title: Press freedom shapes the link between mainstream and social media use for news and climate change understanding: evidence from 30 countries
articles.authors: Laurent Cordonier; Didier Witkowski; Florian Cafiero
articles.abstract: A recent meta-analysis examining the relationship between individuals’ information behaviour and their views about climate change found that, on average, using social media and other user-generated online sources was more strongly associated with science-consistent climate beliefs than using mainstream media. The present study, however, investigates whether these associations vary across countries depending on the level of press freedom, as mainstream journalism is better able to foreground scientific expertise and challenge misleading climate claims when operating freely, whereas social media may provide a partial alternative to constrained domestic mainstream coverage. Accordingly, mainstream media use was hypothesised to be more positively associated with science-consistent climate beliefs and knowledge in countries with greater press freedom than in those with lower press freedom, while the opposite pattern was expected for social media use for news. The analysis draws on a survey of 23,500 respondents in 30 countries. Within each country, survey-weighted models estimated associations between mainstream and social media use for news and four outcomes: belief in the existence of climate change, belief in its anthropogenic nature, belief in its negative consequences, and climate change knowledge, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. Overall, mainstream media use was more often positively associated with science-consistent beliefs and knowledge than social media use. Cross-national analyses then tested whether these country-specific associations varied with press freedom, controlling for socioeconomic development. For each outcome, the association with mainstream media use was more positive in countries with greater press freedom than in those with lower press freedom, whereas the association with social media use for news showed the opposite cross-national pattern. These findings suggest that mainstream media generally contribute more to public understanding of climate change than social media, especially where press freedom is greater, while social media may play a partial compensatory role where domestic journalism is constrained.

articles.title: ‘Intersectionality in the Mind’: Applying an Intersectional Lens to the Study of Lay Perceptions of Inequality
articles.authors: Margherita Cusmano
articles.abstract: Research on lay perceptions of inequality has typically examined economic, gender, and racial inequalities separately and treated social positions additively. Using migrants as a case study, this study employs an intersectional lens to investigate perceptions of inequality. Drawing on interviews and group discussions with 47 participants, the analysis shows, first, that individuals framed different inequalities as interdependent, showcasing what I term ‘intersectionality in the mind’. Second, their intersectional social positions informed how they understood broader patterns of inequality. These findings demonstrate the value of intersectional approaches in analysing the complexity of lay perceptions of inequality. This study points toward methodological and conceptual developments that can better capture both how people cognitively link inequalities and how intersecting social positions inform these perceptions.

articles.title: Systematic Evaluation of Nation-State Propaganda in LLM Outputs
articles.authors: Kevin T. Greene; Jacob N Shapiro
articles.abstract: The rapid growth and usability of AI is creating new risks to information quality, including the possibility that chatbot responses spread propaganda from state-backed influence campaigns. There is little systematic evidence regarding how frequently LLMs spread such narratives when responding to user queries. Previous attempts to assess these risks rely on small numbers of evaluation questions, use opaque query construction procedures, and fail to account for key sources of uncertainty in model responses. We address these gaps with an automated, reproducible pipeline that samples documented state-backed propaganda and news items, programmatically generates evaluation questions, and audits LLM-generated responses. We evaluate whether five prominent models: (1) reproduce arguments aligned with documented Kremlin propaganda narratives; (2) present the Kremlin perspective on events without providing corrective context; and (3) cite known propaganda outlets. We find substantially lower rates of propaganda-aligned responses and propaganda-source citation than prior small-sample work would suggest. These risks are particularly rare for questions resembling ordinary information searches about Ukraine. Our approach enables systematic comparisons across models and issue areas, supports ongoing monitoring, and could be extended to many other hotly-debated topics.

articles.title: Delisting and dispersal: author communities before and after removal from Scopus
articles.authors: Marek Deja
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Delisting removes a journal from an index but not its authors. This study asks whether cohorts disperse or share destinations and whether concentrated inflow is associated with receiving journals' subsequent delisting.

Design/methodology/approach: The analysis reconstructs interval-valued delisting dates from successive Scopus lists, assigns delisted event clocks to matched cohorts, and compares destination overlap with margin-preserving, opportunity-structured, and matched-observed benchmarks. A six-month-landmark discrete-time hazard model handles right censoring and competing exits.

Findings: Delisted-journal output averaged 66.7% below the post-event reference path. For 121 cohorts, median observed-to-expected overlap was 2.40 under the opportunity-structured benchmark. Across 55 matched sets, delisted cohorts overlapped 10.6 percentage points less than references (95% CI [-0.14, -0.07]), a gap that predated delisting and was smaller but present on venues new to the author. An exploratory hazard analysis showed a positive in-sample association between concentrated inflow and receiving journals' subsequent delisting, but extensive censoring and short follow-up preclude a stable magnitude claim.

Research limitations: Delisting is non-random; estimates are descriptive contrasts, benchmark deviations, and conditional in-sample associations.

Practical implications: Synthetic benchmarks establish residual cohort structure; matched observed cohorts test whether it is event-specific.

Originality/value: The study provides a two-stage design for event-specific concentration claims. Pairing a constrained randomisation with matched observed cohorts reversed the substantive conclusion.

articles.title: What the World Studies, Invents and Reports About Urban Heat
articles.authors: Narendra Kumar
articles.abstract: We assemble 20,422 scholarly papers on urban heat islands (1990–2025), read the 17,101 that carry an abstract sentence by sentence, and join them to 96,726 news articles (2021–2025), 4,123 patent families, 14,576 recorded heat incidents, registers of companies, funding rounds and government funding events, and the annual accounts of Indian companies. Eight results stand out. (1) The field grew about 9 times faster than the scholarly literature as a whole, and in 2015–2019 titles naming "extreme heat" overtook those naming "heat island". (2) Of 2,409 papers that attribute urban heat to a cause, 48% name urbanisation and land-use change; attribution to anthropogenic heat fell from 18.4% to 7.7%. (3) Research and news describe different problems: at equal text length, 28% of research openings raise mitigation against 1.6% of news leads, while 22% of news leads are forecasts or warnings against 1.4% of research. (4) They also describe different places: China accounts for 31% of the research and 2.3% of English-language coverage, and Delhi receives 7.4 times the coverage its research share would predict. (5) Invention has outrun science: patent families for cool and permeable pavements grew 12-fold in a decade against 2.4-fold for the research on them. (6) Across 194 studies the median reported cooling from urban trees is 2.0 °C (air temperature 2.0 °C, surface temperature 2.9 °C). (7) Between 2021–22 and 2024–25 news coverage moved from the hazard to the people exposed: workers, schools, the elderly and hospital patients each rose 1.4- to 2.4-fold as a share of heat articles while wildfire and drought fell by about half and climate change — raised in about one article in ten — fell by a quarter. (8) The market record is thin: 140 of 5.05 million companies state a heat or cooling purpose, and recorded capital is $2.7 billion of cooling-infrastructure finance against $48 million of venture funding; larger Indian cooling companies grew revenue 25% a year over three years against 16% for Indian companies generally. Every cause category extracted from the research was tested against an independent second reader; three failed, and no result reported here rests on them.

articles.title: Theravada Buddhism in Contemporary China and Its Followers
articles.authors: Ampere A. Tseng
articles.abstract:
This paper studies the influence of Theravada Buddhism in contemporary China, with a 
focus on the seven ethnic minorities that share a considerable presence of Theravada Buddhism. 
It also considers the populations of Theravada Buddhists among the seven ethnic minorities, as 
well as from another 49 official-recognized ethnicities. It discovers that the Theravada Buddhist 
population increases from 1.3868 million in 2010 to 1.4519 million in 2018 and is expected to 
grow to 1.4786 million by 2027. The present study finds that the Dai ethnicity is not only 
essential for spreading Theravada Buddhism to other ethnicities but it also has the largest 
Theravada Buddhist ethnicity in China, which represents more than 72% of the total Theravada 
Buddhist population. Finally, it discloses that the seven ethnicities each have their own forms of 
folk religions with their faith showing a mix of folk religion with Theravada Buddhism.

articles.title: Agreeing in Principle, Disagreeing on Policy: How Beliefs About the Gender Pay Gap Shape Fairness Concerns and Policy Preferences
articles.authors: Fabian Kalleitner; Jule Adriaans; Ole Brüggemann; Cristóbal Moya; Sandra Bohmann
articles.abstract: Willingness to reduce gender inequalities partly depends on whether people are aware of them and consider them unfair. Extending scholarship centered on inequality misperceptions, we focus on beliefs about the sources of the gender pay gap (GPG), experimentally varying people's ability to attribute pay disparities to women's choices. Preregistered survey experiments in the U.S. and Germany show that information about larger (vs. smaller) and within-job (vs. overall) GPGs independently increases awareness, raises perceived unfairness, and translates into general support for government action. Initially less-supportive groups (conservatives, men) showed some of the largest increases in general support. Yet, updated beliefs did not increase support for specific policies, such as pay transparency laws or gender quotas. These findings suggest that information campaigns can affect beliefs about GPG's size and sources, but even perceiving GPGs as unfair does not bridge the gap between abstract commitment to gender equality and concrete policy support.

articles.title: When Digital Exposure Meets Everyday Buying: Understanding Consumer Behaviour in FMCG
articles.authors: Rithik Bhattacharjee
articles.abstract: Consumers today may discover a product on social media, encounter it repeatedly through digital advertising, and still make the final purchase from a neighbourhood store. This study explores the relationship between digital exposure and everyday consumer behaviour in the fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) sector. Using a consumer survey dataset containing 26 usable responses, the study examines purchase frequency, purchase channels, exposure to social-media promotions, reported influence of online advertising, customer satisfaction, and recommendation intention. The findings show that social-media exposure is relatively common, while reported influence of online advertising is more mixed. Traditional retail remains important, with kirana stores and supermarkets accounting for most reported purchase channels. Mean satisfaction was 3.92 out of 5 among respondents with valid satisfaction scores, while recommendation intention was predominantly positive. Exploratory statistical analysis did not identify a statistically significant association between online-ad influence and recommendation intention (χ² = 0.26, p = 0.61), nor a statistically significant relationship between satisfaction and recommendation intention (Spearman ρ ≈ 0.21, p ≈ 0.31). The findings suggest that digital visibility should not automatically be interpreted as behavioural influence. Consumer decisions appear to involve a broader combination of digital communication, product experience, purchasing convenience, availability, and customer service. Given the small and youth-concentrated sample, the study is exploratory and does not claim population-level generalizability. The paper highlights the need for larger and more diverse studies examining how digital engagement interacts with the wider FMCG consumer journey.

articles.title: The City Multiple: Comparing Geographies of Digital Visibility across Google Maps, Instagram, Facebook, and TikTok
articles.authors: Reza Ardekani Shaker; Justus Uitermark
articles.abstract: Digital platforms have become key geospatial infrastructures through which cities are discovered, experienced, and evaluated. Whereas the extant literature has often focused on single platforms or assumed an undifferentiated platform urbanism, we know very little about how different platforms produce distinct geographies of urban visibility. To address this lacuna, we examine the spatially differentiated regimes of visibility that emerge when platforms mediate urban environments. In doing so, we distinguish between three dimensions of platforms’ geographies of digital visibility: (1) spatial inequality—how each platform distributes visibility across places; (2) spatial articulation—how platform visibilities map onto local urban geographies; and (3) spatial representation—the kinds of places and content that achieve visibility on each platform. Combining computational, geographic, and interpretive methods, we analyse how 6,682 eating and drinking establishments in Amsterdam are represented on TikTok, Instagram, Google Maps, and Facebook, and find strikingly weak correlations between their visibility on the four platforms. We find that each platform produces distinct structures of unequal visibility, with algorithmic-discovery platforms concentrating visibility more intensely than review-based systems. Neighbourhood-level analyses further show that platform-specific spatial articulations correspond to the gentrification and touristification of specific areas. Our findings contribute to the literatures on digital geography and platform urbanism by demonstrating that digital platforms generate multiple instantiations of the same city.

articles.title: Why Politicians Retweet: News Trustworthiness, Emotion, and Partisan Asymmetry in Elite News Sharing among US Congress Members
articles.authors: Apeksha Shetty; Esther Simmendinger; Jula Lühring; Annie Waldherr; David Garcia; Hannah Metzler
articles.abstract: On social media, politicians' retweets can determine which claims gain visibility in online and in wider political debate, yet the factors associated with these retweeting decisions remain poorly understood. Combining natural language processing measures of emotional tone and partisan cues with politician-level characteristics, we analyze the retweeting behavior of United States Members of Congress between 2021 and 2023 using multilevel logistic regression models. Using all news-related retweets during this period, paired with a negative sample of non-retweets, we examine how tweet content and legislators' ideological extremity predict the amplification of tweets linking to more and less trustworthy news domains. We find that partisan identity is a stronger predictor of retweeting than other factors. While politicians generally preferred retweeting content with links to trustworthy sources, this preference weakened when tweets contained party-related references. Anger and fear predicted higher retweeting likelihood when tweets referenced political opponents, while anger predicted lower retweeting likelihood when tweets referenced political allies. Furthermore, ideology conditioned how politicians responded to news trustworthiness: among Republicans, increasing ideological extremity was associated with weaker preference for trustworthy sources, with the most ideologically-extreme Republicans being especially likely to retweet tweets with links to less trustworthy domains. Together, these results suggest that politicians use retweets to reinforce partisan boundaries between 'us' and 'them'. This identity-centered pattern to retweeting explains how information from less trustworthy sources gains traction in polarized digital environments.

articles.title: When the Children’s Rights Normative Culture (CRNC) is Full of Holes: The Child’s Right to Mental Health in Post-Conflict Sool and Sanaag
articles.authors: Guleid Ahmed Jama; Marieke Janne Hopman
articles.abstract: This paper aims to understand the situation of children’s mental health rights in Sool and Sanaag. We apply the Children’s Rights Normative Culture (CRNC) model (Hopman et al. 2026) to a dataset of 85 research conversation conducted between May and November 2025 (40 children, 45 adults) in the two cities. A key finding from the research is that children’s mental health is not recognised as a distinct rights issue within the socio-legal orders applicable in the research area. Moreover, there is no clearly articulated or enforceable socio-legal obligation (from any socio-legal order) concerning the protection of children’s mental health. Nor do the socio-legal norms seem to establish specific remedial measures for children experiencing mental health difficulties. The language of rights is largely absent from people’s understanding of children’s mental health. Across clan, community, religious, and state normative orders, children are mainly seen through the family framework. The paper suggest that 1) children’s mental health should be seen as a children’s rights, 2) families, particularly mothers, and the community, should be engaged as key entry point for societal change, 3) space should be created for children where they can safely share their experiences and views at all levels, including the family, schools, community and post-conflict peacebuilding initiatives.

articles.title: Examination of the News-Finds-Me Perception as an Expanded Bifactor Construct
articles.authors: Toby Hopp
articles.abstract:
Within the mass and political communication literatures, the news-find-me (NFM)
perception has been increasingly used to explain the democratically deleterious implications of a
reliance on incidental, socially mediated news contact. Despite these efforts, there does not
currently exist a consistent means of measuring the NFM construct. This study developed an
expanded NFM measure and evaluated it using a latent bifactor model specification. The results
suggested that a bifactor-(S·I 1) specification fit the data in a plausible manner, and, therein, that
there exist research scenarios where the use of such an approach may confer benefits to
researchers.

articles.title: Orange Cones and Urban Stress: A Population-Based Survey of 1,033 Residents in Greater Montreal
articles.authors: Emmanuel Stip; Marie Claude Delisle; Shekinah Martino; Charles-Édouard Giguère; Jean Caron
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Background: Urban environments expose residents to recurrent low-intensity stressors, including traffic congestion, construction activity, noise, visual overload, disrupted mobility, and unpredictability. In Montreal, orange traffic cones have become an unusually prominent feature of the streetscape and a symbol of construction-related urban disruption. The terms “Montreal syndrome” and “conophobia” were previously proposed as heuristic concepts to explore the psychological significance of this phenomenon. Population-level data, however, have been lacking.
Objective: To examine the frequency of exposure to orange traffic cones among residents of Greater Montreal and characterize associated behavioural responses, emotional reactions, perceived effects on quality of life, and perceptions of their relevance to mental health and well-being.
Methods: A cross-sectional population survey was conducted in collaboration with an independent professional polling company using a general-population panel. A total of 1,033 adults completed a structured questionnaire assessing exposure to orange traffic cones and heavily marked construction zones, behavioural adaptation, emotional reactions, perceived impact on quality of life, and perceived relevance to mental health and well-being. Associations with sociodemographic characteristics were examined using Pearson chi-square tests.
Results: The most unexpected finding concerned perceived mental-health relevance: 56.1% of respondents considered the phenomenon, at least to some extent, a potential mental-health or well-being issue (16.0% “yes, definitely” and 40.1% “yes, to some extent”). Orange-cone exposure was frequent, with 44.1% noticing cones daily or several times per day, and 76.9% reported modifying their behaviour often or sometimes because of cones or heavily marked construction zones. On the multiple-response item, 51.4% of respondents selected slowing down as a precaution, 31.0% changing route or avoiding the area, 27.2% irritation, and 12.3% anxiety or worry. Overall, 67.6% rated the impact on quality of life at the midpoint or higher on a five-point scale. Several sociodemographic associations were observed, particularly for age, employment status, and parental status.
Conclusions: Repeated exposure to orange traffic cones and construction-related disruption is associated with measurable behavioural responses and perceived effects on quality of life in a substantial proportion of Greater Montreal residents. Particularly striking was that more than half of respondents themselves attributed potential mental-health or well-being relevance to the phenomenon. The findings do not establish conophobia as a discrete psychiatric disorder, but provide preliminary population-level support for a measurable dimensional construct of urban environmental stress, ranging from normal adaptation to potentially clinically significant distress.

articles.title: Bandura meets Feminism: Narratives That Normalize and Legitimize Intimate Partner Violence Through Moral Disengagement Mechanisms
articles.authors: Kaja Glomb; Martyna Sekulak; Andrew M. Garcia
articles.abstract: This article undertakes a focused, thematic synthesis of interdisciplinary scientific literature to synthesize existing knowledge on how Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) is legitimized and normalized across diverse sociocultural contexts. Our analysis comprehensively covers physical, psychological, sexual, and controlling behaviours. The effect of this review is a novel hierarchical typology of narratives that frame and justify abuse, which are then analysed through the lens of Bandura’s eight mechanisms of moral disengagement (MD). The core argument proposes that the widespread persistence of IPV is sustained by a system of social coherence, not solely individual pathology. Legitimization operates hierarchically: fundamental societal ideologies provide the foundational Moral Justification, enabling the subsequent activation of individual MD strategies (specifically Dehumanization, Attribution of Blame, and Diffusion of Responsibility) by perpetrators. Crucially, the MD framework is extended to show that these narratives are also mobilized by external observers and social institutions to manage moral discomfort and maintain a predictable social order through defensive attribution and the Belief in a Just World. This model demonstrates that effective prevention must target the underlying cultural narratives and the hierarchical moral architecture that actively license these moral exemptions.

articles.title: Staying Connected: Methodological Insights for Developing Panel Surveys with People Experiencing Homelessness
articles.authors: Caroline Teague; Aryaa Rajouria; Yuanxi Li; Brandon Morande; Hugo Aguas; Nathalie Williams; Jerald Herting; ihsan kahveci
articles.abstract:
Longitudinal research on people experiencing homelessness remains rare due to
challenges in sustained contact, digital access, and institutional trust. This study draws on
three focus groups conducted between September 2024 and January 2025 in King
County, Washington, to explore how to tailor contact modes in longitudinal surveys with
persons experiencing homelessness to improve retention and reduce attrition. Participants
highlighted major barriers to digital contact, including inconsistent access to phones and
service, charging stations, and two-factor authentication. Email was preferred for its
stability. Participants emphasized the need for transparent, scheduled communication and
flexible incentives, such as Cash app. We conclude with a summary of practical
suggestions to improve survey design and discuss how our findings from one particular
setting can be extended more broadly around the country and world.

articles.title: Scrolling the Nation: Banal Digital Nationalism on Short-Form Video Feeds
articles.authors: Mihai Alexandru Bîclea
articles.abstract: This study inquired into the reproduction of banal digital nationalism on the algorithmically curated short-form video feeds. Rather than emphasizing overt nationalist content, I explored how situated, everyday user–platform interactions reproduce banal forms of nationalist ideology. Through digital diaries and post-hoc semi-structured interviews with Romanian users the analysis was attentive at the entanglement of social, affective and technological structures which habitually reinforce the physical and symbolic borders inherent in nationhood. Algorithmic “re-personalization” and “spacetimemattering” through memes, ads and nostalgic content were identified as forms of routine national (re-)production and normalization on the feed, users becoming oriented towards the nation and their being part of it beyond specific ideational contents. By focusing on an underexplored Eastern European context, the study contributes to research on digital nationalism while demonstrating the utility of new materialist sensibilities for investigating banal digital nationalism.

articles.title: The Substitution Trap: Development Aid and the Composition of Government Spending in Indian States
articles.authors: Krishna Vadlamannati; Roberto Iacono
articles.abstract: The question of whether aid supplements or substitutes government spending has long been debated in public finance literature. Building on Vadlamannati and Iacono (2026), who examine how development aid affects discretionary fiscal transfers to Indian states, we address a distinct fiscal question: how does aid exposure affect the composition of subnational government expenditure? Using panel data for 30 Indian states over 1979-2019 (41 years) and an instrumental variable strategy addressing potential endogeneity, we find that greater exposure to aid is associated with a lower share of capital expenditure and a higher share of revenue expenditure. This pattern is consistent with substitution of externally aided projects for domestically financed spending. The effect however varies systematically with electoral incentives. In states with greater electoral competition, aid is more strongly associated with capital expenditure, suggesting that electoral incentives can encourage state governments to channel external resources towards visible capital investments. Our findings extend the evidence on fiscal consequences of aid in India from the allocation of intergovernmental discretionary transfers to the composition of state government expenditure. Our findings reveal that the developmental effects of aid depend not only on how resources reach subnational governments but also on how governments subsequently allocate them.

articles.title: Disaffording the Pedestrian: When Affordances Are Removed
articles.authors: orla fahey
articles.abstract:
Designing for pedestrian road safety is challenging. Designs need to work for a broad and diverse range of pedestrians, while also considering the needs of other vulnerable road users, such as cyclists. Pedestrians are ranked as the most vulnerable in the road user hierarchy and designing for those with protected characteristics is critically important for road safety designers.  One key challenge faced is designing the environment so that safety provisions can align with national and international goals to encourage people to walk or wheel more for health, economic and environmental reasons.

Doctoral research was undertaken to understand whether and how design can improve pedestrian road safety and used key study sites in London to investigate the relationship between safety affordances in public space and pedestrian safety.  One main finding was that often, during a redesign, safety features are removed. The consequences of these changes make it difficult for pedestrians to maintain their safety, particularly those with protected characteristics. Beyond potential physical harm, there are psychosocial impacts: people may avoid a route if they feel it is unsafe or leads to conflict in contested spaces which leaves pedestrians feeling unable to navigate a space confidently. These experiences are not routinely captured within road safety data, which focuses largely on KSI (killed or seriously injured) outcomes.

I have coined this phenomenon of removing an affordance a disaffordance.  The concept comes from over five years of doctoral research into pedestrian road safety in the UK, which focused on pedestrian-only study sites in London that had been redesigned as shared-space zones. Identifying safety affordances and disaffordances in the built environment helps to identify opportunities for broader and more systematic pedestrian participation in the design process. The research also developed GroundMap, a diagnostic approach for identifying and mapping affordances and disaffordances and anticipating the potential consequences of their removal.

At a broader level, the term disaffordance might be extended to identify other environments where the removal of an affordance has significant consequences. While this research applies the concept specifically to pedestrian safety, its wider application across other environments and domains is identified here as a direction for future work.

articles.title: The Influencer I’ll Vote For: Mapping Politicians and Parties on TikTok
articles.authors: Marcos Echevarria-Eirea
articles.abstract: TikTok, and social media generally, continue to rise as important spheres of political communication and information. Mapping how political elites use these platforms thus remains consequential to our understanding of the political arena. However, due to its relative infancy, we have yet to thoroughly study these patterns on TikTok across countries. In response to this shortcoming, this paper introduces Mapping Politicians and Parties on TikTok (MPPTikTok), a dataset of TikTok accounts for national MPs and parties across 17 Western democracies, comprising over 2,190 usernames. Using these to collect ≈260,000 posts, I then describe the supply of content (presence and posting activity) and the engagement it receives across party families. Both radical party families are proportionally more present, post more, and receive more engagement than the Mainstream. The Radical Left leads most clearly in proportional presence and posting activity, while achieving engagement levels comparable to the Radical Right, with differences between them depending on the metric.

articles.title: Calibrating Synthetic Respondents: A Within-Persona Experiment on Public Reactions to Protest in Turkey
articles.authors: MEHMET FUAT KINA; Helin Yaren Ekmen
articles.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate survey respondents, yet the inference pipeline that turns a persona into a response is rarely calibrated for the population and outcome it is applied to. This study makes population- and outcome-specific calibration the research task itself. Using a nationally representative survey in Turkey as the benchmark, we construct persona-conditioned synthetic respondents for all 2,615 survey participants and search a structured space of persona content, sampling strategies, temperatures, model backbones, and prompt framings. Calibration is assessed against two held-out outcomes that carry the response structures on which social movement research typically rests, a rare binary measure of protest participation and a five-point attitude item, and the selected protocols differ between the two. We then run a within-persona synthetic experiment that places the same protest for Kurdish-language education in a political opportunity and a political threat context. The threat context lowers simulated movement legitimacy and willingness to attend, and the simulated contrasts differentiate by political orientation, ethnicity, and education in the directions theory anticipates. Calibration is a precondition for reading synthetic experiments, not a robustness check appended to them.

articles.title: Does exposure to information on ethnic minorities’ greater welfare dependency affect attitudes to welfare and welfare recipients? A pre-registered, population-based survey experiment
articles.authors: Thijs Lindner; Willem de Koster; Jeroen van der Waal
articles.abstract: The relationship between ethnic diversity and welfare attitudes has been the subject of much research. However, little is known about how exposure to information on the overrepresentation of ethnic minority individuals among welfare recipients affects attitudes to welfare recipients in general. We scrutinize a potential information exposure effect, and assess two contrasting scenarios, i.e., exposure to aforementioned information might strengthen either negative stereotypes of welfare recipients or the notion that welfare dependency is the result of structural conditions. Additionally, we hypothesize that the former (latter) response is more likely among those with more (less) ethnocentric attitudes. We tested this by conducting an original pre-registered survey experiment among members of a high-quality probability-based panel designed to represent the Dutch population (n = 1,527). The treatment group was exposed to information depicting the overrepresentation of Dutch citizens with a Moroccan migration background among welfare recipients in the Netherlands, while the control group was not. It was only among the more ethnocentric respondents that exposure to the treatment increased support for the notions that welfare recipients: 1) are lacking work ethic; and 2) are themselves to blame for their condition. There was 3) no treatment effect on support for welfare schemes in general. We discuss the implications of these findings for a variety of academic debates and make suggestions for further research.

articles.title: The Politics of Threat Construction: Securitisation as a Site of Contestation in Georgia’s Public Sphere
articles.authors: Mariam Bibilashvili; Zinaida Bechná; Kornely Kakachia
articles.abstract: Moving beyond studies on contemporary security challenges posed by information manipulation, economic coercion, and military pressure, this article problematises the securitisation of foreign interference narratives by political leaders through the case of Georgia (2023–2025). The analysis draws on 325 social media posts by high-level officials and ten in-depth interviews with civic actors resisting state narratives. It relies on securitisation theory to (1) examine how political elites frame domestic actors as instruments of the Western interference despite the country’s constitutionally anchored pro-European orientation and overwhelming public support for EU integration, and (2) explore how counter-securitisation unfolds among civic actors. The findings reveal a structured securitising narrative grounded in sovereigntist logic, invoking historical memory, identity threats, and conspiracy framings to delegitimise civic actors as rootless and foreign aligned. However, rather than generating stable audience acceptance this securitising move triggers counter-securitisation as civic actors contest the proposed threat hierarchy, reframe Russia and democratic backsliding as primary dangers, and additionally mobilise performative resistance through street protest. The analysis highlights the agency of civic actors who simultaneously occupy the positions of securitised subjects and a segment of the audience and complements post-structuralist understandings of the securitisation as a co-constitutive and iterative rather than a linear process.

articles.title: Regressive Restoration: A Process Model of Belief Rigidity Under Epistemic Destabilization
articles.authors: Mitchell Sanders
articles.abstract: Beliefs do more than represent the world; they can also regulate uncertainty, affect, identity, and significance. This article introduces regressive restoration as a temporal regulatory process in which epistemic destabilization increases reliance on coherence-restoring beliefs, the immediate stabilizing effects of those beliefs reinforce commitment, and that commitment subsequently reduces epistemic flexibility. Epistemic destabilization refers to conditions in which cues for determining what is credible, coherent, or socially shared become fragmented, overloaded, unreliable, or contested. The model proposes that available integrative resources– the momentary attentional, affective, and uncertainty-tolerance resources needed to remain engaged with conflicting information– moderate whether destabilization promotes adaptive accommodation or regressive restoration. The model distinguishes short-term stabilization from maladaptive rigidity. Coherence restoration is context-sensitive and may be functional, whereas rigidity is indicated when closure-oriented responses resist correction or persist across contexts in which reflective integration is possible. Regressive restoration is defined as a process rather than a trait or latent factor, and identity consolidation is treated as an important but nonessential amplifier. Five propositions specify the model’s distinctive predictions concerning regulatory function, temporal ordering, motivational amplification, correction resistance, and cross-context generalization. A focused empirical agenda is proposed to test whether immediate coherence, affective relief, or significance restoration predicts later belief rigidity beyond established informational and motivational mechanisms.

articles.title: Distributed Citizenship in Local-Oriented Online Communities: A Behavioral Repertoire of Civic Roles Across 50 North American City Groups
articles.authors: Yibin Fan
articles.abstract: Local-oriented online communities increasingly serve as informal spaces where residents exchange local knowledge, discuss public issues, and encounter local news. Yet existing research often treats these communities as digital third spaces, with less attention to how civic labor is distributed among participants. This study understands these communities as components of local information infrastructures, examining how civic roles are distributed by analyzing year-long data from 50 highly active North American city subreddits in 2024. Focusing on 43,263 sustained users, we combine media-domain matching, LLM-assisted topic classification, latent profile analysis, and qualitative case comparison. The analysis identifies six behavioral civic roles: National News Commentators, Platform-Native Political Discussants, Local Civic Respondents, Cross-Scale Media Brokers, Local News Brokers, and Peripheral Generalists. The findings show that local-oriented online communities function as local information infrastructures which depend on uneven but complementary forms of resident participation.

articles.title: ThSQCA: Reproducible Threshold-Sweep Workflows for QCA in R
articles.authors: Yuki Toyoda
articles.abstract:
Qualitative Comparative Analysis (QCA) sets thresholds when constructing sets from continuous scales. A standard analysis, however, is fixed to a single set of thresholds, so it does not directly reveal how the sufficiency structure changes across different outcome levels. Researchers can repeat the analysis at individual thresholds, but comparing the emergence and disappearance of configurations, solution fit, and the presence of multiple minimal solutions while keeping settings consistent requires additional implementation.

This article introduces the R package Threshold-Sweep Qualitative Comparative Analysis (ThSQCA), which addresses this gap. ThSQCA uses the QCA package as its computational engine and provides a common workflow to run, aggregate, visualize, and report analyses that systematically vary the outcome threshold, the condition thresholds, or both. In a consumer survey of usage intention toward Starbucks (n = 336), moderate target levels of usage intention yielded multiple sufficient paths, whereas the highest target level left only one narrow path, with solution coverage dropping substantially. Varying the threshold that defines service delivery as high further produced different sufficiency structures, including cases with no solution, for the same high level of usage intention. Such differences cannot be observed in a single-threshold analysis.

ThSQCA does not automatically select the correct threshold. It is a diagnostic and comparative workflow that clarifies, over a research- or practice-relevant range, at which levels a conclusion holds and where it changes. This allows QCA results to be evaluated not as an answer specific to one threshold, but as decision-relevant information that depends on the target level.

articles.title: Who Sees Politics in Sports? Norm Endorsement and Partisan Judgments from the 2026 World Cup
articles.authors: Morgan Wack; Daniel Vogler; Manuel Arrigo; Christian Pipal; Lucas Paulo da Silva
articles.abstract: Most Americans say politics should stay out of sports. Yet whether this norm is truly binding depends on whether people apply it when their own side violates the norm. To test this "apolitical sports" norm, we fielded a two-wave matched panel survey around the 2026 FIFA World Cup (N1=988; N2=699). During the tournament, U.S. President Donald Trump called FIFA to have an American player's red-card suspension lifted. We asked respondents to judge the incident directly and to judge a message on players' shirts, varied to support or protest a contentious U.S. policy. Overall, endorsing the norm predicted lower tolerance for political expression in sports, within each party separately, with a smaller own-side advantage. Following this widely reported violation, Democrats raised their endorsement while Republicans did not. What divided partisans most was what they counted as a violation, with Republicans reporting less political interference. In short, while both sides agreed with the norm, they disagreed about whether it had been broken. Our findings suggest that partisan accommodation can influence how citizens recall and conceive of potentially norm-violating events.

articles.title: Different spaces, different citizens? Explaining online and offline volunteering and citizenship behavior through the Civic Voluntarism Model
articles.authors: Arjen de Wit; Marlou Ramaekers; Stephanie Maas; Rene Bekkers
articles.abstract: Online ways of communication have radically changed the face of volunteerism, often described as ‘virtual volunteering’, ‘online volunteering’ or ‘digital volunteering’. In this paper we examine if those individuals engaged in online spaces, both in formal organizations and in self-organized communities, are different from those engaged in offline (in-person) volunteering. To understand how the four distinct types of voluntary participation (offline volunteers, online volunteers, offline self-organized citizens, online self-organized citizens) attract the same or different individuals, we anchor our analysis in the Civic Voluntarism Model (CVM). Using panel survey data from the Netherlands, we find that offline and online volunteers show higher engagement and especially networks, and this also holds for people who participate as citizens in their neighborhood. ‘Being asked’ to volunteer is the strongest correlate of volunteering, both offline and online, as well as offline citizenship. Recruitment networks are less important for online participation. Strikingly, online self-organized platforms are able to reach new groups of citizens that are not stratified by similar prerequisites for participation. These findings provide valuable insights for volunteer managers, activists, and policy makers who use online channels to recruit and retain volunteers.

articles.title: What Affective Polarization Is Made Of: Components, Targets, Cleavages and Emotions in Five Multiparty Democracies
articles.authors: Mabelle Kretchner; Bendegúz Plesz; Eran Halperin; Julia Elad-Strenger; Sivan hirsch hoefler; Adva Gruenwald; Zsolt Boda
articles.abstract: The more affective polarization (AP) is studied, the clearer it becomes that a single score conceals what it is made of. The score has two sides, ingroup attachment and outgroup hostility, and the two need not be balanced. AP runs toward different targets, it runs along a different divide in each system, and the affect itself is made of distinct emotions. Comparative work has taken up each of these layers, but in the studies we are aware of, never all together, so what any given score is made of is still not known: two democracies with similar AP levels may be facing quite different things. Drawing on preregistered survey data from five multiparty democracies (Germany, Hungary, Italy, Poland, Israel; N = 5,151), we map all four layers in one design: AP and its two sides toward parties, voters, and ideological blocs; where attachment and hostility sit across the parties of each system; and the associations of six discrete emotions with AP. In all countries, AP drew more on ingroup attachment than on outgroup hostility, and disappointment and anger rather than hatred were associated with AP toward parties and voters. What differed was where the affect settled: which parties concentrated it, and whether the ideological bloc carried it at all. Hatred appeared only at the bloc level and only in some systems, at the target whose scores were otherwise among the lowest. We discuss the importance of unfolding these layers together in comparative research, for a better understanding of AP and for addressing it.

articles.title: Resilience in a Hybrid Security Culture: Georgia between Institutional Continuity and Political Realignment
articles.authors: Mariam Bibilashvili
articles.abstract: Challenging the common understanding in the relevant literature, this study reconceptualizes resilience to hybrid threats as a politically mediated process rather than purely a matter of institutional capacity-building. To examine how policy frameworks and political rhetoric interact to shape resilience, it traces Georgia’s security culture in the aftermath of the Russo-Georgian war. Through intertextual discourse analysis, the article cross-examines the institutional architecture of digital resilience, encompassing cybersecurity (systemic), media regulation (protective) and media literacy (empowerment) measures, with the government’s shifting rhetoric (2023–2025), while interview data provide contextual insights. The analysis reveals a hybrid security culture manifested in fragmented governance and discursive struggle over resilience. Although formal policy frameworks normatively align with the West and consistently identify Russia as the principal security threat, governmental rhetoric portrays the same Western actors as sources of foreign interference and prioritizes political autonomy over cooperation while still invoking commitments to the constitutionally enshrined Euro-Atlantic trajectory. This dichotomy between institutional design and political discourse results in strategic ambiguity. It suggests that in hybrid regimes formal frameworks may function symbolically to signal external alignment, while practice is determined by short-term political calculations and discretionary authority, leaving institutions and societies vulnerable to evolving forms of foreign interference.

articles.title: Genital Modifications and Moral Boundary-making: Medical Perspectives on FGM/C versus FGCS in Belgium and the Netherlands
articles.authors: Hannelore Van Bavel
articles.abstract: This chapter investigates how medical professionals who perform female genital cosmetic surgery (FGCS) in Belgium and the Netherlands perceive and negotiate the boundary between FGCS and female genital mutilation (FGM). It draws on in-depth qualitative interviews conducted with 11 medical professionals between March 2024 and August 2025, as part of a broader study of genital self-image, motivations for FGCS, and clinical responses. FGM is criminalised in both countries, whereas FGCS is not, even though some procedures classified as FGCS technically fall within the legal and policy definitions of FGM. In 2008, professional societies in the Netherlands attempted to clarify the distinction but ultimately failed to establish concrete criteria, relying instead on what they regarded as a self-evident difference. Healthcare professionals are therefore left to interpret and navigate this boundary in practice, drawing on their own professional knowledge, moral reasoning, and sociocultural understandings. This ambiguity raises important questions about how medical professionals distinguish between FGM and FGCS in their everyday practice. Do they regard the two as fundamentally different, or do they recognise areas of overlap, and on what grounds? What forms of reasoning, knowledge, and professional or cultural frameworks inform their distinctions? To what extent do their views reflect, reproduce, or resist broader social, cultural, and political discourses?
