articles_hidden.title: Identifying determinants of ecological footprints: A novel application of latent growth curve models (LGM)
articles_hidden.authors: Andrés Beltrán-Hernández; Marcelo Lufin
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigates the determinants of ecological footprint growth trajectories in 112 countries (2004–2017) using latent growth curve models (LGM). Unlike traditional panel methods, LGM captures dynamic trends and country-level heterogeneity in environmental impact over time. The approach integrates economic, institutional, and socio-geographic determinants into a unified causal framework. Results indicate that economic complexity mediates the relationship between economic growth and ecological footprint, promoting technological innovation and sustainable practices. Higher economic complexity also partially offsets environmental impacts from increased fossil fuel consumption. These findings underscore the need for policies fostering innovation, economic diversification, and sustainable urban planning to mitigate environmental degradation.

articles_hidden.title: Determinants of the relationship between growth and CO2 emissions: A novel application utilizing bivariate latent growth curve models (BLGM) across European regions
articles_hidden.authors: Andrés Beltrán-Hernández; Marcelo Lufin
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigates the key determinants shaping the dynamic relationship between economic growth and CO2 emissions in 220 European NUTS2 regions from 2000 to 2021, using a bivariate latent growth curve model (BLGM). Unlike traditional methods, the BLGM framework addresses a critical gap in modeling latent growth processes, variable interactions, and regional heterogeneity, significantly advancing previous methodologies. The approach integrates determinants of regional economic structures, energy consumption patterns, labor market characteristics, and educational attainment. The results highlight the crucial role of financial structure, spatial centrality, and educated development, offering insights for adaptive and effective regional climate and sustainability strategies and emphasizing the need for coordinated policies that integrate technological innovation, territorial planning, labor market diversification, and sustained investment in education.

articles_hidden.title: From Affective Experience to Mechanism: A Critical Realist Case Study Architecture Using Reflexive Thematic Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Varun S. Nair
articles_hidden.abstract:
Studying affective life qualitatively poses a known problem. Burnout, emotional labour, and slow shifts in teacher–class relations are real with measurable effects, yet not directly visible; we infer them from behaviour and language. Interpretation always mediates. How can we claim mechanisms without pretending to observe them?
This paper proposes a case-study architecture using reflexive thematic analysis within a critical realist frame. It integrates five usually separate elements: a multi-perspectival case design; abduction and retroduction as genuinely different inferences; systematic assessment of rival explanations; a procedure for sorting context from mechanism when they do not separate cleanly; and a hierarchy of claims calibrated to evidence. The combination yields what neither purely interpretive nor purely causal work can: fallible mechanism explanations that take meaning and causation equally seriously.
The argument is specified, not demonstrated. Two computational simulations provide proof of concept. The first distinguishes two known ground-truth mechanisms across 40 synthetic cases, with 80% overall recovery (95% CI [68%, 92%]; 85% and 75% per mechanism). The second adds a third rival—perceptual reconstruction, in which teacher behaviour is unchanged but students report change—and distinguishes all three across 60 synthetic cases, with 95% overall recovery (100%, 100%, 85%). The three-way test uses tighter noise parameters than the two-way, so rates are not directly comparable. Both test only one component and neither substitutes for empirical validation on real classroom data, which remains future work.

articles_hidden.title: Ideology on the U.S. District Courts: Reexamining Presidential and Senatorial Appointment Power
articles_hidden.authors: Nicholas O. Howard; David A Hughes; Philip Warncke
articles_hidden.abstract: Unlike U.S. appellate courts, scholars of the American federal judiciary typically lack ideological estimates for district court judges that are derived directly from their behavior. Rather, scholars have primarily relied upon proxy measures based upon the preferences of a  judge's appointing president or those of home-state senators in the event senatorial courtesy is in effect. Nevertheless, senatorial courtesy is a norm, and norms can be broken. It remains an open question  whether home-state senators genuinely constrain the president when it comes to the ideological tenor of appointees to the district courts. We produce novel ideal point estimates for 1,680 U.S.~district court judges appointed between 1913 and 2009 based upon their votes in approximately 100,000 cases, in addition to contextual factors unique to judges and the process by which they were appointed. We map these ideal points into the Judicial Common Space and make them publicly available to American courts scholars. These ideal points differ meaningfully compared to previous proxy measures and improve predictive power in judge voting behavior. Importantly, despite a battery of statistical tests, we find that senatorial courtesy appears to play a minimal role with respect to the revealed preferences of U.S. district court judges compared to the role the president's ideology plays. If senatorial courtesy indeed constrains presidents in the separation of powers game, it is likely on some other, non-ideological dimension.

articles_hidden.title: The Rise of Competitive Authoritarianism in Israel: The Paradox of Uneven Competitive Authoritarianism
articles_hidden.authors: Oded Haklai; Andrew O'Donohue
articles_hidden.abstract: This article evaluates whether Israel crossed the line into competitive authoritarianism under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. To date, scholars and democracy indices disagree over whether prominent cases of autocratization, such as Israel, have crossed this threshold. One reason for these disagreements, we argue, is that there are varieties of competitive authoritarianism. We theorize that competitive authoritarian regimes vary in the degree to which they are uneven across dimensions of democracy and in their levels of repression and competitiveness. We then evaluate empirically whether Israel meets Levitsky and Way’s definition of competitive authoritarianism. We find that by Levitsky and Way’s criteria, Israel crossed the line into competitive authoritarianism after 2023 under Prime Minister Netanyahu, due to the government’s politicization of state institutions, harassment of independent media, and uneven media access. We further show that Israel’s competitive authoritarian regime is uneven, in that autocratization is more severe in some areas than others, and less repressive than many other competitive authoritarian regimes. This regime unevenness has led to Israel’s misclassification as a democracy thus far.

articles_hidden.title: Migration–Citizenship Trajectories and Institutional Incorporation: Long-Term Mental Health Consequences
articles_hidden.authors: Nan Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: Migration does not necessarily produce equivalent changes in institutional membership. This study examines how geographical mobility and institutional citizenship unfold jointly across adulthood and whether differentiated pathways of institutional incorporation are associated with long-term mental health. We analysed longitudinal data from 8,297 adults aged 60–80 in the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS, 2011–2020). Sequence analysis reconstructed joint trajectories of rural–urban residence and institutional citizenship (hukou) between ages 15 and 60, which were linked to depressive symptoms (CES-D-10) using multilevel growth-curve models. Substantial inequalities emerged across migration–citizenship trajectories and persisted throughout later life. Rural–urban migrant workers retaining rural hukou, historically associated with more restricted access to urban social rights and protection, had depressive-symptom levels comparable to lifelong rural residents, whereas trajectories involving urban hukou were associated with more favourable outcomes. Longer migration duration was associated with modestly lower depressive symptoms among women, while the estimated association was essentially flat among men. The findings demonstrate that geographical mobility does not necessarily entail institutional incorporation and that the long-term consequences of migration depend on how geographical and institutional mobility are configured across adulthood.

articles_hidden.title: Data visualization: Spanish results in PISA across  waves by parental educational attainment
articles_hidden.authors: Manuel T. Valdés; Fabrizio Bernardi
articles_hidden.abstract: Using Spanish PISA microdata from 2003–2025, we analyze performance trends in mathematics and reading by parental educational attainment. Results show a steady decline in scores among students from highly educated families, starting as early as 2012 in mathematics and 2015 in reading.

articles_hidden.title: The Unequal Toll of Loneliness on Electoral Participation: Longitudinal Evidence from The Netherlands
articles_hidden.authors: Francesco Marolla; Arturo Bertero; Cristiano Vezzoni
articles_hidden.abstract:
While declining turnout is often attributed to a lack of social integration, the political relevance of
subjective disconnection has only recently drawn scholarly attention. Using eleven waves of the
LISS panel in the Netherlands, we study how social and emotional loneliness relate to electoral
participation, net of objective social position and objective social integration. Lower self-reported
voting propensity is tied specifically to social loneliness, the perceived lack of a broader community
network, whereas emotional loneliness shows no independent association once the social facet is
accounted for. Separating stable between-person differences from within-person change, we find this
gap concentrated among citizens who are chronically high in social loneliness, while within-person
fluctuations show no association, indicating that the relationship is dispositional rather than situational
and consistent with a link between chronic loneliness and weaker voting habits. Crucially, the gap is
substantially narrower among citizens with greater education, political interest, and partisanship. The
participatory cost of loneliness is therefore unevenly distributed across the electorate, falling hardest
on citizens with the fewest civic resources.

articles_hidden.title: Lessons from History:  Historical WaSH Programmes and the Decline of Summer Diarrhoeal Mortality
articles_hidden.authors: Hannaliis Jaadla; Romola Davenport
articles_hidden.abstract: Using high-frequency historical data on mortality (weekly) and temperature (daily), we examine the puzzle of the late decline of infant diarrhoeal mortality in British and Irish cities. While mortality from other faecal–oral diseases began falling before the 1880s alongside investments in urban water supply and waste disposal, large summer epidemics of infant diarrhoea persisted until the 1910s. We analyse a large panel of towns spanning the period 1893–1930 to characterise the temperature-infant mortality nexus and to identify turning points in this relationship. Two-way fixed effects models reveal the roles of flush toilet provision, reductions in fly populations, and infant feeding practices in the decline of infant diarrhoeal mortality. Our findings indicate that preventing lethal summer epidemics among young children required coordinated improvements in both domestic and environmental hygiene.  We suggest that these findings provide historical support for contemporary calls for ‘transformative WaSH’ programmes.

articles_hidden.title: Monetary Policy Transmission in Nepal: A Study of How Central Bank Policy Rates Affect Bank Lending and Economic Activity
articles_hidden.authors: Nirmal Gurung
articles_hidden.abstract:
Monetary policy transmission, the mechanism through which the monetary policy of the central bank impacts bank lending rates and, by extension, the broader economy, is of great interest to policymakers. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the monetary policy transmission mechanism in the Nepalese context. It focuses on the interest rate pass-through channels and associated frictions in the Nepalese monetary policy framework. It uses the information published by NRB, the central bank of Nepal, as well as scholarly research and reports on the topic to perform the study. It highlights that the interest rate pass-through in Nepal is partial and delayed and discusses the reason why monetary policy transmissions in Nepal work as they do.
The paper starts with an introduction to the topic of monetary policy transmission. Then, it proceeds to discuss research questions and objectives, theoretical background, and methodological background. Finally, it presents data analysis and discusses the findings to reach final conclusions and recommendations.

articles_hidden.title: External Debt Sustainability in Nepal: A Case Study Based on Nepal Rastra Bank, IMF, and World Bank Data
articles_hidden.authors: Nirmal Gurung
articles_hidden.abstract: External debt sustainability is a matter of great concern for many developing countries like Nepal since a part of the borrowed money is regarded as the liability that threatens to criticize the value of their local currency and increases their fiscal burden. This paper performs an analysis of the external debt indicators of Nepal and the risk of a debt distress using the information provided by Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank. According to the results, the total public debt in Nepal is expected to reach about Rs 2.97 trillion (USD 19.21 billion) by the end of fiscal year 2025/26, which is equivalent to 45.07 percent of GDP, as compared to 43.79 percent in the previous year. The external debt increased to about 25.3 percent of GDP from 20.6 percent, and that of domestic one remained at about 22-23 percent. Nepal still belongs to the countries with low risk of experiencing a debt distress, according to the joint World Bank-IMF Debt Sustainability Analysis (DSA). However, the study highlights several vulnerabilities in the external debt of Nepal as the present value of the external debt-to-exports ratio exceeds the indicative threshold in the export shock scenario. The Nepali rupee has depreciated by around Rs 8 against the US dollar in the first seven months of FY2025/26, adding Rs 92.96 billion to the external debt of the country. Only around one-third of the capital budget has been spent, which implies that the borrowed money is used for sustaining the recurrent expenditure rather than capital spending. The paper concludes that Nepal’s debt is sustainable in the near term. However, the increasing vulnerabilities in the form of currency depreciation, inadequate revenue mobilization efforts and low efficiency utilization of the borrowed funds should be responded to in order to address long-term sustainability.

articles_hidden.title: Turning Ambition into Action: Lessons from the Italian National Recovery and Resilience Plan
articles_hidden.authors: Alessia Aspide; Lorenzo Mascioli; Gabriele Beretta; Camilla Locatelli
articles_hidden.abstract: The Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) is the primary financial instrument of the EU’s ambitious pandemic response initiative, NextGenerationEU (NGEU). This report examines Italy’s capacity to implement its ambitious National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP) effectively. It opens with a comparative analysis of the NRRPs of the four largest EU economies: Germany, France, Italy, and Spain. Focusing then on Italy, the largest recipient, the report explores how state capacity shapes the implementation of ambitious reforms and investments, emphasizing the challenges of translating NGEU’s transformative goals into tangible outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Issues and Challenges of Poverty and International Labor Migration in Nepal
articles_hidden.authors: Shyam Kumar Karki
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper aims to discuss the opportunity and challenges of the foreign labor market for Nepalese workers and Nepal’s government policy. The study was carried out in the form of a qualitative research method, where secondary data were used. The collected data were analyzed using the content analysis method after a close reading of the sources. This paper discussed the current situation of government policy, manpower agencies, problems of migrant workers, and the way of using the remittance. This research found that the government policy is less effective, and manpower agencies are not following the government rules and regulations. Since the last two decades, remittances have been a significant contributor to the Nepalese economy. Many scholars argued that remittance helps to reduce the country’s poverty rates. However, Nepalese workers face numerous problems in the home country and destination countries. Migrant workers are being charged high service charges and misguided by the local agent and manpower agencies in the home country Nepal. They face problems in destination countries such as low remuneration, sexual abuse, and risky job environment. Most of the remittances are using daily expenses such as purchasing foods. This paper explores these vulnerabilities of migrant workers and suggests stakeholder interventions to make safer migration and sustainably use a remittance.

articles_hidden.title: Women's Land Rights in India: A Learning Document
articles_hidden.authors: ISST; Jahnvi Andharia; Benu Verma; Saee Pawar; Ashmeet Kaur; Kritika Goel
articles_hidden.abstract: Womanity has decided to strategically accelerate gender equality and economic empowerment of women in India by developing and supporting sustainable models that look at women's land rights pathways that can be adapted and scaled across the country. The program focuses on increasing land literacy, women’s land ownership and long-term land access to secure livelihoods for 50,000 women at the community level. Womanity’s Theory of Change (ToC) Document outlines the rationale and the pathway to advance gender equality and economic empowerment of women through sustainable models and strategic interventions. Womanity has outlined three phases to reach 50,000 women – Build, Enhance and Scale. In the Build phase, it seeks to identify challenges, evolve prototype sustainable models, measure effectiveness and impact, support implements, invest in research, and develop a comprehensive evidence plan. This learning document prepared by ISST contributes to the efforts of the Build phase of Womanity. The objective of this document is to capture the learnings of the various partner organizations, key members of the Womanity team, and the other stakeholders (referred as the Womanity ecosystem in India) in the first 18 months of the project period, as well as their future learning needs. Through a thorough analysis of the data collected over six months, a learning framework was expected to map all possible needs for building knowledge and strengthening capacities within the Womanity ecosystem to effectively address various WLR issues

articles_hidden.title: Long-Term Sequences of State-Building and Violent Conflict
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander De Juan
articles_hidden.abstract: A large body of research demonstrates that state capacity is an important correlate of intrastate conflict. However, similar levels of present-day state capacity can result from different historical trajectories of state-building. I argue that specific sequences of state-building can shape the risk of violent conflict in the long run: geographical obstacles can isolate territories from state-building processes for extended periods, strengthening non-state institutions. The risk of violence increases once the state has accumulated sufficient capabilities to close this state-building gap. The extension of authority into peripheral territories triggers resistance from among local elites that mobilize their constituencies against the central state. I exploit exogenous variation in early state-penetration in Nepal to investigate this argument. Areas located below the Himalayan foothills were heavily Malaria-infested preventing the state from establishing meaningful presence until the implementation of a malaria eradication program in the 1950/60s. I make use of this specificity in Regression Discontinuity (RD) estimations. The findings lend support to the primary arguments of the paper and underscore the role of long-term sequences of development.

articles_hidden.title: Rounding and the bill-size gradient in tipping
articles_hidden.authors: Toby Qin; Vrund Gurjar
articles_hidden.abstract: Restaurant tip percentages often decline as bills increase. Rounding is one proposed explanation because a fixed upward adjustment adds more to the tip percentage on a small bill. We examine how much of the observed decline can be explained by adjustments of up to one dollar. We analyzed 22,446 checks with positive recorded tips, no automatic gratuity and bills of $10–$200 from three North Carolina restaurant outlets. For checks with a whole-dollar tip or reconstructed final payment, we allowed the pre-rounding tip to fall anywhere from one dollar below the recorded amount to the recorded amount, with a minimum of zero. We calculated the smallest and largest bill-size coefficients across these possible amounts, controlling for outlet, month, guest count, opening hour and weekday. Bootstrap checks resampled dates, weeks and servers. Each scheme used 999 draws, with the rounding bounds recalculated for each resampled dataset. Tip percentages fell by 4.29 points per bill doubling. Even the adjustments that most reduce this decline leave a coefficient of −1.62 points, which remains negative across all three bootstrap checks. Five-dollar rounding or restricting bills to $30–$200 allows the fitted decline to disappear. Upward dollar rounding cannot fully explain the negative gradient in the primary sample. Larger rounding increments and the exclusion of small bills produce ranges containing zero.

articles_hidden.title: Multiracial young adults’ experiences of Whiteness as a wage and tax
articles_hidden.authors: Monica Heilman
articles_hidden.abstract: Debates persist on the racial position of multiracial Americans, namely whether this population will “become White” or not. However, the premise of this question is predicated on a monoracial paradigm of race that cannot fully account for the experiences of multiracial individuals. Multiracial experiences with Whiteness, including ways they conform to and confound monoracial expectations, have the potential to reshape our understandings of racial constructions, boundaries, and futures, particularly considering shifting racial demographics. One necessary precursor toward these insights lies in the distinctions between how multiracial and monoracial individuals experience Whiteness. Drawing on thirty-seven in-depth interviews with multiracial young adults with White ancestry in the Midwest, I argue that multiracial individuals experience Whiteness as a wage (privileges) and a tax (costs). Like monoracial Whites, multiracial individuals viewed as White can receive public and psychological wages, yet these wages are offset by an inseparable “racial tax,” which is predicated on the contingent and exclusive nature of Whiteness. These results underscore the utility of calling attention to the monoracial structure, as well as recognizing and theorizing beyond its limits.

articles_hidden.title: Antagonistic Predictions
articles_hidden.authors: Christoph Kern
articles_hidden.abstract:
Why do we use models to predict the most likely outcome? Integrating model predictions into high-stakes decision-making pipelines can amplify biases and introduce flawed decisions when human caseworkers and models compete over the same prediction target. Learning to anticipate the most likely outcome risks reproducing biases embedded in historical data, while delivering such predictions in human-AI decision-making raises issues of cognitive biases and algorithmic aversion versus overreliance. 

In this perspective, I argue for Antagonistic Predictions, a structurally different paradigm where models are tasked to act as sparring partners that challenge human pre-conceptions and show reachable futures rather than anticipating the most common pattern. I envision instantiations of Antagonistic Predictions that can counteract historical disadvantages, social stereotyping, and cognitive biases and sketch potential implementations in predictive ML and generative AI settings.

articles_hidden.title: A Geographic Accessibility Database for Health Care Services to Support Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias Exposome Research
articles_hidden.authors: Amber DeJohn; Kyusik Kim; Weining Kan
articles_hidden.abstract: These datasets characterize geographic access to health care providers that are associated with modifiable risk factors for Alzheimer’s Disease and Alzheimer’s Disease-related Dementias (AD/ADRD) for the United States. We offer three measures of geographic access, including the drive time to the closest provider (i.e., nearest facility), how many providers are within a 30, 60, 90, and 120-minute drive (i.e., cumulative opportunity), and the Minimum Attainment Cost (MAC), a new measure that facilitates urban-rural comparisons at a national scale. As an intermediary data product, we provide the origin-destination matrices that are used to generate geographic access measures. We calculate geographic access scores for thirteen types of healthcare facilities at the census block group scale and provide population-weighted aggregate measures at the census tract. Researchers can use these data in tandem with demographic information and other place-based measures to characterize the reachable health care landscape in order to understand how access to care may influence modifiable risk factors for AD/ADRD.

articles_hidden.title: Sustaining Imbalance: International Financial Foundations of Growth Models
articles_hidden.authors: Benjamin Braun; Lucio Baccaro; Joshua Cova
articles_hidden.abstract: Current account imbalances, which have surged again in recent years, are key drivers of global economic instability and conflict. Political economy explanations tend to focus on wage restraint and currency undervaluation. However, in a world of unrestricted cross-border capital mobility, the binding constraint for sustaining imbalances over time is financial flows. To address this gap, we develop a theoretical framework linking current account imbalances, growth models, and domestic financialization. We hypothesize that deep and liquid financial markets enable the reproduction of consumption-led growth by relaxing the current account constraint, while financial underdevelopment favors export-led growth by incentivizing capital exports. We test our theoretical propositions with a series of error correction models and an event history analysis, based on panel data on 55 countries over the period 1970-2022. We find broad support for the theoretical expectations but a dissimilarity in the relationship between growth models and financialization: While financial development is crucial for the long-term maintenance of consumption-led growth in advanced economies especially, results are inconclusive regarding the role of financial underdevelopment as a facilitating factor for export-led growth.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing Funders’ Databases Against Bibliographic Sources: A Study of Interoperability, Metadata Quality, and Coverage Using South Korea’s National R&D Database
articles_hidden.authors: Soohong Eum
articles_hidden.abstract: Comprehensive and reliable funding information is essential for evaluating public research investment, yet funding metadata remain fragmented across heterogeneous data sources maintained by funders and bibliographic platforms. This study examines the interoperability between a national funder database, the National Science and Technology Information Service (NTIS) of South Korea, and two bibliographic sources, Web of Science (WoS) and OpenAlex, in order to assess the quality and coverage of funded publication data. Using a multi-step metadata matching procedure, more than 99% of NTIS records were successfully linked to corresponding documents in WoS and OpenAlex, demonstrating that bibliographic metadata in NTIS records are generally complete and accurate despite incomplete coverage of persistent identifiers such as DOIs. However, limitations arise from NTIS’s exclusive focus on government-funded outputs, overlooking potential co-funding from international or non-governmental sources; its credit-allocation metadata likewise considers only relative contributions among government projects, potentially overestimating government funding’s share and biasing national statistics. Comparison across data sources reveals substantial overlap but also notable differences in coverage and granularity. These differences reflect the distinct collection mechanisms of funders’ databases and bibliographic sources and give rise to complementarities that can be exploited to obtain a more comprehensive picture of funded research outputs and their associated funding sources. The findings carry broader implications for funding agencies seeking to improve interoperability, metadata standardisation, and the analytical utility of research information systems.

articles_hidden.title: What the Balkan Barometer Can and Cannot Rank: A Measurement Audit of the Western Balkans' Flagship Survey
articles_hidden.authors: Milos Kankaras
articles_hidden.abstract: The Balkan Barometer, annual since 2015 with roughly 1,000 face-to-face interviews in each of six Western Balkan economies, is cited across the region as what its citizens think. We evaluate it as a measuring instrument from the Regional Cooperation Council's own released microdata for 2023 to 2025, within a total survey error frame. The published percentages reproduce from the microdata (440 of 444 cells within one point). Of the fifteen pairwise economy differences on each of thirty 2025 headline items, 71 percent are resolvable at a design effect of 2.0, but only 40 percent of adjacent-rank pairs are: six points is the least difference at which two economies of 1,000 can be told apart. The WB6 figure is an unweighted mean of six economies whose populations differ tenfold; under population weights it moves by 6 to 12 points on the most-quoted items, including EU membership (64 versus 58 percent in 2025). Of twenty-three headline series present in all three editions, four are comparable throughout; between 2024 and 2025 the changed series moved by 14 points on average against 6 for the stable ones. The 2025 institutional battery is scalar invariant once two cells are freed, police in Kosovo* and courts in North Macedonia; with them freed, Kosovo*'s raw-score lead disappears and the top three economies cannot be separated. The two published editions score 16 of 32 on a documentation checklist built from what the ESS, the Eurobarometer and the AAPOR Transparency Initiative publish routinely; precision, comparability and limitations score zero. We report two database errors and a file anomaly for correction, and close with the four things a technical report would need to contain.

articles_hidden.title: JCGE: A Modular Julia Framework for Computable General Equilibrium Modelling
articles_hidden.authors: Riccardo Boero
articles_hidden.abstract:
Computable general equilibrium (CGE) modelling requires a workflow beyond
equilibrium specification and solution: data preparation, calibration, model
construction, diagnostics, experiments, and results handling. JCGE is an
Apache-2.0-licensed Julia framework of focused, independently versioned
packages. It provides data and calibration utilities, reusable CGE blocks, a
shared execution specification, diagnostics, outputs, and reference models.
Application packages compose these components while retaining their own data,
closures, and economic assumptions. The runtime constructs JuMP models for
nonlinear and mixed-complementarity formulations without prescribing a solver.
A Model Context Protocol interface supports framework discovery and owner-registered workflows. This paper presents the architecture, quality controls, and reuse potential for
independently developed CGE software.

articles_hidden.title: Neither settling nor conforming: expectations and reactions to low quality jobs of migrant-origin workers in the Netherlands
articles_hidden.authors: Leandro Ivan Canzio; Valentina Di Stasio
articles_hidden.abstract: Migrant-origin workers in Western European countries are more likely to hold low-quality jobs compared to native-origin workers. According to adaptation-level and relative deprivation theories and theories of immigrant socioeconomic integration, this difference may result from migrant-origin workers having lower job quality expectations and weaker reactions to low-quality jobs, due to their awareness of structural labour market disadvantages and lower employability. However, these assumptions have rarely been tested empirically. We provide a direct test using longitudinal, high-quality survey data from the Netherlands (2008-2024) and comparing native-origin workers and first- and second-generation migrants (N = 3744-9671, across model specifications). We hypothesize that migrant-origin workers have lower job quality expectations, experience less job dissatisfaction when those expectations are unmet, and are less likely to translate job dissatisfaction into turnover intentions and subsequent job changes. Based on random- and fixed-effects regression models, we find that migrant-origin workers have similar wage and working hours expectations as native-origin workers. They also report similar or even higher levels of job dissatisfaction when their job quality expectations are unmet. When dissatisfied with their jobs, migrant-origin workers are as likely as native-origin workers to express turnover intentions. Despite their intentions being similar, migrant-origin workers are generally less likely to change jobs in the following year. Overall, our findings indicate that migrant-origin workers neither settle for nor conform to low-quality jobs, and that their structural disadvantage may be better explained by demand-side constraints.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating the discrepancies in funding metadata across bibliographic and administrative databases: the case of South Korea’s public research funding
articles_hidden.authors: Soohong Eum
articles_hidden.abstract: Funding metadata underpins the identification of the relationship between research funding and outputs, yet its coverage and accuracy vary across databases. I examine discrepancies in funding metadata for South Korean government-funded research by comparing records from South Korea’s National Science & Technology Information Service (NTIS) with Web of Science and OpenAlex. Linking NTIS-reported publications across these three sources reveals substantial divergence: few project identifiers and publication-project pairs were captured across all three databases. These discrepancies stem from multiple compounding factors, including incomplete database indexing, optional or inconsistent funder acknowledgement policies, and variations in how project identifiers are described and extracted. Accounting for identifier variations and multi-phase project structures recovers additional matches but does not substantially close the overall gap. A logistic regression model further demonstrates that whether funding sources are acknowledged is linked to structural factors, such as stakeholder complexity regarding the co-authors and institutions involved in a publication. This indicates that acknowledgement omissions are driven not merely by technical limitations in metadata collection, but also by institutional constraints surrounding research funding. Furthermore, acknowledgement lag patterns, where the time gap between project execution and publication active years is virtually zero, point to systemic weaknesses in administrative reporting workflows. The paper concludes by recommending policy actions for funding agencies to ensure the interoperability and reliability of NTIS records. These findings underscore the need to evaluate funding metadata discrepancies not merely as a technical indexing challenge, but as an issue deeply embedded within the institutional structures of research systems.

articles_hidden.title: Between Finality and Accuracy: Vote Recount Institutions in European Democracies
articles_hidden.authors: Ivan Jarabinský; Patrik Mikóczi
articles_hidden.abstract: Vote recounts sit at the intersection of vote counting, dispute resolution, and post-electoral procedure, yet comparative knowledge of how democracies actually conduct them remains scarce. Drawing on a structured, focused comparison across ten European democracies that operate single-instance electoral judiciaries, we examine the institutional settings within which recounts take place. We frame the observed variation through what we term the finality-accuracy dilemma, the tension between treating certified results as settled and ensuring that declared results faithfully reflect voter preferences. Five dimensions structure our analysis, namely standing, threshold conditions, decision-making body, scope, and procedural deadlines. We identify five recurring configurations and find that decision-making body type aligns systematically with position on the finality-accuracy spectrum, with judicial bodies clustering on the finality side and parliamentary bodies adopting accuracy-leaning flexibility. No sampled system employs automatic margin-based triggers, and ordered recounts were partial rather than comprehensive in scope.

articles_hidden.title: Can volunteering substitute for paid work? Unemployment, volunteering, and life satisfaction across the life course
articles_hidden.authors: Arjen de Wit; Heng Qu; Rene Bekkers; Bianca Suanet
articles_hidden.abstract: Unemployment is consistently associated with decreased well-being, but other productive roles may partly compensate for the social and psychological resources lost through job loss. Using a mega-analysis on six longitudinal panel studies covering over 500,000 observations across 20 European countries, we examine how age and volunteer status moderate associations between unemployment and life satisfaction. First-difference models show that transitions into unemployment are associated with declines in life satisfaction, with stronger negative effects observed among younger and middle-aged adults than among older adults. Contrary to expectations, volunteering does not consistently buffer the negative association between unemployment and life satisfaction, although supplementary analyses indicate that the compensatory role of volunteering may vary across age groups and national contexts. These findings indicate that volunteering is not a universal substitute for paid work and that the capacity of alternative productive roles to maintain well-being following job loss depends on broader social and institutional conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating a university micro-placement programme in England: A convergent mixed-methods study of student experiences, attainment and progression
articles_hidden.authors: Isobel Kane; Paulo Ricardo Vieira Braga; Katie Tyrrell; Brandon Harris
articles_hidden.abstract:
Work-integrated learning is associated with improved academic and employment outcomes. However, access to traditional placements remains uneven. Micro-placements offer shorter, paid and potentially more accessible work experience, but evidence concerning their longer-term outcomes is limited. This study evaluated an English university programme in which students completed up to 30 hours of paid work within university teams.
A convergent mixed-methods design combined institutional outcome data with 10 semi-structured interviews. Propensity-score matching and doubly robust augmented inverse probability weighting estimated adjusted associations between participation and two outcomes: degree attainment and employment or further-study status 15 months after graduation. Interview transcripts were analysed separately using Template Analysis.
Qualitative findings indicated that micro-placements supported confidence, workplace awareness, transferable skills, professional networking, and career clarity. Students particularly valued the programme’s flexibility, paid nature, and supportive university environment. However, perceived benefits depended on the relevance, challenge, and quality of placements, alongside opportunities for reflection. Quantitative analyses found no statistically significant association between participation and attainment. An unexpected negative association with progression was observed, although this finding was based on a small sample and remained vulnerable to selection bias and unmeasured confounding.
The findings suggest that micro-placements constitute a valuable and flexible developmental intervention, but that participation alone may be insufficient to improve attainment and progression outcomes without high-quality placement design and structured reflective support.

articles_hidden.title: Designing social tipping interventions: a systematic framework for scaling up behavioural change
articles_hidden.authors: Gian Luca Pasin; Giulia Andrighetto; Eugenia Polizzi di Sorrentino; vito trianni
articles_hidden.abstract: Social tipping, the process by which a new behaviour spreads rapidly upon reaching a critical mass, offers a promising pathway for large-scale behavioural change. However, systematically designing interventions to trigger such tipping points remains a key challenge. This paper introduces a two-phase framework to guide researchers and policymakers in developing effective social tipping interventions. The first phase involves assessing the potential for social tipping by evaluating the prevalence of the target behaviour and the underlying preferences and social expectations that sustain it. We propose a  method for eliciting individual thresholds for changing behaviour, distinguishing between conditional subjects (those who require social proof for changing behaviour) and unconditional subjects (those who are independent of others' decisions). The second phase uses the diagnostic information to inform strategic decisions about whom to target and how to intervene to activate the social tipping process. We analyze the trade-offs between targeting different subpopulations (e.g., amenable vs. resistant individuals) and propose a “stepping stone” approach that breaks down change into manageable steps, which can be particularly effective in populations with polarized individual thresholds. Taken together, our framework offers a roadmap for scaling up large-scale behavioural change through social tipping.

articles_hidden.title: As particularidades da indústria cultural VTuber: um estudo exploratório
articles_hidden.authors: Rafael Dirques David Regis; Julio Cesar Valente Ferreira
articles_hidden.abstract: Em 2016, surgiu no Japão uma nova forma de criar conteúdo de vídeo em tempo real na internet (live stream), chamada de VTubers, ou YouTubers Virtuais. "YouTuber" é a designação em inglês dada a quem cria conteúdo na plataforma, e o “V” refere-se a “virtual”. Esse tipo de criador utiliza artefatos tecnológicos para transmitir conteúdo de forma anônima, por meio de avatares virtuais que refletem seus movimentos e expressões faciais em tempo real. Essa forma de produção tornou-se uma importante indústria cultural dentro e fora do Japão, movimentando mais de USD 100 milhões em doações do público no YouTube entre 2019 e 2021 e alcançando mais de CN¥ 36 bilhões — cerca de USD 4,93 bilhões — em setembro de 2023. Para comparação, todo o mercado audiovisual brasileiro gerou R$ 24,5 bilhões, ou USD 4,91 bilhões, no mesmo período. Tal fenômeno deve-se à capacidade de engajamento dos VTubers, que superam, em termos percentuais, os criadores de conteúdo reais. Além disso, como toda indústria cultural, o setor de VTubers possui particularidades produtivas, lógicas e culturais que constroem seu sucesso, especialmente na formação de comunidades engajadas, que atuam tanto como consumidoras quanto produtoras. Dito isso, este trabalho busca encontrar as diferenças identificáveis entre VTubers e streamers tradicionais, em caráter exploratório, a partir de uma revisão narrativa da literatura. O objetivo é criar uma argumentação estruturada para identificar padrões de diferenciação em áreas como o funcionamento das indústrias, características performáticas, estética e motivadores de engajamento, fornecendo um panorama direto dessa área.

articles_hidden.title: Genital Modifications and Moral Boundary-making: Medical Perspectives on FGM/C versus FGCS in Belgium and the Netherlands
articles_hidden.authors: Hannelore Van Bavel
articles_hidden.abstract: This chapter investigates how medical professionals who perform female genital cosmetic surgery (FGCS) in Belgium and the Netherlands perceive and negotiate the boundary between FGCS and female genital mutilation (FGM). It draws on in-depth qualitative interviews conducted with 11 medical professionals between March 2024 and August 2025, as part of a broader study of genital self-image, motivations for FGCS, and clinical responses. FGM is criminalised in both countries, whereas FGCS is not, even though some procedures classified as FGCS technically fall within the legal and policy definitions of FGM. In 2008, professional societies in the Netherlands attempted to clarify the distinction but ultimately failed to establish concrete criteria, relying instead on what they regarded as a self-evident difference. Healthcare professionals are therefore left to interpret and navigate this boundary in practice, drawing on their own professional knowledge, moral reasoning, and sociocultural understandings. This ambiguity raises important questions about how medical professionals distinguish between FGM and FGCS in their everyday practice. Do they regard the two as fundamentally different, or do they recognise areas of overlap, and on what grounds? What forms of reasoning, knowledge, and professional or cultural frameworks inform their distinctions? To what extent do their views reflect, reproduce, or resist broader social, cultural, and political discourses?

articles_hidden.title: Service Colonisation of the Public Health Model of Bereavement Support: A Critical Review and a Refined Model
articles_hidden.authors: Yong Hao Ng; Bruce Rumbold; Torsten Schwalbach; Samar Aoun
articles_hidden.abstract: The public health model of bereavement support, introduced in 2012, proposed a tiered framework that emphasised community networks’ contributions, informal resources, and shared responsibility across sectors in addition to professional clinical intervention. This study systematically examines how the model has been taken up in the research literature through a combined deductive content analysis and Foucauldian-informed discourse analysis of 252 peer-reviewed articles that cite the model’s foundational papers. The deductive analysis reveals that individually oriented and clinically focused components, particularly triage, epidemiology, and risk factors, dominate the corpus, while community resources and resource allocation remain peripheral. The discourse analysis identifies three interconnected discursive formations: an over-psychologisation that evaluates bereavement as psychiatric risk; an over-professionalisation that positions health professionals as central authorities and renders communities subordinate; and a governmental logic that treats risks, needs, and support as fixed, individually centred categories. Together, these formations constitute what we term service colonisation, in which the institutional norms of the health sciences reshape a broad social framework into a tool for organising clinical resource distribution. This narrowing has material consequences for which services are funded, which populations are recognised as needing support, and whose knowledge is privileged in the design of responses. We propose a refined model that reframes need beyond clinical risk, repositions communities as constitutive agents rather than passive resources, introduces dynamism into the tiered structures, and foregrounds social and structural determinants of bereavement. These findings have implications for how bereavement support is conceptualised, researched, and organised across health and social care systems.

articles_hidden.title: Drivers of household electricity demand in highly electrified markets
articles_hidden.authors: Reza Serati; Anna Kristina Zinn; Siamak Layeghy; Bettina Grün; Marius Portmann; Sara Dolnicar
articles_hidden.abstract: As the world transitions to renewable energies, the structure of national electricity markets will change. Queensland (Australia) is a pioneer market; it is one of the most highly electrified markets internationally. This study analyses drivers of household grid electricity imports using operational smart-meter data from 1,119,389 households and two linked surveys. Solar and battery ownership, dwelling type, household size, pool and electric-vehicle ownership, and climate zone are key drivers. Having a solar system, living in a unit and in smaller households is associated with lower electricity imports. Larger households with a pool and electric vehicles import more electricity. We discuss these findings in the context of previous studies of drivers of household electricity use conducted in more traditional power markets. By distinguishing grid imports from total household consumption, we show how distributed generation and storage reshape network demand and provide new evidence for forecasting and planning in highly electrified markets.

articles_hidden.title: Benefit conditionality, sanction rules and the self-rated health of the unemployed: a longitudinal analysis of European countries
articles_hidden.authors: Christoph Henking; Aaron Reeves
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
The health effects of unemployment vary across European countries. This study examines whether cross-country differences in behavioural conditionality - such as job-search requirements, availability requirements and statutory strictness of sanctions rules - may shape these health effects, and which aspects of conditionality matter most.
Methods
We combined panel data from the European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions (EU-SILC, 2014–2019) with OECD indicators on activation policy strictness in 30 countries. Using first-difference regression models, we estimated the effect of becoming unemployed on changes in self-rated health (five-point scale) and tested whether this effect was moderated by the strictness of each policy dimension. We controlled for individual-level and macroeconomic variables.
Results
Becoming unemployed was linked to a small but significant decline in self-rated health (−0.05, 95% CI[−0.06, −0.04]). This decline was steeper in countries with stricter statutory sanction rules (interaction = −0.04 [−0.08, −0.004]), ranging from −0.053 [−0.098, −0.017] in low-sanction countries to −0.105 [−0.135, −0.078] in high-sanction countries. Job-search and availability requirements showed no significant moderation.
Interpretation
Stricter statutory sanction rules are associated with worse self-rated health among job seekers. Reducing reliance on sanctions and ensuring supportive activation systems could help protect health during unemployment.

articles_hidden.title: Insights from Facilitator Reflections and Participant Feedback: A Cross-Institutional Research Integrity Training Model
articles_hidden.authors: Kate Dunne; Tara Doherty; Sinéad Hanrahan; Ruth Moran; Lorna Walsh; Caragh Tisdall; Ciara McManus; Seán Lacey
articles_hidden.abstract: The Cross-Institutional Research Integrity Training (CIRIT) consortium was established in 2021 by representatives of Irish Research Performing Organisations (RPOs) to collaboratively develop and deliver research integrity (RI) and open science training across the Irish research sector. Underpinning the CIRIT model is a virtue-based approach to RI in which participants work in small groups to engage in dialogue and reflect on moral conflicts and authentic research dilemmas using problem-based learning (PBL) and social constructivist pedagogy. This exploratory mixed-methods case study examined the effectiveness of the CIRIT model and explored its potential as a collaborative cross-institutional approach to RI training. CIRIT facilitators acted as insider researchers, conducting two post-seminar dialogical reflections over a twelve-month period. Seminar participants completed an anonymous post-seminar feedback questionnaire following five CIRIT workshops. A Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats (SWOT) framework informed the analysis of the dialogical reflections, while questionnaire findings were used to contextualise and complement the facilitators' reflections. Findings indicate that the CIRIT model successfully fostered participant engagement, dialogue, and reflective discussion while supporting the development of a collaborative RI community of practice. The findings suggest that collaborative cross-institutional, virtue-based approaches offer a promising model for strengthening RI training and provide a transferable framework that could be adapted within other national research systems, while highlighting the importance of adequate resourcing and institutional recognition.

articles_hidden.title: Rethinking Revictimization
articles_hidden.authors: Joyce Mok
articles_hidden.abstract: Survivors of childhood abuse have a heightened risk of experiencing adulthood interpersonal violence. Existing theories explain revictimization through the victim’s deficits and past experiences of violence. These theories fail to explain the causes of revictimization, can lead to ineffective interventions, and can harm victims. This article presents a secondary analysis of the qualitative literature inspired by Eve Tuck’s formulation of desire-based research, which originally aimed to address similar narratives in the fields of education research and Indigenous studies. This analysis shows the benefits of a theoretical approach that situates the individual’s motivations within an interpersonal, social, and cultural context.

articles_hidden.title: Соотношение финансового и реального секторов как драйверов развития экономики: систематизация теоретических моделей в рамках 9-слойной схемы системы разделения труда // The Relationship between the Financial and Real Sectors as Drivers of Economic Development: Systematization of Theoretical Models within a Nine-Layer Scheme of the Division of Labor
articles_hidden.authors: Maksim Tsepkov
articles_hidden.abstract:
This meta-research is devoted to the systematization and conceptual comparison of key economic concepts that consider either the real sector and technological innovation, the financial sector, or state institutions as the fundamental drivers of economic development. Comparing traditional models is complicated by the fact that most authors focus on individual factors, ignoring complex interrelated relationships.

To overcome this limitation, nine-layer scheme of the division of labor of Petr Shchedrovitsky is used as an integrative analytical framework, encompassing levels from natural resources and production technologies to knowledge accumulation institutions and monetary systems. The study spatially visualizes the theoretical perspectives of Karl Marx, R. Hilferding, V. Lenin, J. Keynes, H. Minsky, J. Schumpeter, and C. Perez, as well as those of Latin American structuralism, Japanese "knowledge capitalism," and the Chinese school of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Positioning these concepts on a single map allows us to demonstrate their mutual complementarity at different phases of technological and financial cycles and lay the foundations for the synthesis of a comprehensive socioeconomic theory.

The study also identified four main phases of technological and economic cycles, during each of which the role of the financial sector shifts from stimulating to destructive. It is shown that state and national-institutional mechanisms (the Chinese model, the Japanese J-firm) are capable of blocking the speculative separation of the ninth layer from the real sector.

articles_hidden.title: Representation Without Power: Far Right Electoral Success and Violence in Weimar Germany
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Haass; Alexander De Juan; Daniel Bischof; Henry Thomson
articles_hidden.abstract: Far right parties often win elections without gaining access to power. Do such outcomes pacify extremist movements, or can they fuel violence? We study this question in Weimar Germany after the July 1932 Reichstag election, when the Nazi Party became the largest parliamentary force but remained outside government. We digitize Nazi candidate lists and Prussian police records on street violence, linking riots to candidates' home towns. Using a regression discontinuity design around district list cutoffs, we compare towns whose Nazi candidates narrowly entered parliament with towns whose candidates narrowly missed. Post-election Nazi-communist violence was substantially higher in towns represented by elected Nazi MPs, while no discontinuity appears before the election. Mechanism evidence from perpetrator coding, stormtrooper mood reports, and membership records suggests that representation without power redirected frustration toward the movement's violent wing. The findings show that electoral representation can intensify anti-democratic violence when far right parties win mandates but remain excluded from power.

articles_hidden.title: Что такое жертва? Концептуализация виктимизации в опросах
articles_hidden.authors: Ruslan Kuchakov; Dmitriy Serebrennikov
articles_hidden.abstract: В статье рассматриваются основные подходы к концептуализации и операционализации понятия жертвы в виктимизационных опросах. На основе обзора более чем полувековой исследовательской традиции выделяются нормативный и конструктивистский подходы к определению жертвы и анализируются их следствия для дизайна опросных инструментов. Во второй части работы реконструируются три традиции операционализации виктимизации на материале пяти опросов: NCVS, CSEW, SES, ICVS и Всероссийского опроса жертв преступлений (RCVS). Авторы предлагают рассматривать эти исследования через матрицу двух измерений: фиксация факта (или стилизованного факта) виктимизации и фиксация самооценки респондента в качестве жертвы. Показано, что выбор стратегии измерения предполагает поиск баланса между юридической строгостью, обеспечивающей сопоставимость с официальной статистикой, и конструктной валидностью — способностью улавливать реальный опыт виктимизации, в том числе не распознанный самим респондентом. Другой компромисс — уже ресурсный — образует своего рода невозможную триаду: при ограниченном бюджете и времени интервью нельзя одновременно максимизировать содержательную широту опросника, лонгитюдную глубину и статистическую точность (надёжность) оценок. При этом сама лонгитюдная глубина достигается по-разному — от повторных кросс-секционных срезов, где каждая волна опрашивает новую выборку из той же совокупности, до панельных дизайнов, отслеживающих одних и тех же респондентов. Именно последние — панели с наблюдением за одними и теми же людьми — из-за бюджетных ограничений по сей день остаются редкостью.

articles_hidden.title: The China Mirror  Learning through Difference in the Digital Age
articles_hidden.authors: Stéphane Grumbach
articles_hidden.abstract: Under conditions of rapidly increasing societal complexity, understanding other civilizations might become an epistemological necessity for fostering adaptive capacities. Drawing on Weber's Verstehen, Jullien's method of the écart, Luhmann's theory of observation, and Koselleck's conceptual history, we propose a method of differential displacement to compare not simply different situations, but their dynamics, with the aim of exposing implicit assumptions. As a case study, following Jullien, we examine what the categories through which China approaches the digital transformation can reveal to Europeans about its purposes and governance. The goal is neither to endorse nor to criticize China, but to move beyond the simplistic duality of democracy and authoritarianism and examine what the difference reveals about Europe's own categories. We further argue that persistent misunderstanding of others can progressively feed a misunderstanding of one's own transformation. Under conditions of complexity surge, comparison can become a mechanism of collective intelligence and adaptive learning.

articles_hidden.title: An Overview of Public Administration Research: Insights From Publications in Leading Journals (2000–2024)
articles_hidden.authors: Vener Garayev
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines paradigmatic changes, thematic developments and authorship patterns in public administration research by analyzing 4,317 articles published in Public Administration Review, Public Management Review, and Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory between 2000 and 2024. Using natural language processing (NLP) techniques through Python software to analyze content of titles, abstracts, and metadata, the article identifies key thematic clusters and paradigmatic shifts across the period, shaped by global events, contextual challenges, and technological advancements. The findings reveal a transition from bureaucratic efficiency to participatory governance, from reform to resilience, and from administrative theory to data-driven governance. Additionally, analysis of authorship patterns reveals increasing collaboration and concentration of scholarly output among top prolific contributors. This study contributes to a growing body of literature on bibliometric and content analytical studies in public administration, offering a comprehensive, data-driven perspective on the field’s intellectual evolution over the past quarter-century.

articles_hidden.title: The chilean health model in the context of latin america. 40 years of economic crises, spending policies and reforms
articles_hidden.authors: Camilo Cid Pedraza; Mauricio Matus-Lopez
articles_hidden.abstract: This chapter analyzes the relationship between economic crises and health reforms in Latin America, with an in-depth focus on the Chilean case, from the origins of its health model to the present day, including a reflection on its possible future developments. The Chilean health model, as it is known today, was designed amid the international crises of 1975 and 1982 and the political crisis of the dictatorship, and it was consolidated during the economic growth of the 1990s. Its most significant reform, developed following the Asian crisis of 1997, resulted in the AUGE Plan, adopted in 2005, which increased access to a defined set of health conditions without changing the model's underlying structure. The 2008 global financial crisis, and later the 2019 social crisis, opened a new stage of debate over structural change, in which the segmentation between the public insurer (FONASA) and the private insurers (ISAPRES) has come to be seen as the central obstacle to an equitable and solidarity-based health system. The regional analysis shows that this relationship between crises and reforms is not unique to Chile, but follows a broader Latin American pattern, moving from market-oriented reforms in the 1980s and 1990s toward a growing consensus, strengthened by the COVID-19 pandemic, in favor of universal, solidarity-based public health systems.

articles_hidden.title: Are geographical and socioeconomic contexts exchangeable? On simple means versus random effects in the study of health inequalities
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Merlo; Kani Khalaf
articles_hidden.abstract: Multilevel random-effects (RE) models are standard in social and geographical epidemiology. They rest on the assumption of exchangeability, which means that, before seeing the data, we have no reason to distinguish one group from another: group means become draws from one common distribution. RE models were developed for repeated measurements within individuals where a shared physiology underwrites the assumption, and partial pooling improves prediction. A silent transfer later applied the same machinery to schools, hospitals, neighbourhoods and, recently, to intersectional strata. There exchangeability fails twice: individuals are not repeated measurements of their group, and groups are social positions produced by directional forces such as racism, not draws from a common distribution. We review strict, conditional and tolerant readings of exchangeability and show that they agree: social and intersectional categories are not exchangeable, as this would paradoxically require the absence of the unjustified inequalities which are the very object of study. In many intersectional analyses, shrinkage erases the small and deviating strata, where inequality lives. Modelling injustice as dispersion around a mean domesticates rather than denounces it. For describing realised health inequalities we recommend Simple-Means MAIHDA (S-MAIHDA). Here, each stratum is estimated from its own individuals, and uncertainty is reported openly rather than smoothed. RE models keep their legitimate uses, such as prediction, cluster-randomised trials and the propensity models of causal S-MAIHDA. Exchangeability is not a property of the software. It is a claim about the world, to be justified in every application.

articles_hidden.title: One meal, not the next: a two-day RCT testing effects of increased plant-based availability on direct and later food choice
articles_hidden.authors: Lotte Patricia de Lint; Wilhelmina Elisabeth Adriana Metje van Rookhuijzen; Rachelle de Vries; Emely de Vet
articles_hidden.abstract: Replacing animal-sourced foods with plant-based alternatives benefits the environment, animal welfare, and public health. Nudges have been found to promote plant-based selection in the moment, but whether they influence later, non-targeted behaviors remains underexplored. Effects on non-targeted behavior could make interventions more effective if they promote consistency in later plant-based choice, or less effective if they trigger compensatory animal-based choice. In a two-day randomized controlled trial (n = 200), we evaluated a Nudge plus intervention delivered on day 1. The intervention combined an increased availability of plant-based to meat sandwich varieties (3:1 vs. 1:3) with a post-choice identity cue informing plant-based choosers that their choice signaled they care about the environment. We assessed intervention effects on targeted behavior (day-1 plant-based lunch choice) and non-targeted behavior (day-2 plant-based lunch choice and 24-hour animal product consumption). Furthermore, we tested whether such effects were mediated by environmental self-identity or moderated by plant-based eating motivation. The increased availability tripled targeted plant-based choice, from 22% in the Reference condition to 66% in the Intervention condition. We detected no main effects of the intervention on either non-targeted outcome, with equivalence tests indicating a negligible effect on 24-hour animal product consumption. There was no evidence of mediation via environmental self-identity or moderation by plant-based eating motivation. Increasing plant-based availability produced a large immediate positive effect on plant-based choice, while the Nudge plus produced no detectable compensatory shifts in non-targeted behavior. These findings support increasing the relative availability of appealing plant-based over meat-based options in food service settings.

articles_hidden.title: Peace or Push? Understanding Global Patterns of Refugee Return
articles_hidden.authors: Mae MacDonald
articles_hidden.abstract: Return is the main way refugee crises end, yet there have been few cross-national studies of when it actually occurs. A central expectation of the refugee regime is that refugees remain abroad while home is unsafe and return as security improves. Yet using a novel global dataset, I show that most returns occur during ongoing conflict, while many refugees remain abroad long after wars end. To explain these patterns, I argue that asylum countries and international organizations play major and underrecognized roles in shaping return, largely overlooked by existing micro-level research focused on refugees’ concerns about security at home. Return is substantially higher when refugees face exclusion policies or conflict in asylum countries, and when donor-funded UNHCR assistance lowers the costs of return. I introduce the Global Refugee Return Dataset, covering 293 origin--asylum dyads from 1980 to 2023, which documents returns systematically undercounted by UNHCR and provides new global data on de facto refugee conditions and UNHCR financing.

articles_hidden.title: Dangers  of  non-objective constructions and  interpretations of history: Important assertions and  takeaways from an Indian context
articles_hidden.authors: Sujay Rao Mandavilli
articles_hidden.abstract:
This short and very brief paper in a way extends our previous papers and publications on historiography, 
though it is in many ways quite important to our core mission. Its importance cannot also not be 
discounted based on our general observation that non-objective and non-purposeful constructs of 
history are widely prevalent across the intellectual spectrum, and both from the left and the right, and 
various errors of omission and commission to this effect and deeply and foundationally entrenched. 
Therefore, it goes without saying that course-corrections are in order, and that the dangers of non
objective and highly biased and prejudiced constructs of history, especially those driven and propelled 
by ideology must be driven home to the broader and larger public. These assume added importance and 
significance in the Indian context for several reasons. Firstly, it precludes a scientific temper being 
inculcated among the laity, as they cannot trust mainstream scholarship any longer. Scientific constructs 
of history are also so important to relegate religion to the background eventually, and keep it in its 
place. Such constructs also lead to a culture of non-objectivity becoming deeply entrenched and it 
invariably begets counter-reactions from other ideologically driven groups. In addition, it is bound to 
severely compromise interdisciplinary approaches and integration across multiple periods and 
geographies all of which are so essential to the healthy growth of scholarship. In situations and 
circumstances where there are ideologically-driven ding dong battles as is presently the case, we may 
even need to adopt an outside in approach and educate the general public about non-objective and 
non-scientific constructs of history first. We are also at a loss to understand why a culture of service of 
historians to science, society, and the education system is not well-entrenched, and immediate course
corrections are in order to promote objectivity in mindset at all costs, and under all circumstances.
